subjects.title: Programming and Data Structures
subjects.description: C programming, recursion and core data structures

questions.prompt: In a zero-based array of n elements stored contiguously, what is the worst-case number of elements shifted to insert a new item at index 0 when capacity is available?
answer: n
questions.explanation: Every existing element must move one position right to open index zero, so n elements are shifted in the worst case.

questions.prompt: Why does direct access to A[i] in a contiguous array take constant time under the usual RAM model?
options: Its address is computed from the base address and i times the element size
The array is searched sequentially until index i
The element is copied to the beginning first
The array stores a linked pointer for each index
answer: Its address is computed from the base address and i times the element size
questions.explanation: The address calculation is base+i*element_size and takes constant arithmetic operations, independent of the array length.

questions.prompt: A row-major matrix has 12 columns and elements of 4 bytes. What is the byte offset of element A[7][5] from A[0][0], using zero-based indices?
questions.explanation: The linear index is 7*12+5=89. Multiplying by four bytes per element gives an offset of 356 bytes.

questions.prompt: For an R by C row-major matrix with zero-based indices, which formula gives the linear element index of A[i][j]?
answer: i*C+j
questions.explanation: Each preceding row contributes C elements, then j elements in the current row, giving i*C+j.

questions.prompt: A C matrix A has row-major layout. Which loop order accesses a[i][j] with good spatial locality in the inner loop?
answer: i outer and j inner
questions.explanation: In row-major storage, consecutive columns within a row are adjacent in memory. Keeping j in the inner loop walks contiguous elements and uses cache lines effectively.

questions.prompt: A row-major three-dimensional array B[2][3][4] is flattened to one-based element positions. What is the one-based position of B[1][2][3] using zero-based subscripts?
questions.explanation: The zero-based linear index is ((1*3)+2)*4+3=23. Converting to a one-based position gives 24.

questions.prompt: How many bytes are required for a row-major 4 by 7 integer matrix when each integer occupies 4 bytes and no extra padding is stored between elements?
questions.explanation: The matrix contains 4*7=28 integer elements. At four bytes each, the storage is 28*4=112 bytes.

questions.prompt: An array of n elements must be left-rotated by k positions in place using the reversal method. Which sequence performs the rotation with O(1) extra space?
options: Reverse [0,k-1], reverse [k,n-1], then reverse the whole array
Sort the array, then reverse it
Shift every element left k times using a temporary array of size n
answer: Reverse [0,k-1], reverse [k,n-1], then reverse the whole array
questions.explanation: Reversing each partition and then the full array restores the order within both blocks while moving the first k items to the end. It uses constant auxiliary storage and linear time.

questions.prompt: For a sorted array of n elements, what is the worst-case number of comparisons for binary search?
answer: Theta(log n)
questions.explanation: Each comparison discards approximately half the remaining interval, so the number of levels grows logarithmically.

questions.prompt: Which statements about searching an unsorted array of n values are correct?
options: An absent key may require examining all n entries
A linear scan has worst-case time Theta(n)
Binary search is correct without any ordering or preprocessing
A scan has worst-case time O(log n)
answer: An absent key may require examining all n entries
A linear scan has worst-case time Theta(n)
questions.explanation: When the key is absent, a scan cannot stop early and must inspect every item. Without order or preprocessing, binary search cannot safely discard a half.

questions.prompt: An array-based list with spare capacity inserts an element at index k. Which expression best describes the number of elements shifted in the worst case?
answer: n-k
questions.explanation: Elements at indices k through n-1 shift right, which is n-k items. Inserting at the end requires no shifts.

questions.prompt: Which statements about deleting an item from a packed array while preserving order are correct?
options: Deleting index k shifts n-k-1 later entries left
Deleting the last entry requires no suffix shift
Deleting any index always takes O(1) time
Compaction can preserve the relative order of remaining entries
answer: Deleting index k shifts n-k-1 later entries left
Deleting the last entry requires no suffix shift
Compaction can preserve the relative order of remaining entries
questions.explanation: All items after k move left to fill the gap, except when k is last. This compaction preserves the order but can take linear time.

questions.prompt: A dynamic array doubles capacity whenever it is full. Which statements about appending are correct?
options: An individual resizing append can take Theta(n) time
Append has amortized O(1) time over a sequence of operations
The total number of copied elements over m appends is O(m)
Every append has worst-case O(1) time
answer: An individual resizing append can take Theta(n) time
Append has amortized O(1) time over a sequence of operations
The total number of copied elements over m appends is O(m)
questions.explanation: A resize copies the current array, causing a linear worst-case operation. Geometric growth makes the total copies linear over many appends, yielding constant amortized cost.

questions.prompt: An initially empty dynamic array doubles capacity from 1 whenever full. After 9 appends, what is its capacity?
questions.explanation: The capacities after growth are 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16. The ninth item requires growth from 8 to 16.

questions.prompt: Which statements about contiguous arrays are correct?
options: They support constant-time indexed access under the RAM model
Inserting at the front can require shifting all existing elements
Every middle insertion is constant time
Their elements are individually allocated as linked nodes
answer: They support constant-time indexed access under the RAM model
Inserting at the front can require shifting all existing elements
questions.explanation: Indexing is calculated arithmetically from the base. Opening space near the front shifts later entries, while array elements are contiguous rather than separate linked nodes.

questions.prompt: A prefix-sum array P is defined by P[0]=0 and P[i+1]=P[i]+A[i]. How many array accesses are needed to answer a range-sum query A[l..r] after preprocessing?
options: Two prefix accesses and one subtraction
One access per array element in A
Theta(log n) accesses using binary search
answer: Two prefix accesses and one subtraction
questions.explanation: The range sum is P[r+1]-P[l], so two prefix values and one subtraction answer each query in constant time.

questions.prompt: For A=[3,-2,5,1,-4], define P[0]=0 and P[i+1]=P[i]+A[i]. What is the sum of A[1..3]?
An array A of length n is rotated left by k positions, where 0<=k<n. Which original index becomes the first element?
answer: k
questions.explanation: A left rotation by k moves the original element at index k to index zero.

questions.prompt: An in-place reversal algorithm swaps symmetric elements until the indices meet. How many swaps are required for an array of length n?
answer: floor(n/2)
questions.explanation: Each swap handles two elements, so exactly floor(n/2) symmetric pairs are exchanged.

questions.prompt: A loop executes for i=0; i<n; i+=3. How many iterations occur for positive n?
answer: ceil(n/3)
questions.explanation: The visited indices are 0,3,6,... strictly below n. Their count is the ceiling of n divided by 3.

questions.prompt: A nested loop runs for i=1..20 and j=1..i, inclusive. How many total inner iterations occur?
questions.explanation: The total is 1+2+...+20=20*21/2=210 iterations.

questions.prompt: A loop uses i=1; while (i<n) i*=2. What is its time complexity as a function of n?
answer: Theta(log n)
questions.explanation: The loop variable doubles each iteration, so it reaches n after logarithmically many iterations.

questions.prompt: Which operations on a fixed-size contiguous array can require worst-case Theta(n) work?
options: Searching an unsorted array for an absent key
Inserting at index zero while shifting elements
Deleting at index zero while preserving order
Reading an element at a known index
answer: Searching an unsorted array for an absent key
Inserting at index zero while shifting elements
Deleting at index zero while preserving order
questions.explanation: An absent-key scan inspects all values. Front insertion and ordered deletion shift a linear number of entries; known-index access is constant time.

questions.prompt: A matrix A has 4 rows and 7 columns in row-major storage. How many elements precede A[3][2]?
questions.explanation: There are 3 complete rows before row 3, contributing 21 elements, plus two elements before column 2 in that row: 23.

questions.prompt: For a nonnegative array, a sliding window is used to find the longest subarray whose sum is at most K. Why can the left endpoint move only forward when the current sum exceeds K?
options: Removing elements from the left cannot increase the sum
The array is sorted by value
The sum is always unchanged by removal
The right endpoint must move backward
answer: Removing elements from the left cannot increase the sum
questions.explanation: With nonnegative entries, removing the leftmost element cannot increase the window sum. Therefore advancing the left endpoint restores feasibility without revisiting earlier positions.

questions.prompt: A two-pointer method searches for a pair summing to X in a sorted increasing array. If the current sum is too small, which pointer moves?
options: The smaller value is replaced by X
answer: The left pointer moves right
questions.explanation: Moving the left pointer to a larger value is the only direction that can increase the sum while preserving the candidate order.

questions.prompt: Two sorted arrays of lengths m and n are merged into one sorted array by the standard two-pointer procedure. What is the worst-case time?
answer: Theta(m+n)
questions.explanation: Each input element is copied once, so the total work is linear in the combined lengths.

questions.prompt: A sorted array [1,2,2,2,5,5,8] is compacted in place to unique values while preserving order. How many elements remain?
questions.explanation: The distinct values are 1, 2, 5, and 8. Stable compaction retains one occurrence of each, leaving four elements.

questions.prompt: In stable in-place compaction of a sorted array, what invariant does a write index typically maintain?
options: The prefix before it contains exactly the unique values seen so far
It always equals the current read index squared
It marks the smallest unseen value
It stores the number of duplicate pairs in the suffix
answer: The prefix before it contains exactly the unique values seen so far
questions.explanation: After processing a prefix, the write region contains the unique elements from that prefix in original sorted order.

questions.prompt: For an array A of length n, what is the worst-case number of comparisons needed to find its maximum by a single scan?
questions.explanation: The first element initializes the maximum. Each of the remaining n-1 elements is compared once against the current maximum.

questions.prompt: What is the worst-case number of comparisons required to find both minimum and maximum using the simple independent-scan approach?
questions.explanation: One scan performs n-1 comparisons for the maximum and another n-1 for the minimum, totaling 2n-2. Pairwise methods can improve this bound.

questions.prompt: Why can pairwise min-max scanning use fewer comparisons than two independent scans?
options: Each pair is first compared internally, then its smaller and larger values update separate extrema
It sorts the whole array first
It relies on the array being sorted
answer: Each pair is first compared internally, then its smaller and larger values update separate extrema
questions.explanation: For each pair, one comparison identifies a local low and high; only these candidates are compared with the global minimum and maximum.

questions.prompt: Kadane's algorithm for maximum subarray sum maintains a current ending sum. What update is applied at each element x?
answer: max(x, current+x)
questions.explanation: The best subarray ending here either starts at x or extends the prior ending subarray. Taking the maximum handles negative accumulated sums.

questions.prompt: For A=[-3,4,-1,2,-6,5], what is the maximum contiguous subarray sum?
questions.explanation: The subarray [4,-1,2] sums to 5. The final singleton 5 also gives 5, and no other contiguous segment is larger.

questions.prompt: An array of n integers is scanned once while maintaining a running sum and the best sum seen. What is the auxiliary space usage?
answer: Theta(1)
questions.explanation: Only a fixed number of scalar variables are maintained, so extra storage is constant with respect to n.

questions.prompt: An array has a length n and an element is accessed by a known index. Which property is required for the usual O(1) access bound?
options: The elements are stored contiguously with known element size
The array length is a power of two
answer: The elements are stored contiguously with known element size
questions.explanation: Contiguous storage lets the address be calculated from the base and index without traversing preceding elements.

questions.prompt: A circular buffer of capacity C maps a logical index i to a physical array slot. Which common mapping handles wraparound?
answer: i mod C
questions.explanation: Modulo capacity wraps indices back to the beginning of the backing array when they reach its end.

questions.prompt: A circular buffer has capacity 11 and head index 8. After advancing the head by 7 positions, what is its new physical index?
questions.explanation: The wrapped index is (8+7) mod 11=15 mod 11=4.

questions.prompt: A sorted array is rotated at an unknown pivot. Which property can support logarithmic search for a key?
options: At least one of the two halves around the midpoint is sorted
The minimum element is always at index zero
The array must contain no duplicates in every variant
answer: At least one of the two halves around the midpoint is sorted
questions.explanation: A midpoint divides the array so at least one side remains sorted, allowing elimination of a half based on the key range. Duplicates can complicate progress.

questions.prompt: In an array with all distinct elements, how many comparisons are sufficient to find a peak using binary search on the slope between adjacent entries?
answer: O(log n)
questions.explanation: Comparing adjacent values indicates a direction containing a peak. Repeatedly discarding half the range gives logarithmic search.

questions.prompt: A difference array D represents range additions to A. To add x to every A[l..r], what two updates are made when a sentinel slot exists?
options: Add x to every D index in [l,r]
answer: D[l]+=x and D[r+1]-=x
questions.explanation: The prefix sum of D reconstructs A. Starting an addition at l and canceling it after r uses +x at l and -x at r+1.

questions.prompt: A difference array receives +5 on range [2,6] and -3 on range [4,8]. What net addition applies at index 5?
questions.explanation: Index 5 lies in both ranges. Its net change is +5-3=+2.

questions.prompt: For an array A, let P[i] be the sum of elements before index i. Which formula gives the sum on half-open interval [l,r)?
answer: P[r]-P[l]
questions.explanation: The prefix through positions before r minus the prefix before l leaves exactly A[l] through A[r-1].

questions.prompt: For a two-dimensional prefix-sum table P, which combination gives the sum of rectangle rows r1..r2 and columns c1..c2, inclusive?
questions.explanation: Subtract the strips above and left of the rectangle, then add back their overlap once. This inclusion-exclusion formula gives the rectangle sum.

questions.prompt: After O(RC) preprocessing of a two-dimensional prefix-sum table, what is the query time for one axis-aligned rectangle sum?
questions.explanation: Four table values and a constant number of additions/subtractions return the rectangle sum, independent of its area.

questions.prompt: What is the standard time complexity of multiplying two dense n by n matrices using the classical triple loop?
answer: Theta(n^3)
questions.explanation: There are n^2 output cells and each accumulates n products, producing n^3 arithmetic operations.

questions.prompt: For matrix multiplication C[i][j]+=A[i][k]*B[k][j] in row-major storage, which loop order gives contiguous access to B in the innermost loop?
options: i outer, k middle, j inner
i outer, j middle, k inner
j outer, i middle, k inner
k outer, j middle, i inner
answer: i outer, k middle, j inner
questions.explanation: With j innermost, B[k][j] and C[i][j] advance across adjacent columns, improving spatial locality in row-major layouts.

questions.prompt: Which statements about transposing a square matrix in place are correct?
options: Each off-diagonal pair A[i][j], A[j][i] is swapped once
Diagonal entries remain in their original positions
Restricting swaps to i<j avoids processing each pair twice
Every matrix entry must be moved into a temporary array
answer: Each off-diagonal pair A[i][j], A[j][i] is swapped once
Diagonal entries remain in their original positions
Restricting swaps to i<j avoids processing each pair twice
questions.explanation: The transpose exchanges symmetric off-diagonal cells. Diagonal cells are unchanged, and iterating over one triangle swaps each pair exactly once.

questions.prompt: A sorted array contains duplicate keys. What is the worst-case time to find the first occurrence with a modified binary search?
answer: O(log n)
questions.explanation: After finding an equal value the search continues left, halving the remaining interval until the boundary is identified.

questions.prompt: To count occurrences of x in a sorted array with duplicates in O(log n), what should be found?
options: The first index of x and the first index greater than x
One occurrence and then a full scan
The minimum and maximum array values
The insertion position of every distinct key
answer: The first index of x and the first index greater than x
questions.explanation: Two binary searches find the half-open interval of x values. Subtracting the boundary indices gives the count.

questions.prompt: In a sorted array, the first occurrence of 6 is at index 4 and the first element greater than 6 is at index 11. How many occurrences of 6 are present?
questions.explanation: The matching entries occupy indices 4 through 10, so the half-open range length is 11-4=7.

questions.prompt: A fixed-width window of length k slides one position. After its first sum is known, what constant-time update advances it?
options: Subtract the outgoing value and add the incoming value
Recompute all k values and divide by k
Multiply the prior sum by k
answer: Subtract the outgoing value and add the incoming value
questions.explanation: Removing the leaving element and adding the entering element updates the sum in O(1), rather than scanning the entire window.

questions.prompt: For A=[4,-1,2,10,3], what is the largest sum among contiguous subarrays of length exactly 3?
questions.explanation: The three window sums are 5, 11, and 15. The last window [2,10,3] yields 15.

questions.prompt: Why does a sliding-window greedy method for sum-at-most-K constraints generally fail with negative array elements?
options: Removing a negative left element can increase the window sum
Negative values make array indexing invalid
Prefix sums cannot represent negative values
answer: Removing a negative left element can increase the window sum
questions.explanation: With negatives the sum is not monotone under removal: discarding a negative element can raise it, so the usual feasibility argument breaks.

questions.prompt: An equilibrium index i has equal sums strictly to its left and right. Given total sum and a running left sum, what is the time to find one?
answer: O(n)
questions.explanation: At each index, the right sum is total-left-A[i]. One pass updates the left sum and checks equality.

questions.prompt: For A=[2,-1,4,3,-2], what is an equilibrium index using zero-based indexing, if one exists?
questions.explanation: At index 2, the left sum is 2-1=1 and the right sum is 3-2=1.

questions.prompt: A two-dimensional prefix table stores sums over top-left rectangles. How many table entries are needed to answer one arbitrary rectangle-sum query?
answer: Four
questions.explanation: Inclusion-exclusion uses the prefix values at the lower-right, above, left, and overlapping corner positions.

questions.prompt: A sparse n by n matrix is stored as one (row,column,value) triple per nonzero. Ignoring metadata, when is this smaller in scalar slots than dense storage?
answer: When 3z<n^2 for z nonzeros
questions.explanation: Dense storage uses n^2 scalar values; triplet storage uses about 3z scalars. It is smaller under this model when 3z<n^2.

questions.prompt: A loop executes for i=1; i<=64; i*=2. How many body executions occur?
questions.explanation: The values are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, and 64: seven executions.

questions.prompt: Two separate loops each run n iterations with constant work per iteration. What is their combined asymptotic time?
answer: Theta(n)
questions.explanation: Their costs add to n+n=2n, which is Theta(n). Sequential loops are not multiplied as nested loops are.

questions.prompt: A single pass stably compacts retained array items in place, reading each item once and writing each retained item once. What is the running time?
answer: Theta(n)
questions.explanation: There is constant work for each of the n input entries, so the total is linear.

questions.prompt: A permutation on n positions has k disjoint cycles including fixed points. How many swaps suffice to realize it?
answer: n-k
questions.explanation: A cycle of length l requires l-1 swaps. Summing over cycle lengths gives n-k swaps.

questions.prompt: A permutation of 8 positions has nontrivial cycle lengths 3 and 2; the remaining positions are fixed. How many swaps suffice?
questions.explanation: There are five cycles total: lengths 3, 2, 1, 1, 1. The minimum swap count is 8-5=3.

questions.prompt: An array has distinct values from 1 through n except for one missing value. Which calculation recovers the missing value?
options: The array product divided by n
The array length squared minus its sum
answer: n(n+1)/2 minus the array sum
questions.explanation: The expected sum of 1 through n is n(n+1)/2; subtracting the observed sum leaves the missing value.

questions.prompt: The values 1 through 8 appear in an array except one value; the array sum is 33. What is missing?
questions.explanation: The complete sum is 8*9/2=36. The absent value is 36-33=3.

questions.prompt: How much work is needed to sum the main diagonal of a square n by n matrix?
answer: Theta(n)
questions.explanation: The algorithm visits the n diagonal cells exactly once and performs constant work at each.

questions.prompt: In a naive row-major matrix transpose, what is the primary locality issue?
options: One of the read or write traversals may stride through noncontiguous memory
The output contains twice as many values
Every element changes its numeric value
The matrix cannot be traversed by columns
answer: One of the read or write traversals may stride through noncontiguous memory
questions.explanation: A row-major layout places columns far apart by row width. A transpose often reads or writes one side with a stride, reducing spatial locality.

questions.prompt: Which statements about array prefix-sum techniques are correct?
options: A 1-D prefix table answers static range sums in O(1) after O(n) preprocessing
A 2-D prefix table answers rectangle sums using four table values
A prefix table alone supports arbitrary range updates in O(1)
A range query must visit every element in the range
answer: A 1-D prefix table answers static range sums in O(1) after O(n) preprocessing
A 2-D prefix table answers rectangle sums using four table values
questions.explanation: Prefix tables answer static sums by subtracting boundary sums; two-dimensional inclusion-exclusion uses four entries. Updates may require rebuilding or a different data structure.

questions.prompt: A strictly increasing array is rotated at an unknown pivot. Why can binary search discard one half when looking for a key?
options: At least one half is sorted and its value range can be checked
The pivot is always the midpoint
The minimum remains at index zero
answer: At least one half is sorted and its value range can be checked
questions.explanation: With distinct values, one side of the midpoint is sorted. Comparing the key with that side's endpoints reveals whether it can lie there.

questions.prompt: A sorted array search returns the first index whose value is at least x, or n if none exists. What is that position called?
options: The count of values greater than x
answer: The lower-bound insertion position
questions.explanation: The lower bound divides values less than x from those at least x, giving the insertion position that preserves sorted order.

questions.prompt: A merge-based algorithm counts inversions while sorting an array. What is its running time?
answer: Theta(n log n)
questions.explanation: It divides the input recursively and counts cross-inversions during linear merges, yielding logarithmic levels of linear work.

questions.prompt: In a sorted-array pair-sum search, the current endpoint values sum to more than X. Which pointer moves?
answer: The right pointer moves left
questions.explanation: Decreasing the larger endpoint is the move that can lower the sum while retaining every potentially valid pair.

questions.prompt: With randomized pivots, what is the expected time of quickselect for finding the kth smallest item?
answer: Theta(n)
questions.explanation: Expected partition sizes shrink geometrically, so total work is linear, though a poor sequence of pivots can take quadratic time.

questions.prompt: If quickselect repeatedly partitions an n-item array into sizes 0 and n-1, what is its worst-case running time?
answer: Theta(n^2)
questions.explanation: The work sums n+(n-1)+...+1 when each partition removes only one element, producing a quadratic sum.

questions.prompt: For i=0..n-1, an inner loop runs j=i..n-1. How many inner iterations occur in total?
questions.explanation: The counts are n,n-1,...,1. Their sum is n(n+1)/2.

questions.prompt: An outer loop doubles its index each pass and an inner loop scans n elements. What is total time?
answer: Theta(n log n)
questions.explanation: There are logarithmically many outer iterations and each inner scan costs linear time.

questions.prompt: For dense matrices A(m by n) and B(n by p), what is the classical multiplication time?
answer: Theta(mnp)
questions.explanation: There are m*p output cells and each accumulates n products, for m*n*p arithmetic operations.

questions.prompt: Let A have dimensions m by n and B have dimensions n by p. Which statements about their classical matrix product are correct?
options: A*B is defined and has dimensions m by p
The classical algorithm takes Theta(mnp) arithmetic operations
The product is defined only when m=p
answer: A*B is defined and has dimensions m by p
The classical algorithm takes Theta(mnp) arithmetic operations
The result contains m*p entries
questions.explanation: The shared inner dimension n makes the product valid. It has m rows and p columns; each of its m*p entries uses n multiply-add terms.

questions.prompt: What are the dimensions of the transpose of an R by C matrix?
answer: C by R
questions.explanation: Transposition exchanges rows and columns, so R rows and C columns become C rows and R columns.

questions.prompt: In row-major storage, which pair of entries in the same row is adjacent in memory?
answer: A[i][j] and A[i][j+1]
questions.explanation: A row is stored contiguously, so neighboring column positions are consecutive elements in memory.

questions.prompt: In a row-major matrix with C columns and element size s bytes, what is the byte stride between A[i][j] and A[i+1][j]?
answer: C*s
questions.explanation: Moving down one row advances C elements. Multiplying the row width by the element size gives a stride of C*s bytes.

questions.prompt: Why must a product-except-self algorithm handle zeros separately if it uses total-product division?
options: Division by a product containing zero is invalid
answer: Division by a product containing zero is invalid
questions.explanation: If any element is zero, the total product is zero and division cannot recover each position. Counting zeros or using prefix/suffix products avoids this issue.

questions.prompt: An array contains n+1 values drawn from 1..n and has at least one repeated value. Which statements are correct?
options: A duplicate is guaranteed by the pigeonhole principle
A functional graph can be formed by mapping each index to the value stored there
Floyd cycle detection can find a duplicate with O(1) extra space under the stated constraints
A hash set requires O(1) total space for arbitrary n
answer: A duplicate is guaranteed by the pigeonhole principle
A functional graph can be formed by mapping each index to the value stored there
Floyd cycle detection can find a duplicate with O(1) extra space under the stated constraints
questions.explanation: There are more entries than possible values, so a duplicate exists. The value mapping creates a cycle structure; Floyd detects it without a growing auxiliary set.

questions.prompt: An array of n elements is reversed in place by swapping symmetric pairs. Which statements are correct?
options: The number of swaps is floor(n/2)
A temporary array of length n is necessary
answer: The running time is Theta(n)
The auxiliary space is O(1)
The number of swaps is floor(n/2)
questions.explanation: Each symmetric pair is swapped once, producing floor(n/2) swaps and linear time. A temporary scalar is sufficient, so auxiliary space is constant.

questions.prompt: How many nonempty contiguous subarrays does an array of length 12 have?
questions.explanation: There are n(n+1)/2 choices of start and end with start<=end: 12*13/2=78.

questions.prompt: For an array of n elements, how many contiguous subarrays have length exactly k, where 1<=k<=n?
answer: n-k+1
questions.explanation: The starting index ranges from 0 through n-k, giving n-k+1 possible windows.

questions.prompt: An array has length 20. How many contiguous subarrays have length exactly 6?
questions.explanation: The possible starting positions are 0 through 14, so the count is 20-6+1=15.

questions.prompt: How many unordered index pairs (i,j) with i<j exist in an array of n elements?
questions.explanation: Choose two distinct indices without ordering; the count is n choose 2.

questions.prompt: How many unordered pairs of distinct indices are there in an array of length 15?
questions.explanation: An array of length 15 has 15*14/2=105 unordered pairs of distinct indices. Each pair corresponds to one choice of two different positions.

questions.prompt: A sequence is queried frequently by random index and rarely modified in the middle. Which representation is usually suitable?
answer: A contiguous array
questions.explanation: An array provides constant-time indexed access with low per-element overhead, matching frequent random reads and few middle updates.

questions.prompt: An ordered array maintains sorted order. What is the worst-case time to insert a new item while preserving that order?
answer: Theta(n)
questions.explanation: Binary search locates the insertion point quickly, but the suffix may require a linear number of moves.

questions.prompt: A stored prefix-sum array P is explicitly maintained. What is the worst-case time to update P after changing A[k]?
answer: Theta(n)
questions.explanation: Every later prefix includes A[k], so direct maintenance may require updating a linear suffix of P.

questions.prompt: Which formula gives the number of nonempty contiguous subarrays of an n-element array?
questions.explanation: Each subarray is determined by a start and end with start<=end; summing by start yields n+(n-1)+...+1.

questions.prompt: In a row-major matrix, which nested-loop order generally gives sequential accesses for the innermost loop?
answer: Rows outer, columns inner
questions.explanation: A row is contiguous in memory, so iterating columns in the inner loop accesses neighboring cells.

questions.prompt: How many element slots are needed for a dense R by C matrix representation?
answer: R*C
questions.explanation: A dense matrix stores one value for every row-column pair, yielding R times C entries.

questions.prompt: Which statements about binary search on an array are correct?
options: The searched range must be ordered by the comparison relation
Each midpoint comparison can eliminate about half the remaining candidates
Its worst-case comparisons are Theta(log n)
It is correct on every unsorted array without preprocessing
answer: The searched range must be ordered by the comparison relation
Each midpoint comparison can eliminate about half the remaining candidates
Its worst-case comparisons are Theta(log n)
questions.explanation: Sorted order supports discarding a half based on a midpoint comparison. The remaining interval shrinks geometrically, giving logarithmic worst-case comparisons.

questions.prompt: A dynamic-array append triggers a resize and copies n existing elements. What is the time of that individual append?
answer: Theta(n)
questions.explanation: A resizing append can allocate a new block and copy all current entries, which is linear for that operation even though amortized append is constant.

questions.prompt: A stable partition groups elements by a predicate. What property does stable guarantee?
options: Relative order is preserved within each group
The algorithm uses O(1) extra space
answer: Relative order is preserved within each group
questions.explanation: Stability preserves the original order among elements assigned to each group; it does not sort within the groups.

questions.prompt: For a row-major matrix, what is the locality effect of traversing a column top-to-bottom?
options: The access stride is the row width, so locality is worse than row traversal
Every access is to an adjacent element
The traversal is impossible without transposing
The algorithm visits only diagonal entries
answer: The access stride is the row width, so locality is worse than row traversal
questions.explanation: A fixed-column traversal jumps by C elements between rows, unlike consecutive-column accesses within a row.

questions.prompt: Why is appending to a dynamic array with geometric capacity growth amortized O(1)?
options: The total copied elements over many resizes is bounded by a geometric sum
Each append always copies exactly one element
A resize copies only the first element
answer: The total copied elements over many resizes is bounded by a geometric sum
questions.explanation: Doubling makes the total copied elements over m appends O(m), so average append cost is constant.

questions.prompt: A max-heap is represented in a zero-based array. For a node at index i, its parent index is
answer: floor((i-1)/2)
questions.explanation: In a zero-based heap array, the parent of a nonroot node i is floor((i-1)/2).

questions.prompt: In a zero-based binary heap array, what is the right child index of node 6?
questions.explanation: The right child index is 2i+2, so for i=6 it is 14.

questions.prompt: In a max-heap, which relation holds between every parent and its children?
options: Parent key is at least each child key
Parent key is at most each child key
Keys increase from left to right at every level
Every node is greater than every node in the next level
answer: Parent key is at least each child key
questions.explanation: The max-heap property constrains each parent to be no smaller than its children; it does not sort nodes within a level or across subtrees.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the array representation of a binary heap is true?
options: It is a complete binary tree
It is always a full binary tree
Every leaf has the same depth
answer: It is a complete binary tree
questions.explanation: A binary heap is structurally complete, with the final level filled from left to right, enabling compact array storage.

questions.prompt: A binary heap contains 31 elements. What is the index of its last element in a zero-based array?
questions.explanation: With n elements, occupied indices are 0 through n-1; the last index for 31 elements is 30.

questions.prompt: The maximum element in a max-heap is found in
answer: the root
questions.explanation: Every parent is at least its descendants by repeated heap inequalities, so the global maximum is at the root.

questions.prompt: Inserting an element into a binary heap with n elements takes worst-case time
answer: O(log n)
questions.explanation: The new element is placed at the next complete-tree position and may bubble up at most the heap height, which is O(log n).

questions.prompt: A complete binary heap has 63 nodes. What is its height in edges?
questions.explanation: A perfect tree of height 5 has 2^6-1=63 nodes, so the heap height is 5.

questions.prompt: During max-heap insertion, the new key is repeatedly swapped with its parent while
answer: the parent key is smaller
questions.explanation: To restore max-heap order, a newly inserted key moves upward while it exceeds its parent; the process stops when the parent is at least as large or root is reached.

questions.prompt: A max-heap has height 4. What is the maximum number of swaps needed to bubble up one inserted key?
questions.explanation: An insertion starts at a leaf at depth at most four and can swap once per edge on the path to the root.

questions.prompt: Removing the maximum element from a max-heap takes
answer: O(log n)
questions.explanation: After removing the root, the last element is moved to the root and sifted downward at most the heap height, which is logarithmic.

questions.prompt: After deleting the root of a max-heap, which element is moved to the root before heap restoration?
options: The last element in level-order array storage
answer: The last element in level-order array storage
questions.explanation: Removing the final array element preserves completeness. Moving it to the root leaves one position to restore with sift-down.

questions.prompt: A max-heap root has children 14 and 18. During sift-down, which child should it be compared/swapped with first?
questions.explanation: To preserve the max-heap order, sift-down swaps with the larger child, which is 18.

questions.prompt: Which operations on a binary max-heap have O(log n) worst-case time?
options: Increase the key of a known node
answer: Insert a key
Extract the maximum
Increase the key of a known node
questions.explanation: Insertion, extract-max, and increase-key can follow a path of heap height. Finding an arbitrary key has no ordering shortcut and may scan all n elements.

questions.prompt: Building a heap by inserting n keys one at a time has worst-case time
answer: O(n log n)
questions.explanation: Each insertion may take O(log n), so n successive insertions have O(n log n) worst-case total time.

questions.prompt: Bottom-up build-heap on an array of n keys runs in
answer: O(n)
questions.explanation: Most nodes are near leaves and sift down only a few levels. Summing node-height costs across all levels yields linear total time.

questions.prompt: Bottom-up build-heap on an array of 15 elements starts heapifying at what zero-based index?
questions.explanation: The last internal node is floor(n/2)-1. For n=15 this is floor(15/2)-1=6.

questions.prompt: In bottom-up heap construction, which nodes need sift-down processing?
options: Internal nodes, in reverse level order
Nodes from the root downward in preorder
answer: Internal nodes, in reverse level order
questions.explanation: Leaves already satisfy heap order. Processing internal nodes bottom-up ensures child subtrees are heaps before each parent is sifted down.

questions.prompt: Which statements about bottom-up heap construction are true?
options: It can be faster asymptotically than n successive insertions
It starts with leaves as trivial heaps
Its worst-case time is Theta(n log n)
answer: It is O(n) time
It can be faster asymptotically than n successive insertions
It starts with leaves as trivial heaps
questions.explanation: Leaves are already heaps; internal nodes are processed bottom-up. The sum of potential sift-down distances is linear, whereas successive insertion has O(n log n) bound.

questions.prompt: A max-heap stores distinct values. If its root is 100, what can be concluded about the second-largest value?
options: It is one of the root's children
It is the last array element
answer: It is one of the root's children
questions.explanation: Any node other than the root is below one of its children in the heap tree, and the largest nonroot key must be one of the root's immediate children.

questions.prompt: A min-heap supports extract-min in
answer: O(log n)
questions.explanation: The minimum is at the root. Replacing it with the final element and sifting down takes at most the heap height, O(log n).

questions.prompt: In a min-heap, the key at the root is
options: no greater than any other key
no smaller than any other key
answer: no greater than any other key
questions.explanation: The min-heap property ensures every parent is no greater than its children, so the root is a global minimum.

questions.prompt: A complete binary min-heap has 127 elements. What is its height in edges?
questions.explanation: Since 127=2^7-1, it is perfect with levels 0 through 6, so height is 6.

questions.prompt: Which array index range contains leaves of a zero-based heap with n elements?
answer: floor(n/2) through n-1
questions.explanation: An index i is a leaf when its left child 2i+1 is outside the occupied range. This begins at floor(n/2).

questions.prompt: A zero-based heap has 20 elements. What is the last internal-node index?
questions.explanation: The last internal node is floor(n/2)-1=floor(20/2)-1=9.

questions.prompt: Which statements about a binary heap are true?
options: Its array supports O(1) access to the root
A search for an arbitrary key is O(log n) worst case
answer: Its shape is complete
Its array supports O(1) access to the root
questions.explanation: Completeness allows compact array storage and provides the root at index zero. Heap order does not sort the array, and arbitrary-key search may be linear.

questions.prompt: A max-heap array is [50,30,40,10,20,35]. Is it a valid max-heap?
options: Yes, every parent is at least its children
No, the array must be sorted
answer: Yes, every parent is at least its children
questions.explanation: The root 50 exceeds children 30 and 40; node 30 exceeds 10 and 20; node 40 exceeds 35. All parent-child constraints hold.

questions.prompt: A max-heap array is [40,25,35,10,30,20]. Which change is required to make it a valid max-heap?
answer: Swap 25 and 30
questions.explanation: At index 1, parent 25 is smaller than child 30 at index 4, violating heap order. Swapping these values fixes that relation without breaking the others.

questions.prompt: A min-heap array is [3,7,5,12,9,8]. What is the minimum number of parent-child violations?
questions.explanation: The root 3 is below 7 and 5; 7 is below 12 and 9; 5 is below 8. No parent-child relation violates min-heap order.

questions.prompt: In a max-heap, a key at index i is increased. Which repair is generally needed?
options: Swap it with the root unconditionally
answer: Sift it upward
questions.explanation: Increasing a key can make it larger than its parent, so the violation is along the parent path and is repaired by sift-up.

questions.prompt: In a max-heap, a key at a known index is decreased. Which repair is generally needed?
options: Move it to the final index
answer: Sift it downward
questions.explanation: Decreasing a key may make it smaller than one or both children. Sifting down restores parent dominance along a downward path.

questions.prompt: A max-heap has height 5. A key is decreased at the root. What is the maximum number of downward swaps required?
questions.explanation: A root-to-leaf path contains at most five edges, so sift-down performs at most five swaps.

questions.prompt: Which key updates in a max-heap may violate heap order in the upward direction?
options: Increase a key at a known node
Decrease a key at a known node
Replace a key by a larger value
Replace a key by a smaller value
answer: Increase a key at a known node
Replace a key by a larger value
questions.explanation: Increasing a key or replacing it by a larger value may exceed its parent and require sift-up. Decreasing a key can instead violate order with children.

questions.prompt: A binary heap is not a search tree because
options: siblings and subtrees are not ordered by key ranges
it is stored in an array
answer: siblings and subtrees are not ordered by key ranges
questions.explanation: Heap order compares each parent only with its children; it does not require all keys in one subtree to be ordered relative to another subtree.

questions.prompt: The k-th largest element can be found by repeated extract-max from a max-heap in
options: O(n+k log n) including heap construction
answer: O(n+k log n) including heap construction
questions.explanation: Build the heap in O(n), then perform k extractions at O(log n) each, for O(n+k log n).

questions.prompt: A max-heap contains 100 elements. After extracting the maximum 4 times, how many elements remain?
questions.explanation: Each extraction removes exactly one element, leaving 100-4=96.

questions.prompt: A priority queue implemented by a binary heap provides which typical operation bounds?
options: Insert and extract-priority in O(log n), peek in O(1)
Search and delete arbitrary key in O(log n) without extra indexing
Build-heap in O(n log n) only
answer: Insert and extract-priority in O(log n), peek in O(1)
questions.explanation: Heap insertion and extraction traverse a height path; the root provides constant-time peek. Arbitrary search is not logarithmic without additional indexing.

questions.prompt: In heapsort using a max-heap, after swapping the root with the last unsorted element, the heap size is
answer: reduced by one
questions.explanation: The maximum is placed at the end of the array, which is excluded from the active heap. The remaining heap shrinks by one and is restored with sift-down.

questions.prompt: Which properties hold for heapsort on an array using an in-place binary heap?
options: Worst-case time is O(n log n)
It is stable in its standard form
answer: Worst-case time is O(n log n)
Auxiliary space can be O(1)
It sorts in-place
questions.explanation: Heapsort runs in O(n log n) worst-case time, sorts in-place with O(1) auxiliary space, and is not stable in its standard form.

questions.prompt: Heapsort with a max-heap produces the sorted array in
answer: nondecreasing order
questions.explanation: Repeatedly moving the maximum to the final unsorted position places values from largest to smallest at the array's right end, yielding ascending order overall.

questions.prompt: A d-ary heap is a complete tree in which each internal node can have at most
answer: d children
questions.explanation: The branching factor d specifies the maximum number of children per node. A binary heap is the special case d=2.

questions.prompt: In a d-ary heap, increasing d generally
options: reduces height but increases the number of children inspected during sift-down
answer: reduces height but increases the number of children inspected during sift-down
questions.explanation: Larger branching factors reduce the number of levels for n nodes, but choosing the best child during sift-down requires inspecting up to d children.

questions.prompt: A perfect 4-ary tree has height 2 measured in edges. How many nodes does it contain?
questions.explanation: A full 4-ary tree through depth 2 has 1+4+16=21 nodes.

questions.prompt: A binary min-heap is used to implement a priority queue. Which element is removed by extract-min?
answer: The root
questions.explanation: The root stores the minimum by heap order. Extract-min removes it, then repairs the heap after moving the final element to root.

questions.prompt: A binary min-heap stores 12 elements. How many elements are removed after 5 successful extract-min operations?
questions.explanation: Each extract-min removes one item, so five successful operations remove five elements.

questions.prompt: Which operations on a binary heap have O(1) worst-case time?
options: Read the heap size when maintained
Return the array element at a given index
answer: Read the root priority
Read the heap size when maintained
Return the array element at a given index
questions.explanation: The root, a maintained size counter, and an array element at a supplied index can be read directly in constant time. Searching for an arbitrary key may require scanning the heap.

questions.prompt: A max-heap's root is removed and the heap has n>1 elements. Why is sift-down necessary after moving the last element to root?
options: The moved element may be smaller than a child
The tree may cease to be complete
The root must always be the most recently inserted key
answer: The moved element may be smaller than a child
questions.explanation: The last element may not dominate its children, violating max-heap order at the root. The complete shape is preserved because the final slot is removed.

questions.prompt: A min-heap contains distinct values. What is the second-smallest element guaranteed to be?
answer: One of the root's children
questions.explanation: The minimum is at root; the second-smallest must be the minimum among its children because any deeper node has an ancestor child no greater than it.

questions.prompt: A min-heap root has children 4 and 9, and all other nodes are descendants of these children. What is the second-smallest key?
questions.explanation: The minimum is the root. The least remaining value must be among root's children, and min(4,9)=4.

questions.prompt: A heap's array representation allows parent and child positions to be computed in
answer: O(1) time
questions.explanation: Index arithmetic computes parent and child locations directly without traversing pointers, requiring constant time.

questions.prompt: A min-heap array is [2,5,3,9,7,8]. Which operation can return a value in O(1) time?
answer: Find the minimum
questions.explanation: The minimum is at the root, array index zero. The maximum and median are not generally known from heap order without additional work.

questions.prompt: A max-heap has 16 elements. How many leaves does its complete binary tree contain?
questions.explanation: In a zero-based heap, leaves occupy indices floor(n/2) through n-1. For n=16, there are 8 leaves.

questions.prompt: Which statements about a complete binary tree with n nodes stored in a heap array are correct?
options: All occupied indices form a prefix starting at zero
The final level, if partial, is filled left to right
Every node has exactly two children
answer: All occupied indices form a prefix starting at zero
The final level, if partial, is filled left to right
The height is floor(log2 n)
questions.explanation: The array occupies a prefix and the final tree level is left-packed. A complete binary tree has logarithmic height floor(log2 n); nodes can have fewer than two children.

questions.prompt: A binary heap with n elements has height
answer: floor(log2 n)
questions.explanation: The last occupied level is depth floor(log2 n), since a complete tree has 2^h through 2^(h+1)-1 nodes at height h.

questions.prompt: A complete binary heap has 100 elements. What is its height in edges?
questions.explanation: Since 2^6=64<=100<128=2^7, the height is floor(log2 100)=6.

questions.prompt: In a max-heap, after a new key is appended at the end, which direction can restore heap order?
answer: Upward toward the root
questions.explanation: The new key is a leaf, so it cannot violate order with its children. Only its relationship to ancestors can be invalid, repaired by sift-up.

questions.prompt: In a min-heap, after replacing the root with the last element, which direction is used to restore heap order?
answer: Downward toward a leaf
questions.explanation: The root's children may be smaller than the replacement, while there is no parent above root. Sift-down addresses the possible violation.

questions.prompt: A binary heap has height 7. What is the maximum number of comparisons of children during one sift-down, assuming one comparison selects the better child at each level?
questions.explanation: At most one child-selection comparison is made at each of the seven levels traversed, giving seven such comparisons (excluding parent comparison).

questions.prompt: A heap is built from an array using repeated insertions. If each insertion costs O(log n), what is the resulting upper bound for n insertions?
answer: O(n log n)
questions.explanation: Summing n logarithmic upper bounds gives O(n log n). Bottom-up build-heap improves this to O(n), but that is a different construction method.

questions.prompt: Which are advantages of a binary heap for priority-queue implementation?
options: O(1) access to the top-priority item
O(log n) search for any arbitrary key
answer: Compact array storage
O(1) access to the top-priority item
O(log n) insertion and extraction
questions.explanation: A heap uses compact array storage, provides constant-time access to the top priority, and supports logarithmic insert/extract. Arbitrary-key search is not logarithmic in general.

questions.prompt: A max-heap stores priorities 90,70,80,20,50,60,75 in level order. What is the array after extracting the maximum and restoring heap order?
questions.explanation: Move last key 75 to root and remove 90. Compare 75 with children 70 and 80, swap with 80; the resulting heap is [80,70,75,20,50,60].

questions.prompt: A min-heap array is [4,8,6,12,10,9]. After inserting 3, what is the resulting heap array?
questions.explanation: Append 3 at index 6, swap with parent 6 at index 2, then swap with root 4. This yields [3,8,4,12,10,9,6].

questions.prompt: A max-heap array is [40,25,35,10,20,30]. After inserting 50 and bubbling up, what is the root value?
questions.explanation: 50 swaps with parent 35 at index 2, then with root 40, so the root becomes 50.

questions.prompt: A heap insertion of a value performs swaps along a root-to-leaf path. What is the maximum path length for n elements?
answer: O(log n)
questions.explanation: A complete binary tree has logarithmic height, so a bubble-up path contains at most O(log n) edges.

questions.prompt: Which statements about extracting from a max-heap are true?
options: The final array element is moved to the root
The active heap size decreases by one
Sift-down may swap with the smaller child
answer: The root is the maximum
The final array element is moved to the root
The active heap size decreases by one
questions.explanation: The root is maximum, the final element replaces it, and the active size decreases by one. Sift-down in a max-heap chooses the larger child, not the smaller.

questions.prompt: When sifting down in a max-heap, if a node is smaller than both children, it should be swapped with
answer: the larger child
questions.explanation: Swapping with the larger child ensures the promoted value remains at least as large as the other child, maintaining heap order at that level.

questions.prompt: A max-heap node has children 12 and 17, and its key is 9. Which value becomes the parent after one sift-down swap?
questions.explanation: The larger child 17 is promoted to the parent's position during max-heap sift-down.

questions.prompt: A min-heap's sift-down operation chooses the smaller child because
options: the promoted child must be no greater than its sibling
the larger child is always a leaf
the root must be the largest
answer: the promoted child must be no greater than its sibling
questions.explanation: Promoting the smaller child keeps it no greater than the sibling, which is necessary for both children to remain at least the new parent in a min-heap.

questions.prompt: A min-heap node has children 6 and 11 and key 15. Which child is selected for a sift-down swap?
questions.explanation: For min-heap restoration, choose the smaller child, 6, so the parent remains no greater than both children.

questions.prompt: A binary heap permits finding an arbitrary value by scanning its array. What is the worst-case time?
answer: O(n)
questions.explanation: Heap order does not locate a target by key range; the key may be at any index, so a worst-case scan checks all n elements.

questions.prompt: A max-priority queue stores tasks by priority in a max-heap. If equal priorities are allowed, does heap order guarantee FIFO among tied tasks?
options: No, additional sequence information or tie-breaking is needed
Only when the heap has odd size
answer: No, additional sequence information or tie-breaking is needed
questions.explanation: Heap order constrains priority values but not the relative order of equal-priority items. Stable tie handling requires explicit arrival-order data and comparison rules.

questions.prompt: Which information can be included in heap keys to provide deterministic tie-breaking?
options: Current array index only, if indices change after swaps
answer: Priority value
Insertion timestamp or sequence number
Unique task identifier
questions.explanation: Priority is the primary field; a sequence number can preserve FIFO among ties, and a unique identifier can complete deterministic comparison. Array index changes during swaps, so it is not stable tie information.

questions.prompt: A stable priority queue can compare pairs (priority, sequence). For equal priority, which sequence order preserves FIFO?
options: Compare the task payload alphabetically only
answer: Earlier sequence number first
questions.explanation: Assigning increasing sequence numbers at insertion and favoring the smaller number among equal priorities preserves arrival order.

questions.prompt: A heap has 10 items and uses a one-based array with index 1 as root. What is the left-child index of node 6?
questions.explanation: With one-based heap indexing, the left child index is 2i=12.

questions.prompt: A one-based heap array has a node at index i. Its right child is at index
questions.explanation: One-based indexing gives left child 2i and right child 2i+1.

questions.prompt: A one-based heap stores n elements at indices 1 through n. Which index range contains leaves?
answer: floor(n/2)+1 through n
questions.explanation: Indices greater than floor(n/2) have left-child indices beyond n, so they are leaves.

questions.prompt: A one-based heap has 17 elements. What is the last internal-node index?
questions.explanation: The last internal node is floor(n/2)=floor(17/2)=8.

questions.prompt: The bottom-up heapify process can start at index floor(n/2)-1 because
options: the root is always a leaf
all earlier indices are already heaps
the array is sorted from the midpoint onward
answer: all later indices are leaves
questions.explanation: In zero-based storage, nodes from floor(n/2) onward have no children. They are trivial heaps, so processing begins at the last internal node.

questions.prompt: Which facts explain why bottom-up heap construction is linear?
options: There are about n/2 leaves with zero sift-down distance
Only about n/4 nodes can move down one level
Only about n/8 nodes can move down two levels
Every node moves down log n levels
answer: There are about n/2 leaves with zero sift-down distance
Only about n/4 nodes can move down one level
Only about n/8 nodes can move down two levels
questions.explanation: About n/2 leaves have zero height; fewer nodes can descend one or more levels as distance grows. The geometric weighted sum is O(n), unlike moving every node log n levels.

questions.prompt: The root of a max-heap is 100. What is the minimum possible key among all other nodes?
options: It may be arbitrarily smaller subject to the key domain
It must be one of the root's children
answer: It may be arbitrarily smaller subject to the key domain
questions.explanation: Heap order imposes an upper-bound relation from parent to child, but a descendant can have a very small value; there is no global lower bound from the root.

questions.prompt: A min-heap is used for Dijkstra's algorithm with adjacency lists and decrease-key support. What is the heap operation required when a shorter distance to a vertex is found?
answer: Decrease its key
questions.explanation: A shorter tentative distance decreases that vertex's priority key in a min-priority queue, requiring decrease-key and upward repair.

questions.prompt: A binary heap priority queue without a direct handle to a vertex uses lazy insertion in Dijkstra's algorithm. How is a stale extracted entry recognized?
options: Compare its stored distance with the current best distance
Check whether it is the last array element
Compare it with the heap root's parent
answer: Compare its stored distance with the current best distance
questions.explanation: When an old pair is extracted, if its distance exceeds the current best recorded distance for that vertex, it is stale and can be skipped.

questions.prompt: A shortest-path implementation inserts 3 tentative distance entries for the same vertex into a heap. If the best known distance is 12 and an extracted entry has distance 17, what is the distance gap indicating staleness?
questions.explanation: The extracted value exceeds the current best by 17-12=5, so it is stale.

questions.prompt: Which statements about using a binary heap in Prim's minimum spanning tree algorithm are correct?
options: The heap can store candidate vertices keyed by best incident edge weight
Extract-min chooses a next vertex with minimum current key
A key decrease may be needed when a cheaper connecting edge is found
The heap itself guarantees the resulting graph is connected
answer: The heap can store candidate vertices keyed by best incident edge weight
Extract-min chooses a next vertex with minimum current key
A key decrease may be needed when a cheaper connecting edge is found
questions.explanation: The heap stores each candidate vertex keyed by its best connecting edge; extract-min selects the cheapest candidate, and decrease-key updates improved edges. Connectivity depends on the graph, not the heap.

questions.prompt: For a binary heap with n entries, decrease-key on a known node handle takes
answer: O(log n)
questions.explanation: A decreased key in a min-heap bubbles upward along a root path whose length is O(log n).

questions.prompt: A min-heap node at depth 3 has its key decreased enough to reach the root. What is the maximum number of swaps?
questions.explanation: A node at depth three has three edges to the root, so at most three upward swaps are needed.

questions.prompt: A binary heap is complete, but does that imply its array is sorted?
options: No, only parent-child heap order is required
Only if the heap has an even size
answer: No, only parent-child heap order is required
questions.explanation: Completeness describes shape; heap order is local. Siblings and cousins are not necessarily sorted relative to each other.

questions.prompt: A max-heap array [90,70,80,20,60,75,65] is valid because
options: each parent is at least its children
answer: each parent is at least its children
questions.explanation: Root 90 exceeds 70 and 80; 70 exceeds 20 and 60; 80 exceeds 75 and 65. These parent-child checks establish a valid max-heap.

questions.prompt: A min-heap array [2,6,4,9,8,7,5] has how many parent-child violations?
questions.explanation: Each parent is no greater than its children: 2<=6,4; 6<=9,8; and 4<=7,5. Thus there are no violations.

questions.prompt: In heapsort, the heap is built from an arbitrary array and then repeatedly reduced. What is the total worst-case running time?
answer: Theta(n log n)
questions.explanation: Bottom-up build is O(n), followed by n extract-max operations costing O(log n) each. The total is Theta(n log n).

questions.prompt: Which structures can implement a priority queue with different operation trade-offs?
answer: Unsorted array
Sorted array
Binary heap
Linked list
questions.explanation: Unsorted arrays/lists, sorted arrays/lists, and binary heaps all support priority queues with different insertion and extraction costs.

questions.prompt: A priority queue implemented by an unsorted array supports insert in
questions.explanation: Appending an item to an unsorted array takes constant time, while extraction of an extreme priority generally requires a linear scan.

questions.prompt: A priority queue implemented by a sorted array supports find-min in
options: O(1) if the minimum is kept at an endpoint
answer: O(1) if the minimum is kept at an endpoint
questions.explanation: If the array is maintained in sorted order, the minimum lies at a known endpoint and is accessible in constant time; insertion may require shifting O(n) items.

questions.prompt: An unsorted array priority queue contains 40 elements. In the worst case, how many key comparisons are needed to extract the maximum?
questions.explanation: A linear scan can initialize the candidate from one element and compare the other 39 elements against it.

questions.prompt: A binary heap's height is logarithmic because it is
answer: complete
questions.explanation: Completeness ensures every level except the last is full and the last is left-packed, giving logarithmic height in the number of nodes.

questions.prompt: A max-heap supports delete-key for an arbitrary node in O(log n) when
options: a handle to its array index is available
answer: a handle to its array index is available
questions.explanation: With a handle, replace the target by the last element, remove the last slot, and sift up or down as needed, taking heap-height time.

questions.prompt: A heap has height 8. An arbitrary key replacement may require either sift-up or sift-down. What is the maximum number of swaps along one repair path?
questions.explanation: The repair follows at most one root-to-leaf path, whose length is bounded by heap height eight.

questions.prompt: After replacing a heap element at index i by a new key, which repair direction is needed in a max-heap?
options: Up if it exceeds its parent; otherwise down if below a child
Both up and down in separate full traversals
answer: Up if it exceeds its parent; otherwise down if below a child
questions.explanation: Only one side of the local ordering can be violated based on the new key relative to its parent and children; the corresponding path is repaired.

questions.prompt: Which comparisons identify whether a changed key in a max-heap requires sift-up or sift-down?
options: Compare it with its parent when i is not root
If it is smaller than a child, sift-down may be needed
If it is greater than its parent, sift-up may be needed
Compare it with every heap element
answer: Compare it with its parent when i is not root
If it is smaller than a child, sift-down may be needed
If it is greater than its parent, sift-up may be needed
questions.explanation: The parent comparison detects whether a larger value violates upward order; child comparisons detect a smaller value that may violate downward order. A full scan is unnecessary for a known index.

questions.prompt: A min-heap stores all distinct values 1 through 15. Which value is guaranteed at the root?
questions.explanation: The root of a min-heap is the global minimum, which among these distinct keys is 1.

questions.prompt: Assume int is 4 bytes and row-major layout. What is the byte offset of a[2][1] in int a[4][3], from a[0][0]?
questions.explanation: The linear element offset is 2*3+1=7. At four bytes per int, the byte offset is 7*4=28.

questions.prompt: For int a[7]={0}; in the same scope, what does sizeof(a)/sizeof(a[0]) evaluate to?
questions.explanation: sizeof(a) includes all seven int elements; sizeof(a[0]) is one int. Their ratio gives the element count.

questions.prompt: For char text[]="GATE"; what value does sizeof(text) return?
questions.explanation: The array stores four visible characters plus the terminating null character, so sizeof reports five bytes.

questions.prompt: For char text[]="GATE"; what does strlen(text) return before modification?
questions.explanation: strlen counts characters up to but excluding the null terminator.

questions.prompt: Let int a[9]; int *p=&a[2] and int *q=&a[8]. What is q-p?
questions.explanation: Pointer subtraction for elements of the same array returns their element-index difference: 8-2=6.

questions.prompt: For int a[4]; int *p=&a[3]; which operation is defined?
options: Forming p+1 as a one-past pointer
answer: Forming p+1 as a one-past pointer
questions.explanation: C permits a pointer one past an array end for comparison or subtraction, but it cannot be dereferenced or advanced farther.

questions.prompt: In a function parameter declaration void f(int values[20]), what type does values have inside f?
answer: int *
questions.explanation: Array parameters are adjusted to pointer parameters. The function receives an int pointer; the bound 20 does not automatically enforce a runtime length.

questions.prompt: A function void inc(int x) executes x=x+1. The caller passes variable n. What is guaranteed about n after the call?
options: The call does not modify n through x
The result depends on stack layout
answer: The call does not modify n through x
questions.explanation: C passes the scalar value by value. The function changes its local parameter copy, not the caller object.

questions.prompt: A block-scope static int counter starts without an initializer and is incremented once per call. What is its value after 9 calls?
questions.explanation: A static-storage object is zero-initialized once and retains its value between calls. Nine increments produce 9.

questions.prompt: What initial value does a file-scope int object without an explicit initializer have?
options: The value of the first input read
questions.explanation: Objects with static storage duration are zero-initialized when no initializer is provided.

questions.prompt: A function declares static int calls; and increments calls every invocation. What happens to calls between invocations?
options: Its value is retained for the program duration
It is recreated with value zero on every call
It becomes a global variable visible to all translation units
It is stored in the caller stack frame
answer: Its value is retained for the program duration
questions.explanation: A block-scope static object has static storage duration. Its name remains block-scoped, but its stored value persists across calls.

questions.prompt: What is the status of reading an uninitialized automatic int local variable?
options: It has an indeterminate value and using it can have undefined behavior
It is guaranteed to be zero
It is guaranteed to equal the last value at that stack address
It is implementation-defined but always safe
answer: It has an indeterminate value and using it can have undefined behavior
questions.explanation: An automatic object without an initializer is not zero-initialized. Evaluating its indeterminate value is not a portable operation.

questions.prompt: At file scope, what does extern int total; normally declare?
options: An object defined elsewhere without defining storage here
answer: An object defined elsewhere without defining storage here
questions.explanation: A file-scope extern declaration refers to an externally linked object. Without an initializer, it is a declaration rather than a tentative definition.

questions.prompt: What does static on a file-scope function declaration specify?
options: Internal linkage within that translation unit
External linkage across the whole program
Automatic storage duration for each call
answer: Internal linkage within that translation unit
questions.explanation: A file-scope static function name is not visible to other translation units; static changes linkage in this context.

questions.prompt: Given int a[3], b[3]; what does the statement a=b; do in standard C?
options: It violates a constraint because arrays are not assignable
It copies the address of b
answer: It violates a constraint because arrays are not assignable
questions.explanation: Array objects are not modifiable lvalues and cannot be assigned wholesale. Elements must be copied individually or through a library routine.

questions.prompt: For int a[2][5], what is the type of a+1 after array conversion?
options: Pointer to an array of 5 int
Pointer to an array of 2 int
answer: Pointer to an array of 5 int
questions.explanation: The outer array decays to a pointer to its first row. Each row has type int[5], so adding one advances by one row.

questions.prompt: Inside a function, sizeof applied to a parameter declared int x[] yields what?
options: The size of an int pointer
The total size of the caller array
The size of the first int
answer: The size of an int pointer
questions.explanation: The parameter is adjusted to int *x. sizeof measures that pointer object; the array length must be passed separately.

questions.prompt: For char s[4]="GATE"; which statement is correct?
options: The initializer cannot fit because the null terminator needs a fifth element
It is valid and stores the complete string including terminator
It silently truncates the last character
answer: The initializer cannot fit because the null terminator needs a fifth element
questions.explanation: The string literal has five char elements including its terminator. An array of four cannot hold the full initializer as written.

questions.prompt: Which printf conversion is intended for a value of type size_t returned by sizeof?
answer: %zu
questions.explanation: sizeof has type size_t. The z length modifier with u is the matching standard conversion for an unsigned integer type such as size_t.

questions.prompt: For int a[]={3,5,8,12}; int *p=a; what value does p[2] designate?
questions.explanation: p[2] is *(p+2). Since p points to a[0], it selects a[2], whose value is 8.

questions.prompt: For int a[4]; int *p=&a[1]; which expression denotes the address of a[3]?
questions.explanation: Starting at a[1], advancing the pointer by two elements yields a[3].

questions.prompt: For char *p="abc";, which operation has undefined behavior?
options: Passing p to a function taking const char *
answer: Attempting to modify p[0]
questions.explanation: A string literal is not modifiable. Reading its characters is allowed, but writing through p has undefined behavior.

questions.prompt: For int a[3]={1,2}; what value is stored in a[2]?
questions.explanation: Aggregate initialization supplies zero values for array elements omitted from the initializer list.

questions.prompt: Which C function counts characters in a null-terminated string s, excluding its terminator?
answer: strlen(s)
questions.explanation: strlen counts characters before the first null byte. sizeof may measure an array or just a pointer, depending on context.

questions.prompt: For char word[]="net"; what is sizeof(word)?
questions.explanation: The array contains n, e, t, and a terminating null character, so it has four char elements.

questions.prompt: For int a[5], what is the result of 2[a]?
answer: The same element as a[2]
questions.explanation: C defines a[i] as *(a+i). Pointer addition is commutative, so 2[a] is equivalent to a[2], though it is unusual style.

questions.prompt: In a function parameter written int x[static 8], what does static require of each call?
options: The argument provides access to at least eight int elements
The function allocates eight ints automatically
The argument has static storage duration
The parameter becomes a global array
answer: The argument provides access to at least eight int elements
questions.explanation: The static array-parameter qualifier expresses a minimum accessible element count; it does not allocate storage.

questions.prompt: In the declaration int (*p)[6], what does p point to?
options: An array of six int pointers
answer: An array of six int
questions.explanation: Parentheses make p a pointer to an array of six int, rather than an array of pointers.

questions.prompt: Which declaration is an array of four pointers to char?
answer: char *names[4];
questions.explanation: Array subscripting binds more tightly than unary *, so names is an array whose elements are char pointers.

questions.prompt: Assume 8-bit unsigned char. What value results from unsigned char x=250; x+=10; ?
questions.explanation: The compound assignment converts the sum back to an 8-bit unsigned type. 260 modulo 256 is 4.

questions.prompt: Assume 32-bit unsigned int. What value does 0u-1u produce?
questions.explanation: Unsigned arithmetic is modulo 2^32, so zero minus one yields 2^32-1.

questions.prompt: Assume 32-bit signed int with x=INT_MAX. What happens when x is incremented?
options: The behavior is undefined due to signed overflow
It is guaranteed to wrap to INT_MIN
answer: The behavior is undefined due to signed overflow
questions.explanation: C does not define signed overflow. Hardware wraparound does not make the expression portable.

questions.prompt: Assume unsigned char is 8 bits and int can represent 0 through 255. What value does the expression (unsigned char)255 + 1 have before assignment to any narrower object?
questions.explanation: The unsigned char operand is promoted to int because int represents its full range. The addition therefore occurs as int and yields 256; it does not wrap at 8 bits.

questions.prompt: For unsigned int x, which expression tests whether its least significant bit is set?
questions.explanation: Bitwise AND with one isolates the low bit. Comparing that masked result with zero tests whether it is set.

questions.prompt: Given int a[]={4,9,13}; int *p=a; then execute int first=*p++; followed by int second=*p; what values are stored in first and second?
answer: 4 and 9
questions.explanation: Each statement is a separate full expression. The first reads a[0] and advances p; the next reads a[1], so the values are 4 and 9.

questions.prompt: If p points to a modifiable int, what does (*p)++ do?
options: Increment the pointer by one byte
answer: Increment the pointed-to int
questions.explanation: Parentheses make indirection occur first, so postfix increment applies to the int object reached through p.

questions.prompt: Which uses of an array expression avoid array-to-pointer conversion?
options: Passing a as an int * argument
answer: sizeof a
questions.explanation: The operand of sizeof is an exception to array conversion when it is not a variable-length array type. Other listed contexts use the array as a pointer.

questions.prompt: For int a[4]; int *p=&a[0]; int *q=&a[3]; what is q-p?
questions.explanation: Pointer subtraction within one array is measured in elements. The index difference is 3, independent of int byte size.

questions.prompt: Which operation on int a[5] is defined when p=&a[4]?
answer: Compare p+1 with a+5
