questions.explanation: p+1 is the one-past pointer and equals a+5. It may be formed but not dereferenced or advanced farther.

questions.prompt: Which declaration denotes a pointer to a function taking int and returning int?
answer: int (*fp)(int);
questions.explanation: Parentheses bind the pointer declarator to fp before the function parameter list. Without parentheses, int *fp(int) declares a function returning int pointer.

questions.prompt: What does const int *p allow?
options: Changing p to point elsewhere but not modifying the int through p
Modifying p but not changing the int value
Neither changing p nor modifying the int
Changing both p and the int freely
answer: Changing p to point elsewhere but not modifying the int through p
questions.explanation: The pointed-to type is const-qualified through this access path, but p itself is not const and may be reassigned.

questions.prompt: What does int * const p mean?
options: p cannot be reassigned, but the pointed-to int may be modified
p points to a const int
Both p and the int are const
answer: p cannot be reassigned, but the pointed-to int may be modified
questions.explanation: The const qualifier applies to the pointer object itself. It does not qualify the int that p points to.

questions.prompt: What guarantee does volatile provide by itself?
options: It does not make accesses atomic or thread-safe
answer: It does not make accesses atomic or thread-safe
questions.explanation: volatile affects optimization assumptions about accesses but is not an atomicity or synchronization mechanism.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes restrict in C99 and later?
options: It is an aliasing promise about access to an object through a pointer
It means the pointer cannot be null
It makes the pointed-to object const
It requests that the pointer be stored in a register
answer: It is an aliasing promise about access to an object through a pointer
questions.explanation: restrict communicates a restricted access association for an object during a block execution. Violating that promise can yield undefined behavior.

questions.prompt: Assume struct S { char c; int x; } with int alignment 4 and natural padding. What is sizeof(struct S)?
questions.explanation: c uses byte 0; padding aligns x at offset 4; the int ends at offset 8. Struct size is rounded to its maximum member alignment, four.

questions.prompt: Why may memcmp on two structures report different bytes even when their members compare equal?
options: C stores a pointer in every structure
The structures must have different types
answer: Padding bytes may differ
questions.explanation: Padding can be part of the object representation without being a member value. Member-wise comparison avoids relying on unspecified padding bytes.

questions.prompt: For a union with members int i and char c, which is true about their storage?
options: The members overlap and begin at the same address
The union stores both in separate consecutive areas
Its size is always the sum of member sizes
Only the first member can ever be selected
answer: The members overlap and begin at the same address
questions.explanation: Union members share storage. The union has enough size and alignment for its largest member, rather than adding all member sizes.

questions.prompt: An enum is declared enum E {P=4, Q, R=9, S}; what value does S have?
questions.explanation: An enumerator without an explicit value is one greater than its predecessor. R is 9, so S is 10.

questions.prompt: Which statements about C structure and union objects are correct?
options: Compatible structures may be assigned as whole values
A structure may contain padding between members
All structure types are compared by memcmp
answer: Compatible structures may be assigned as whole values
Union members share overlapping storage
A structure may contain padding between members
questions.explanation: Structure assignment copies compatible structure values. Union members overlap in storage, and implementations may insert padding between structure members; bytewise comparison can therefore differ even when member values match.

questions.prompt: Which pointer type may inspect the object representation of an arbitrary object byte by byte?
options: A pointer to void after direct dereference
answer: A pointer to character type
questions.explanation: Character-type lvalues are allowed to inspect object representation. A void pointer must be converted to an object pointer type before dereferencing.

questions.prompt: What can happen when an object is accessed through an incompatible pointer type, outside specified exceptions?
options: It can violate effective-type rules and cause undefined behavior
The compiler always converts the representation safely
The object is copied to a temporary of the new type
It is safe whenever pointer sizes match
answer: It can violate effective-type rules and cause undefined behavior
questions.explanation: C restricts access to object storage through compatible types, with specified exceptions such as character types.

questions.prompt: Which statement about function pointers is correct?
options: A function pointer can be called with arguments matching its function type
A function pointer can be dereferenced to read machine code bytes portably
All object pointers and function pointers must have identical representations
A function pointer is an array of instructions
answer: A function pointer can be called with arguments matching its function type
questions.explanation: A function pointer designates a function and may be invoked through a compatible function type. Its representation need not match object pointers.

questions.prompt: Which declarations can represent a pointer to an array of five int?
answer: typedef int Row[5]; Row *p;
questions.explanation: Both the parenthesized declarator and the typedef form declare a pointer to an array of five int. An array of pointers and a pointer-to-pointer are different types.

questions.prompt: What does p->member mean for a pointer p to a structure object?
answer: (*p).member
questions.explanation: The arrow operator is equivalent to first dereferencing p, then selecting the named structure member.

questions.prompt: Evaluate 0x35u & 0x0Fu and give its decimal value.
questions.explanation: The mask keeps the low four bits of 0x35; 0101 in binary is decimal 5.

questions.prompt: Evaluate 0x35u ^ 0x0Fu and give the hexadecimal result.
questions.explanation: Hexadecimal XOR gives 0x35 XOR 0x0F = 0x3A because only corresponding equal bits become zero.

questions.prompt: Assume 32-bit unsigned int. What is the value of 1u << 5?
questions.explanation: Left-shifting unsigned one by five positions gives 2^5, which is 32.

questions.prompt: For a 32-bit unsigned int, which shift count makes x << count undefined?
questions.explanation: The shift count must be less than the width of the promoted left operand. A count of 32 is invalid for a 32-bit value.

questions.prompt: In C17, what can be concluded about right-shifting a negative signed integer?
options: It is always a logical shift
It is always division rounded toward zero
It is undefined on every implementation
answer: The result is implementation-defined
questions.explanation: C17 leaves right shift of a negative signed value implementation-defined. Portable code should not assume a particular sign-extension result.

questions.prompt: A function int inc(int x) returns x+1. If int (*fp)(int)=inc; what value does fp(6) return?
questions.explanation: fp stores a pointer to a function with compatible parameter and result types. Calling fp(6) invokes inc with 6 and returns 6+1=7.

questions.prompt: What is sizeof(int[3]) in bytes when sizeof(int) is 4?
questions.explanation: The type is an array of three int objects. Its size is 3*4=12 bytes.

questions.prompt: A variable-length array int a[n] has a run-time bound n. When is sizeof(a) determined?
options: At run time from the value of n
It is not permitted for a VLA
answer: At run time from the value of n
questions.explanation: A variable-length array has a bound evaluated at run time, and sizeof on its VLA type reflects that bound.

questions.prompt: Which type may control a switch statement in C after integer promotions?
answer: An integer type
questions.explanation: The controlling expression must have integer type after the permitted integer promotions.

questions.prompt: A break statement is inside a switch that itself is inside a while loop. What does break exit?
options: Both the switch and while loop
The current while iteration and then the switch
answer: The switch only
questions.explanation: break exits only the innermost enclosing switch or loop. Execution continues after the switch, still within the while body.

questions.prompt: In a for loop, where does continue transfer control?
options: To the iteration expression, then the next condition check
To the loop body start without checking the condition
answer: To the iteration expression, then the next condition check
questions.explanation: For a for loop, continue executes the iteration expression before evaluating the condition for the next iteration.

questions.prompt: What is guaranteed about sizeof(char) in C?
options: It is implementation-defined and may be zero
answer: It equals 1
questions.explanation: sizeof measures in C bytes, and a char always occupies exactly one such byte. A byte may have more than eight bits.

questions.prompt: What does CHAR_BIT from limits.h specify?
options: The number of bits in a byte
The number of bytes in an int
The number of bits in a pointer
The maximum number of chars in a string
answer: The number of bits in a byte
questions.explanation: CHAR_BIT defines how many bits are in one C byte; the standard does not require every byte to have exactly eight bits.

questions.prompt: Which statement about null pointers is guaranteed by C?
options: A null pointer compares unequal to every pointer to an object or function
A null pointer is represented by all zero bits
A null pointer always has type int *
A null pointer can be dereferenced to obtain zero
answer: A null pointer compares unequal to every pointer to an object or function
questions.explanation: Null pointer semantics are defined by comparisons and conversion rules, not by a required all-zero representation.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between the null character and a null pointer?
options: The null character is a character value; a null pointer is a pointer value that designates no object or function
They are the same value and type
A null pointer terminates a C string
The null character can only appear in pointer objects
answer: The null character is a character value; a null pointer is a pointer value that designates no object or function
questions.explanation: The null character terminates strings. A null pointer is a special pointer value; the concepts have different types and uses.

questions.prompt: For char s[]="CS";, what storage does s contain?
options: C, S, and a terminating null character
A pointer to immutable literal storage
Only C and S with no terminator
The address of the literal as an integer
answer: C, S, and a terminating null character
questions.explanation: Array initialization copies the literal into a modifiable three-element char array including its terminator.

questions.prompt: A six-element int array uses the designated initializer {[3]=9} and has no other initializers. What is the sum of all its elements?
questions.explanation: The designated initializer sets only element 3 to 9. Every omitted element of the aggregate is zero-initialized, so the total sum is 9.

questions.prompt: Which statements about C strings are correct?
options: A string is terminated by a null character
strlen excludes the terminating null character
strcpy copies the terminating null character
Every char array is automatically a valid null-terminated string
answer: A string is terminated by a null character
strlen excludes the terminating null character
strcpy copies the terminating null character
questions.explanation: A C string is a character sequence ending at a null byte. strlen excludes that byte, while strcpy copies it to terminate the destination string.

questions.prompt: Which C17 expression-order statements are correct?
options: The left operand of && is evaluated before the right operand
The condition of ?: is evaluated before one selected branch
The operands of + have no specified left-to-right order
Arguments to a function are evaluated left to right
answer: The left operand of && is evaluated before the right operand
The condition of ?: is evaluated before one selected branch
The operands of + have no specified left-to-right order
questions.explanation: Logical AND and the conditional operator impose sequencing rules. Ordinary addition and function arguments do not have a general left-to-right evaluation order in C17.

questions.prompt: What can be concluded about the exact nonzero value returned by strcmp?
options: It is always the ASCII difference
It is the difference in string lengths
answer: Only its sign is specified
questions.explanation: strcmp specifies whether its result is negative, zero, or positive; the exact nonzero magnitude is not fixed.

questions.prompt: What is the behavior of printf("%d", 3.5) in a variadic call?
options: It prints the double bit pattern
A diagnostic is required in every implementation
answer: Undefined because %d expects an int
questions.explanation: Variadic arguments are not converted according to the format string. A double argument mismatched with %d has undefined behavior.

questions.prompt: An object pointer p is passed to printf with the %p conversion. Which argument form satisfies the required pointer type?
answer: (void *)p
questions.explanation: The %p conversion expects a void pointer argument. An object pointer can be converted to void * explicitly before passing it through the variadic argument list.

questions.prompt: What happens to a float argument in the unnamed portion of a variadic function call?
options: It is promoted to long double
answer: It is promoted to double
questions.explanation: The default argument promotions convert float to double for arguments corresponding to an ellipsis.

questions.prompt: Which is the safe pattern when realloc must preserve the old allocation if it fails?
options: Store the result in a temporary pointer and update the owner only on success
Assign the result directly to the only copy of p
answer: Store the result in a temporary pointer and update the owner only on success
questions.explanation: On failure realloc returns NULL and leaves the old allocation valid. A temporary pointer avoids losing the original address.

questions.prompt: What argument must be passed to free for a block returned by malloc?
options: The original allocation pointer or NULL
An interior pointer to its last byte
The first value stored in the block
Any pointer with the same numeric address after arithmetic
answer: The original allocation pointer or NULL
questions.explanation: free accepts the allocation pointer itself or NULL. Interior pointers and repeated frees are invalid.

questions.prompt: What does calloc guarantee about the bytes of a successful allocation?
options: They are all set to zero bits
Every pointer member is guaranteed to be a null pointer
Every floating member is guaranteed to equal 0.0
Each object is initialized by a constructor
answer: They are all set to zero bits
questions.explanation: calloc fills bytes with all-bits-zero; C does not require that representation to encode null pointers or floating zero for every type.

questions.prompt: Why is gets unsafe for reading input into a fixed-size array?
options: It has no parameter limiting how many bytes are stored
It always reads only one character
answer: It has no parameter limiting how many bytes are stored
questions.explanation: gets cannot enforce the destination bound and was removed from the C standard. fgets accepts an explicit size limit.

questions.prompt: For #define SQR(x) x*x, what does SQR(1+2) expand to and evaluate as?
answer: 1+2*1+2, which is 5
questions.explanation: Macro substitution is textual. Without parentheses the expansion is 1+2*1+2, which evaluates to 5 by operator precedence.

questions.prompt: Which definition protects a square macro from precedence errors?
answer: #define SQR(x) ((x) * (x))
questions.explanation: Parenthesizing each argument use and the complete expansion preserves grouping in surrounding expressions.

questions.prompt: What risk remains for SQR(i++) with a macro defined as ((x)*(x))?
options: The side effect can occur twice
The macro is converted to a function automatically
answer: The side effect can occur twice
questions.explanation: The argument text appears twice in the replacement, so i++ can be evaluated twice. Parentheses do not remove repeated side effects.

questions.prompt: What does typedef unsigned long Size; do?
options: Introduces Size as an alias for unsigned long
answer: Introduces Size as an alias for unsigned long
questions.explanation: typedef introduces a type name alias; it does not allocate storage or create a distinct representation by itself.

questions.prompt: In hosted C99 and later, what happens if main reaches its closing brace?
options: It is equivalent to returning zero
It returns the last local value
answer: It is equivalent to returning zero
questions.explanation: The standard gives main a special rule: reaching its closing brace returns zero. This rule does not apply to arbitrary non-void functions.

questions.prompt: Which return type is required for main in a hosted C program?
answer: int
questions.explanation: A hosted program defines main with return type int in one of the standard forms.

questions.prompt: What does the prototype int f(void); specify?
options: f takes no parameters and returns int
f accepts any number of parameters
answer: f takes no parameters and returns int
questions.explanation: The parameter list containing void explicitly specifies no parameters; the result type is int.

questions.prompt: A function returns the address of an automatic local variable. What is the problem after return?
options: The pointed-to object lifetime has ended
answer: The pointed-to object lifetime has ended
questions.explanation: An automatic local object ceases to exist when its block ends. Using the returned pointer to access it is invalid.

questions.prompt: What is guaranteed about the representation of a null object pointer?
options: It need not consist of all zero bits
It is always all zero bits
It has the same representation as the null character
answer: It need not consist of all zero bits
questions.explanation: C specifies null-pointer value semantics, not a required bit pattern.

questions.prompt: What values can standard C _Bool store?
answer: 0 or 1
questions.explanation: Conversion to _Bool produces zero if the value compares equal to zero and one otherwise.

questions.prompt: Which declaration makes f a function taking no parameters and returning a pointer to int?
answer: int *f(void);
questions.explanation: The declarator is a function named f with a void parameter list; its return type is int pointer. Parentheses around *f would instead make f a function pointer object.

questions.prompt: What does sizeof applied to a function designator do in standard C?
options: It is not permitted for a function type
It returns a function pointer size
answer: It is not permitted for a function type
questions.explanation: sizeof cannot be applied to function types. A pointer to function is a distinct object type and can be measured.

questions.prompt: For enum E {A=3, B, C=10, D}; what value does D have?
questions.explanation: An enumerator without an explicit value follows its predecessor by one. C is 10, so D is 11.

questions.prompt: Why can a program not apply unary & to a bit-field member?
options: A bit-field is not an independently addressable object
A bit-field is always a pointer
The operator is valid only on arrays
answer: A bit-field is not an independently addressable object
questions.explanation: C prohibits taking a bit-field address because the field may not occupy an independently addressable object.

questions.prompt: Which statements about C storage duration and linkage are correct?
options: A block-scope static object retains its value between calls
A file-scope static function has internal linkage
An ordinary automatic local object ends its lifetime at block exit
extern always defines a new object
answer: A block-scope static object retains its value between calls
A file-scope static function has internal linkage
An ordinary automatic local object ends its lifetime at block exit
questions.explanation: Static duration preserves a local static value. File-scope static restricts linkage; ordinary locals end at block exit. extern alone does not define storage.

questions.prompt: Which statements about malloc and realloc are correct?
options: malloc returns suitably aligned storage for object types
A failed nonzero-size realloc leaves the original allocation valid
free sets the caller pointer to NULL
realloc accepts an interior pointer to a block
answer: malloc returns suitably aligned storage for object types
A failed nonzero-size realloc leaves the original allocation valid
questions.explanation: malloc returns suitably aligned storage. If a nonzero realloc request fails, the old block remains allocated; free does not overwrite the caller pointer.

questions.prompt: What does the declaration const int *p prevent?
options: Modifying the pointed-to int through p
answer: Modifying the pointed-to int through p
questions.explanation: The pointed-to type is const-qualified through p, so writes through it are disallowed; p itself may be reassigned.

questions.prompt: Which statement about errno after a successful library call is correct?
options: The function is not generally required to clear errno on success
It is guaranteed to be zero
It always equals the return value
It cannot be changed by a library function
answer: The function is not generally required to clear errno on success
questions.explanation: A function may leave errno unchanged after success. Inspect it only according to that function's documented error convention.

questions.prompt: Which expressions have defined sequencing between their relevant evaluations?
options: The left-to-right short-circuit evaluation of a && b
The two operands of i++ + i
Function arguments are guaranteed left to right
answer: The comma expression (i++, i+1)
The left-to-right short-circuit evaluation of a && b
questions.explanation: The comma operator sequences its left operand before the right; && sequences left before right. Addition and function arguments have no general left-to-right order.

questions.prompt: An undirected simple graph has n vertices. What is the maximum possible number of edges?
questions.explanation: A simple undirected graph has at most one edge per unordered pair of distinct vertices. There are n choose 2 such pairs.

questions.prompt: A simple undirected graph has 8 vertices and 11 edges. What is the sum of all vertex degrees?
questions.explanation: By the handshaking lemma, the degree sum is twice the edge count: 2*11=22.

questions.prompt: An undirected graph has degree sequence 3,2,2,1. How many edges does it have?
questions.explanation: The degree sum is 3+2+2+1=8. Each undirected edge contributes two to the degree sum, so there are 8/2=4 edges.

questions.prompt: For a directed graph, the sum of all out-degrees is equal to
options: the sum of in-degrees times two
answer: the number of edges
questions.explanation: Each directed edge contributes exactly one to the out-degree of its tail, so the out-degree sum equals the edge count. The in-degree sum does too.

questions.prompt: A directed graph has 9 edges. What is the sum of all in-degrees?
questions.explanation: Each directed edge contributes one to the in-degree of its head, so the sum of in-degrees is nine.

questions.prompt: An undirected graph is connected if
options: every pair of vertices is joined by a path
every vertex has degree at least two
answer: every pair of vertices is joined by a path
questions.explanation: Connectivity requires a path between each pair. A connected graph may have leaves, may have cycles, and needs at least n-1 edges but not exactly n-1.

questions.prompt: A connected undirected graph with n vertices and n-1 edges is necessarily
answer: a tree
questions.explanation: A connected graph with n-1 edges is acyclic; if it had a cycle, removing a cycle edge would keep it connected with fewer than n-1 edges, impossible.

questions.prompt: A tree has 15 vertices. How many edges does it have?
questions.explanation: Every tree with n vertices has n-1 edges, giving 14 for n=15.

questions.prompt: Which statements about trees are true for a finite undirected tree with n>=2 vertices?
answer: It is connected
It is acyclic
It has n-1 edges
questions.explanation: A finite tree is connected, acyclic, and has n-1 edges. A tree with n>=2 has leaves of degree one, so not every vertex has degree two.

questions.prompt: A forest has n vertices and c connected components. How many edges does it have?
answer: n-c
questions.explanation: Each tree component with vi vertices has vi-1 edges. Summing across c components gives n-c edges.

questions.prompt: A forest has 20 vertices and 4 connected components. How many edges does it have?
questions.explanation: A forest with n vertices and c components has n-c edges, so 20-4=16.

questions.prompt: An adjacency matrix for a simple undirected graph with n vertices uses
answer: Theta(n^2) space
questions.explanation: The matrix stores one entry for each ordered pair of vertices, requiring n squared cells even if the graph is sparse.

questions.prompt: An adjacency-list representation of an undirected graph with n vertices and m edges uses
answer: Theta(n+m) space
questions.explanation: It stores a list header per vertex and two adjacency entries per undirected edge, yielding Theta(n+m) storage.

questions.prompt: An undirected graph has 10 vertices and 7 edges. How many adjacency-list edge entries are stored in total?
questions.explanation: Each undirected edge appears once in each endpoint's adjacency list, so seven edges produce fourteen entries.

questions.prompt: Which operations are O(1) in an adjacency-matrix representation, assuming vertex indices are known?
options: Read the degree of u by scanning its row
answer: Test whether edge (u,v) exists
Add an edge (u,v)
questions.explanation: A matrix cell directly tests an edge and can be updated to insert one in O(1). Degree and neighbor enumeration scan the row and take O(n).

questions.prompt: For a graph with n vertices and m edges, BFS using adjacency lists runs in
answer: O(n+m)
questions.explanation: Each vertex is enqueued once and each adjacency entry is examined once, for O(n+m) total time.

questions.prompt: An undirected graph has 9 vertices and 7 edges. How many adjacency-list edge entries will a full BFS inspect?
questions.explanation: Each undirected edge appears in both endpoints' adjacency lists, so seven edges produce 2*7=14 entries that are examined during a full traversal.

questions.prompt: BFS in an unweighted graph finds a shortest path because it explores vertices in
options: nondecreasing number of edges from the source
answer: nondecreasing number of edges from the source
questions.explanation: A FIFO queue processes all vertices at distance d before newly discovered vertices at distance d+1, so first discovery minimizes edge count.

questions.prompt: DFS on a graph with adjacency lists runs in
answer: O(n+m)
questions.explanation: A standard DFS marks each vertex once and scans each adjacency entry once, producing O(n+m) time.

questions.prompt: A connected undirected graph has 9 vertices and 12 edges. How many adjacency entries will a full DFS inspect?
questions.explanation: Each undirected edge contributes two adjacency entries, so 12 edges produce 24 entries inspected in a full traversal.

questions.prompt: In BFS, a vertex should typically be marked visited
options: after all its neighbors are processed
only if it is a leaf
answer: when it is enqueued
questions.explanation: Marking on enqueue prevents multiple neighbors from inserting the same vertex repeatedly and ensures each vertex enters the queue at most once.

questions.prompt: In DFS on an undirected graph, an edge from a vertex to an already visited ancestor is commonly called a
answer: back edge
questions.explanation: In DFS of an undirected graph, non-tree edges connect a vertex to an ancestor and are classified as back edges; undirected graphs do not have forward/cross edges in the same way as directed DFS classification.

questions.prompt: Which data structures are commonly used by iterative graph traversals?
options: Priority queue for ordinary unweighted BFS
answer: Queue for BFS
Stack for DFS
Visited set or array
questions.explanation: BFS uses a queue and DFS uses a stack (explicitly or through recursion). Both require visited state. Ordinary unweighted BFS does not need a priority queue.

questions.prompt: A graph has V vertices and E edges. An adjacency matrix traversal of all possible neighbors for every vertex takes
questions.explanation: For each vertex, the algorithm scans an entire matrix row of V entries, for V rows total V squared work.

questions.prompt: An adjacency matrix for a graph with 7 vertices contains how many cells?
questions.explanation: An adjacency matrix has one cell for each ordered pair of vertices, so it contains 7*7=49 cells.

questions.prompt: A simple undirected graph's adjacency matrix is
options: filled with ones on the diagonal
answer: symmetric with a zero diagonal
questions.explanation: Undirected adjacency is reciprocal, so A[u][v]=A[v][u]. A simple graph has no self-loops, giving zeros on the diagonal.

questions.prompt: Which statements about adjacency lists for an undirected simple graph are true?
options: The sum of list lengths is 2m
An isolated vertex still has a list header
Testing adjacency may take O(degree(u)) by scanning u's list
Space is Theta(n^2) regardless of m
answer: The sum of list lengths is 2m
An isolated vertex still has a list header
Testing adjacency may take O(degree(u)) by scanning u's list
questions.explanation: Each undirected edge contributes two entries; isolated vertices retain list headers; adjacency testing can scan one endpoint list. Space is O(n+m), not always quadratic.

questions.prompt: A graph is sparse when
options: the number of edges is much smaller than V^2
it has more than V^2 edges
answer: the number of edges is much smaller than V^2
questions.explanation: A sparse graph has relatively few edges compared with the maximum possible quadratic number; trees are sparse examples but not the only ones.

questions.prompt: A simple undirected graph with 6 vertices is complete. How many edges does it have?
questions.explanation: A complete simple graph has n(n-1)/2 edges. For n=6 this is 6*5/2=15.

questions.prompt: A complete graph K_n has degree of every vertex equal to
questions.explanation: Each vertex is adjacent to all other n-1 vertices, with no self-loop.

questions.prompt: A bipartite graph is one whose vertices can be partitioned into two sets such that
options: every edge crosses between the sets
every pair in each set has an edge
answer: every edge crosses between the sets
questions.explanation: A bipartite graph admits a two-coloring in which every edge joins opposite color classes. It may have odd-length paths, but it has no odd cycle.

questions.prompt: Which conditions imply an undirected graph is bipartite?
answer: It contains no odd cycle
It is 2-colorable
Every cycle has even length
questions.explanation: Bipartiteness is equivalent to 2-colorability and to having no odd cycle, which also means every cycle is even. Connectivity is not required.

questions.prompt: A cycle graph C_n is bipartite exactly when
options: n is a power of two
answer: n is even
questions.explanation: An even cycle alternates between two color classes and returns consistently; an odd cycle creates a conflict at its closing edge.

questions.prompt: Is the cycle C_9 bipartite? Use 1 for yes and 0 for no.
questions.explanation: C_9 has odd length, so alternating two colors around the cycle forces adjacent endpoints to share a color. It is not bipartite.

questions.prompt: A graph with an odd cycle cannot be
answer: bipartite
questions.explanation: Every cycle in a bipartite graph alternates between two partitions and therefore has even length, so an odd cycle rules bipartiteness out.

questions.prompt: A connected acyclic undirected graph with at least two vertices has
options: at least two vertices of degree one
answer: at least two vertices of degree one
questions.explanation: Every finite tree with at least two vertices has at least two leaves, which can be shown by taking endpoints of a longest simple path.

questions.prompt: A tree has 10 vertices. What is the average vertex degree?
questions.explanation: Its degree sum is 2(n-1)=18, so average degree is 18/10=1.8.

questions.prompt: In an undirected graph, a vertex of degree zero is called
answer: isolated
questions.explanation: A degree-zero vertex has no incident edge and is isolated. A pendant vertex has degree one.

questions.prompt: Which statements about graph connectivity are true?
options: A graph with one connected component is connected
A connected graph has a path between every vertex pair
An isolated vertex forms a connected component
A disconnected graph must have a cycle
answer: A graph with one connected component is connected
A connected graph has a path between every vertex pair
An isolated vertex forms a connected component
questions.explanation: A connected component is a maximal connected set, so an isolated vertex is a component of size one. Disconnected graphs need not contain cycles.

questions.prompt: The number of connected components of an undirected graph can be found by
options: repeated BFS/DFS from each unvisited vertex
answer: repeated BFS/DFS from each unvisited vertex
questions.explanation: Start a traversal from each unvisited vertex. Each traversal discovers one component, and the total traversal work remains O(V+E).

questions.prompt: A directed graph is strongly connected if
options: every vertex can reach every other vertex
the underlying undirected graph is a tree
every vertex has equal in-degree and out-degree
answer: every vertex can reach every other vertex
questions.explanation: Strong connectivity requires a directed path from each vertex to every other vertex; the undirected underlying graph alone does not suffice.

questions.prompt: A directed graph is weakly connected if
options: its underlying undirected graph is connected
each vertex has out-degree at least one
answer: its underlying undirected graph is connected
questions.explanation: Weak connectivity ignores edge directions and asks whether the underlying undirected graph is connected.

questions.prompt: A directed graph has 6 vertices and is strongly connected. What is the minimum possible number of edges?
questions.explanation: Each vertex must have at least one incoming and outgoing edge; a directed cycle through all six vertices achieves strong connectivity using six edges.

questions.prompt: Which statements about directed graphs are true?
options: The sum of out-degrees equals the number of edges
The sum of in-degrees equals the number of edges
A strongly connected graph is weakly connected
A weakly connected graph is always strongly connected
answer: The sum of out-degrees equals the number of edges
The sum of in-degrees equals the number of edges
A strongly connected graph is weakly connected
questions.explanation: Each directed edge contributes once to the out-degree sum and once to the in-degree sum. Strong connectivity implies weak connectivity, but not vice versa.

questions.prompt: A directed acyclic graph (DAG) is a directed graph with
options: equal in-degree and out-degree at every vertex
answer: no directed cycle
questions.explanation: A DAG has no directed cycle. It may contain multiple sources and undirected paths.

questions.prompt: A topological ordering of a directed graph exists if and only if the graph is
answer: a DAG
questions.explanation: A topological order places every edge's source before its destination; such an ordering exists precisely when no directed cycle prevents a consistent order.

questions.prompt: Which algorithms can produce a topological ordering of a DAG?
answer: Kahn's indegree-based algorithm
DFS finishing-time order reversed
questions.explanation: Kahn removes zero-indegree vertices; reverse DFS finishing-time order is also topological for a DAG. Dijkstra and Prim solve different graph problems.

questions.prompt: Kahn's algorithm for topological sorting repeatedly selects a vertex with
answer: indegree zero
questions.explanation: A vertex with indegree zero has no remaining prerequisite edge, so it can be emitted next and its outgoing edges removed.

questions.prompt: A DAG has vertices A,B,C with edges A->B and A->C. How many valid topological orders are there?
questions.explanation: A must appear first, while B and C can appear in either order, giving two topological orders.

questions.prompt: If Kahn's algorithm stops with vertices remaining, the graph contains
answer: a directed cycle
questions.explanation: In a remaining nonempty subgraph where every vertex has positive indegree, following predecessor edges must eventually repeat a vertex, forming a directed cycle.

questions.prompt: A graph is represented by adjacency lists. A DFS can detect a cycle in a directed graph using
answer: visited and recursion-stack/gray-state information
questions.explanation: An edge to a currently active (gray) vertex indicates a back edge and therefore a directed cycle. A simple visited flag alone cannot distinguish active from completed vertices.

questions.prompt: A directed graph has a DFS back edge to a gray vertex. Does this prove a directed cycle exists? Use 1 for yes and 0 for no.
questions.explanation: A gray vertex is an ancestor on the active DFS path. The back edge plus the tree path back to that ancestor forms a directed cycle.

questions.prompt: In an undirected DFS, a visited neighbor should be treated as a cycle edge only if it is not
answer: the parent vertex
questions.explanation: The edge back to the DFS parent is the same undirected tree edge and does not form a cycle. A visited non-parent neighbor indicates a cycle.

questions.prompt: Which statements about graph traversal forests are true?
options: A DFS forest of a disconnected graph has one tree per component
A BFS from one source reaches only its connected component in an undirected graph
Starting BFS from each unvisited vertex can visit every component
A single BFS always visits every vertex in a disconnected graph
answer: A DFS forest of a disconnected graph has one tree per component
A BFS from one source reaches only its connected component in an undirected graph
Starting BFS from each unvisited vertex can visit every component
questions.explanation: A traversal from one source covers only its component. Repeating from unvisited vertices creates a forest with one traversal tree per component and covers all vertices.

questions.prompt: A spanning tree of a connected undirected graph with n vertices contains
answer: n-1 edges
questions.explanation: A spanning tree is connected and acyclic on all n vertices, so it has exactly n-1 edges.

questions.prompt: A connected graph has 11 vertices. How many edges are in any spanning tree?
questions.explanation: Every spanning tree on n vertices has n-1 edges, giving ten.

questions.prompt: A graph with n vertices has a spanning forest with c components. How many forest edges are there?
answer: n-c
questions.explanation: Each component tree contributes vi-1 edges; summing yields total vertices minus component count.

questions.prompt: A graph with 8 vertices has a spanning forest of 5 edges. How many connected components does it have?
questions.explanation: A spanning forest with n vertices and c components has n-c edges. Here 5=8-c, so c=3.

questions.prompt: Which are valid ways to represent a weighted graph?
options: A single degree number per vertex
answer: Adjacency matrix storing weights
Adjacency lists storing neighbor-weight pairs
Edge list storing endpoint-weight triples
questions.explanation: A weighted graph can store weights in a matrix, neighbor-weight adjacency lists, or endpoint-weight edge tuples. Degree counts alone lose weight and endpoint information.

questions.prompt: For an unweighted graph, an adjacency matrix entry A[u][v] is commonly
answer: 1 if edge (u,v) exists and 0 otherwise
questions.explanation: The basic adjacency matrix records edge presence (or absence); distances and traversal times require separate computations or data.

questions.prompt: A connected undirected graph has a bridge e. Removing e
options: increases the number of connected components
answer: increases the number of connected components
questions.explanation: A bridge is an edge whose removal disconnects its component, increasing the number of components by one.

questions.prompt: A vertex is an articulation point if removing it and its incident edges
options: increases the number of connected components
decreases the number of edges by exactly one
answer: increases the number of connected components
questions.explanation: An articulation vertex is a cut vertex whose removal increases the number of connected components of the graph.

questions.prompt: Which conditions characterize a tree on n vertices?
options: It is connected and has n-1 edges
It is acyclic and has n-1 edges
There is exactly one simple path between every pair of vertices
answer: It is connected and has n-1 edges
It is acyclic and has n-1 edges
There is exactly one simple path between every pair of vertices
questions.explanation: For a finite undirected graph, connected plus n-1 edges, acyclic plus n-1 edges, and a unique simple path between every pair are equivalent tree characterizations.

questions.prompt: A tree has 18 vertices and is rooted at one vertex. How many parent-child edges does the rooted tree have?
questions.explanation: Rooting changes no edges; a tree with 18 vertices has 17 edges.

questions.prompt: In a connected undirected graph, a DFS tree edge is
options: an edge used to first discover a vertex
any edge between two visited vertices
answer: an edge used to first discover a vertex
questions.explanation: A DFS tree edge is the edge through which a previously unvisited vertex is discovered from its parent.

questions.prompt: BFS tree distance from the source in an unweighted graph equals
options: shortest-path length in number of edges
minimum total weight for any weights
answer: shortest-path length in number of edges
questions.explanation: BFS levels correspond to minimum edge-count distances from the source in an unweighted graph.

questions.prompt: An unweighted graph has shortest distance 4 edges from source s to vertex v. At what BFS level is v discovered, with source at level 0?
questions.explanation: BFS level counts the number of edges in a shortest path; a four-edge path places v at level 4.

questions.prompt: For a weighted graph with nonnegative edge weights, which algorithm finds single-source shortest paths?
answer: Dijkstra's algorithm
questions.explanation: Dijkstra repeatedly finalizes the closest tentative vertex and supports nonnegative weights. BFS applies when all edges have equal unit cost.

questions.prompt: Why can ordinary BFS fail to find a minimum-weight path when edge weights differ?
options: It minimizes number of edges, not sum of weights
It ignores all vertices with degree one
It only works on directed graphs
answer: It minimizes number of edges, not sum of weights
questions.explanation: BFS orders by hop count. A path with fewer edges can have greater total weight than one with more edges.

questions.prompt: Which algorithms are intended for finding a minimum spanning tree of a connected weighted undirected graph?
answer: Kruskal's algorithm
Prim's algorithm
questions.explanation: Kruskal and Prim construct minimum spanning trees for connected weighted undirected graphs. Dijkstra and Bellman-Ford compute single-source shortest paths.

questions.prompt: Kruskal's algorithm considers edges in
answer: nondecreasing weight order
questions.explanation: It adds the lightest edge that joins different components, so edges are considered in nondecreasing weight order.

questions.prompt: A spanning tree on 9 vertices contains how many edges?
questions.explanation: A spanning tree has n-1 edges, so with nine vertices it contains eight.

questions.prompt: Kruskal's algorithm uses a disjoint-set union structure primarily to
options: test whether an edge's endpoints are already connected
find the shortest path between endpoints
answer: test whether an edge's endpoints are already connected
questions.explanation: If both endpoints are in the same component, adding the edge creates a cycle; DSU supports component checks and unions efficiently.

questions.prompt: A union-find structure with path compression and union by rank has amortized operation time
answer: near-constant, O(alpha(n))
questions.explanation: The combination has inverse-Ackermann amortized time per operation, which is effectively constant for practical input sizes.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Kruskal's algorithm are true?
options: It can process edges sorted by weight
It rejects edges that create a cycle
It produces a minimum spanning forest for a disconnected graph
It requires all edge weights to be distinct for correctness
answer: It can process edges sorted by weight
It rejects edges that create a cycle
It produces a minimum spanning forest for a disconnected graph
questions.explanation: Kruskal sorts edges, rejects cycle-forming edges, and on disconnected input returns a minimum spanning forest. Tied weights are allowed and may yield multiple valid optimal forests.

questions.prompt: Prim's algorithm grows a tree by repeatedly selecting
options: the minimum-weight edge crossing from the current tree to an outside vertex
an arbitrary edge in the graph
the minimum degree vertex regardless of edge weight
answer: the minimum-weight edge crossing from the current tree to an outside vertex
questions.explanation: Prim maintains a cut between included and excluded vertices and adds a minimum-weight crossing edge.

questions.prompt: For a connected graph with V vertices and E edges, Prim's algorithm with a binary heap and adjacency lists runs in
answer: O((V+E) log V)
questions.explanation: Heap operations for vertex priorities contribute O(log V) each across edge updates; standard binary-heap bound is O((V+E) log V).

questions.prompt: A minimum spanning tree has total edge weight 23. If one edge of weight 8 is replaced by an alternative edge of weight 11 while preserving a spanning tree, what is the new total weight?
questions.explanation: The replacement increases total weight by 11-8=3, giving 23+3=26.

questions.prompt: The cut property for MSTs states that a minimum-weight edge crossing a cut
options: belongs to some MST (and if unique, every MST)
can never be in an MST
must be the heaviest edge globally
is irrelevant to Prim and Kruskal
answer: belongs to some MST (and if unique, every MST)
questions.explanation: A lightest edge crossing any cut is safe to include in an MST; if uniquely light, it belongs to every MST.

questions.prompt: The cycle property for a weighted undirected graph says a unique heaviest edge on a cycle
answer: belongs to no MST
questions.explanation: The unique heaviest edge can be omitted: the rest of the cycle provides a path between its endpoints with lower maximum weight, so it cannot be required in an MST.

questions.prompt: A graph with negative edge weights but no negative cycles is handled by which single-source shortest-path algorithm among these?
answer: Bellman-Ford
questions.explanation: Bellman-Ford supports negative edge weights and can detect negative cycles reachable from the source. Dijkstra's correctness requires nonnegative weights.

questions.prompt: Bellman-Ford relaxes every edge V-1 times because
options: a shortest simple path uses at most V-1 edges
it must visit each cycle V-1 times
answer: a shortest simple path uses at most V-1 edges
questions.explanation: A shortest path without a negative cycle can be made simple and therefore contains at most V-1 edges; each pass propagates paths one edge longer.

questions.prompt: A graph has 7 vertices. How many full edge-relaxation passes are sufficient for Bellman-Ford after initialization?
questions.explanation: The standard bound is V-1 passes; with V=7, six passes suffice.

questions.prompt: Which statements about shortest-path algorithms are true?
options: BFS finds shortest paths by edge count in unweighted graphs
Bellman-Ford can detect a reachable negative cycle
Prim computes shortest paths from a source
answer: BFS finds shortest paths by edge count in unweighted graphs
Dijkstra requires nonnegative edge weights
Bellman-Ford can detect a reachable negative cycle
questions.explanation: BFS minimizes edge count in unweighted graphs, Dijkstra assumes nonnegative weights, and Bellman-Ford can detect reachable negative cycles. Prim is an MST algorithm.

questions.prompt: A shortest-path relaxation for edge (u,v,w) updates dist[v] when
options: v has greater degree than u
answer: dist[u]+w<dist[v]
questions.explanation: Relaxation replaces the current estimate when the path through u yields a strictly smaller candidate distance.

questions.prompt: In a directed graph, a negative cycle is relevant to source s shortest paths when
options: all its edges have equal weights
answer: it is reachable from s
questions.explanation: Only a negative cycle reachable from the source can be traversed after starting at s and make path costs arbitrarily small.

questions.prompt: A directed graph has a negative cycle in a component unreachable from source s. Does it make shortest-path distances from s undefined? Use 1 for yes, 0 for no.
questions.explanation: A source cannot reach that cycle, so paths from s cannot traverse it; it does not make source-reachable shortest distances undefined.

questions.prompt: A topological ordering of a DAG can be computed in
answer: O(V+E)
questions.explanation: Kahn's algorithm or DFS scans each vertex and edge a constant number of times, giving linear time in the adjacency-list size.

questions.prompt: A DAG has 8 vertices and 10 edges. What is the time order of Kahn's algorithm using adjacency lists?
questions.explanation: The running time is O(V+E); the sum V+E for this instance is 8+10=18 units of asymptotic input work.

questions.prompt: A DAG has a unique topological ordering if
options: at each Kahn step there is exactly one zero-indegree vertex available
answer: at each Kahn step there is exactly one zero-indegree vertex available
questions.explanation: If multiple zero-indegree choices exist at a step, choosing them in either order yields distinct topological orders. A unique choice at each step ensures uniqueness.

questions.prompt: Which statements about topological orderings are true?
options: Every directed edge goes from an earlier to a later vertex
A directed cycle prevents a topological ordering
A DAG may have multiple valid topological orders
Every DAG has exactly one source
answer: Every directed edge goes from an earlier to a later vertex
A directed cycle prevents a topological ordering
A DAG may have multiple valid topological orders
questions.explanation: Topological order respects every directed edge; a directed cycle makes such an order impossible. A DAG can have several valid orders and can have multiple sources.

questions.prompt: A directed graph has edges A->C, B->C, and C->D. Which sequence is a valid topological ordering?
answer: A,B,C,D
questions.explanation: A and B must precede C, and C must precede D. A,B,C,D satisfies all precedence constraints.

questions.prompt: A DAG has two independent vertices A and B and no edges. How many topological orders does it have?
questions.explanation: With no precedence constraints, either A,B or B,A is valid, giving two orders.

questions.prompt: A directed graph's strongly connected components partition its vertices so that within each component
options: every vertex is reachable from every other vertex
there are no paths between any vertices
answer: every vertex is reachable from every other vertex
questions.explanation: Strong connectivity is mutual reachability; maximal sets of mutually reachable vertices form disjoint SCCs covering the graph.

questions.prompt: Contracting each strongly connected component of a directed graph produces a condensation graph that is
options: strongly connected unless there is one component
answer: a DAG
questions.explanation: If the component graph had a directed cycle, all SCCs on that cycle would be mutually reachable and should be one component. Therefore condensation is acyclic.

questions.prompt: Which algorithms compute strongly connected components in O(V+E) time?
answer: Kosaraju's algorithm
Tarjan's algorithm
questions.explanation: Kosaraju and Tarjan compute SCCs in O(V+E). Kahn topologically sorts a DAG, while Kruskal constructs a minimum spanning forest.

questions.prompt: Kosaraju's SCC algorithm performs DFS on the graph transpose in the order determined by
options: decreasing finishing time from a first DFS
answer: decreasing finishing time from a first DFS
questions.explanation: The first DFS finishing order is reversed; processing the transpose in decreasing finish time separates SCCs correctly.

questions.prompt: A directed graph has 5 vertices, each reachable from every other vertex. How many strongly connected components does it have?
questions.explanation: All vertices are mutually reachable, so the entire graph is a single maximal strongly connected component.

questions.prompt: A directed graph with V vertices is strongly connected if
options: for every ordered pair u,v there is a directed path u to v
answer: for every ordered pair u,v there is a directed path u to v
questions.explanation: Strong connectivity requires directed reachability for every ordered pair, not a specific degree or edge count.

questions.prompt: A graph algorithm uses a visited array initialized false. Why should each vertex be marked before recursively exploring its neighbors?
options: To prevent infinite recursion on cycles and duplicate processing
To ensure adjacency lists are sorted
To reduce the number of graph edges
answer: To prevent infinite recursion on cycles and duplicate processing
questions.explanation: Marking on discovery prevents revisiting a vertex through cycles or multiple paths and limits processing to once per vertex.

questions.prompt: A singly linked list contains keys 1,2,...,n in this order. Which operation can delete the node containing key n in O(1) time if only a pointer to that node is given?
options: Yes, by setting its next to null
Yes, by copying its predecessor's next value
answer: None in general
questions.explanation: Without the predecessor pointer, the previous link cannot be changed; copying the successor's data fails for the tail. The head pointer also does not identify the predecessor.

questions.prompt: A pointer p addresses a non-tail node in a singly linked list. Which method deletes p in O(1) time when node payloads may be copied?
options: Copy successor payload into p and bypass successor
answer: Copy successor payload into p and bypass successor
questions.explanation: Copying the successor's payload into p and linking p to the successor's successor removes the logical element in constant time, provided p is not the tail and payload copying is allowed.

questions.prompt: A singly linked list has 20 nodes. Starting only at head, how many next-pointer traversals are needed to reach the node at zero-based position 7?
questions.explanation: The head is at position zero, so exactly k links are followed to reach position k.

questions.prompt: A circular singly linked list has a tail pointer t and n>=1 nodes. Which pointer identifies its first node?
answer: t.next
questions.explanation: In a circular list, the tail's next link points to the head; this provides head access in constant time.

questions.prompt: A singly linked list supports insertion at the front and deletion at the front. What is the worst-case time for each?
answer: O(1) and O(1)
questions.explanation: Insertion changes the new node's next and the head pointer. Deletion advances head to head.next. Both take constant pointer operations.

questions.prompt: A singly linked list is unsorted and has no tail pointer. Which operations have worst-case O(1) time?
options: Insert a node at the head
Append a node at the tail
Find whether a given key occurs
answer: Insert a node at the head
Delete the head node
questions.explanation: Head insertion and head deletion require constant pointer updates. Appending without a tail pointer and searching may require traversing all n nodes.

questions.prompt: A linked list has 25 nodes. A complete traversal follows the next pointer of every node except the last. How many next-pointer traversals occur?
questions.explanation: Each of the first n-1 nodes links to its successor; the last node has no successor link to follow.

questions.prompt: Two nonempty singly linked lists are concatenated in O(1) time when both head and tail pointers are maintained. Which update is required?
options: First tail.next becomes second head, then first tail becomes second tail
No update is possible in O(1)
answer: First tail.next becomes second head, then first tail becomes second tail
questions.explanation: The first tail is linked to the second head, and the resulting tail is the second list's tail. Both list endpoints are available directly.

questions.prompt: A singly linked list is represented only by a head pointer. What is the worst-case time to append one node?
answer: O(n)
questions.explanation: The implementation must traverse to the last node to set its next field. Without a tail pointer this scan is linear.

questions.prompt: For a doubly linked list with head and tail pointers, which operations take O(1) time?
options: Insert before a node when its pointer is given
Delete a node when its pointer is given
Find the predecessor of a node when its pointer is given
Find a key by value in an unsorted list
answer: Insert before a node when its pointer is given
Delete a node when its pointer is given
Find the predecessor of a node when its pointer is given
questions.explanation: Both neighbor links permit constant-time local insertion, deletion, and predecessor access. Value search remains linear in the worst case.

questions.prompt: A doubly linked list node x is deleted from a nonempty list. Which pair of neighbor updates is generally required?
answer: x.prev.next=x.next and x.next.prev=x.prev
questions.explanation: For an interior node, reconnecting the predecessor to the successor and the successor to the predecessor removes x. Boundary cases update head or tail instead.

questions.prompt: A circular singly linked list contains 7 nodes. Starting at head, how many next-pointer traversals return to head for the first time?
questions.explanation: A cycle through all seven distinct nodes returns to its starting node after exactly seven link traversals.

questions.prompt: Floyd's tortoise-and-hare algorithm starts both pointers at the head of a list with a cycle of length lambda and a noncyclic prefix of length mu. What is its worst-case time order?
answer: O(mu+lambda)
questions.explanation: The pointers advance one and two links per iteration. They meet within O(mu+lambda) steps, requiring linear time in the prefix plus cycle length.

questions.prompt: Floyd's cycle-detection algorithm uses two pointers advancing by one and two links. Which statement is correct for an acyclic list of n nodes?
options: It terminates after O(n) steps without a meeting
It always meets at the tail
answer: It terminates after O(n) steps without a meeting
questions.explanation: On an acyclic list the fast pointer eventually reaches null (or its next is null), so the algorithm terminates after linear traversal with constant extra space.

questions.prompt: A singly linked list has a cycle consisting of 5 nodes. Once Floyd's slow and fast pointers are both within the cycle, what is the maximum number of iterations until they meet?
questions.explanation: Their relative speed is one node per iteration modulo the cycle length. Any initial separation is removed in at most lambda iterations, here five.

questions.prompt: A list is reversed iteratively using prev, cur, and next pointers. After processing the first k nodes of an n-node list, which invariant holds?
options: prev heads the reversed prefix and cur heads the untouched suffix
prev is always null and cur heads the reversed prefix
The original head still heads the whole list
The tail points to the original head
answer: prev heads the reversed prefix and cur heads the untouched suffix
questions.explanation: Each processed link is reversed toward prev, so prev is the head of the reversed prefix and cur begins the remaining original-order suffix.

questions.prompt: A singly linked list of 9 nodes is reversed iteratively. How many next pointers of existing nodes must be redirected?
questions.explanation: Every original edge between consecutive nodes is reversed; a list of nine nodes has eight such edges.

questions.prompt: To find the middle node of a singly linked list in one pass using slow and fast pointers, how should they advance?
options: Slow by one and fast by two links
Slow by two and fast by one link
Fast by three and slow by two links
answer: Slow by one and fast by two links
questions.explanation: The fast pointer traverses twice as quickly. When it reaches the end, slow has traversed approximately half the list.

questions.prompt: A list has 8 nodes. With slow initialized at head and fast at head, and the loop condition fast!=null && fast.next!=null followed by slow=slow.next and fast=fast.next.next, where does slow stop?
answer: At zero-based index 4
questions.explanation: For an even-length list under this initialization and loop, slow advances four times and stops at index 4, the second of the two central nodes.

questions.prompt: Which statements about singly linked-list traversal are true?
options: Accessing position k from head takes O(k) time
Finding the predecessor of a given node pointer may require O(n) time
A tail pointer alone makes arbitrary indexed access O(1)
Searching an unsorted list is O(n) in the worst case
answer: Accessing position k from head takes O(k) time
Finding the predecessor of a given node pointer may require O(n) time
Searching an unsorted list is O(n) in the worst case
questions.explanation: Links provide sequential access, so indexed access and predecessor search may scan linearly. A tail pointer only helps at the end, and unsorted key search is linear.

questions.prompt: Two sorted singly linked lists of lengths m and n are merged into sorted order using only pointer relinking. What is the worst-case time?
answer: Theta(m+n)
questions.explanation: At each step the smaller current head is removed from one list and appended to output. Each node is examined and linked a constant number of times, giving linear time in the total length.

questions.prompt: Two sorted lists contain 12 and 9 nodes. During a standard merge, how many node selections are made if their keys interleave and the final remaining suffix is attached without examining its nodes?
questions.explanation: Until one list empties, 20 nodes are selected individually; the remaining one node is attached as a suffix without a comparison.

questions.prompt: A singly linked list is sorted by key. Which sorting algorithm is most appropriate when stable sorting and O(1) auxiliary pointer storage are desired?
options: Heap sort in an array copy
answer: Merge sort
questions.explanation: Merge sort is stable and can be implemented by relinking nodes with constant auxiliary pointer storage. Its worst-case time is O(n log n).

questions.prompt: Why is insertion sort often efficient on a nearly sorted linked list?
options: Few nodes need to be moved through the list
It uses binary search to locate every insertion point
It always performs O(log n) comparisons
answer: Few nodes need to be moved through the list
questions.explanation: In a nearly sorted sequence, each element moves only a small distance. Linked-list insertion itself is constant time once the position is reached, though locating it still entails traversal.

questions.prompt: A linked-list merge sort splits the list using slow and fast pointers. What should be done before recursively sorting the two halves?
options: Cut the link at the midpoint
Copy all nodes to an array
answer: Cut the link at the midpoint
questions.explanation: The midpoint link must be set to null so that recursive calls receive disjoint finite lists and each recursion level reduces the problem size.

questions.prompt: A top-down merge sort on a list of 64 nodes splits into halves until singleton lists. How many split levels are there?
questions.explanation: Repeated halving gives sizes 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1, which is six splits before singleton leaves.

questions.prompt: Which properties hold for a correctly implemented linked-list merge sort?
options: Worst-case time is O(n log n)
It can use O(1) auxiliary node storage aside from recursion stack
It requires O(1) time to access the middle node
answer: Worst-case time is O(n log n)
It can be stable
It can use O(1) auxiliary node storage aside from recursion stack
questions.explanation: Each merge level processes all nodes and there are logarithmically many levels. Choosing from the left list on equal keys preserves stability; midpoint finding is linear per level.

questions.prompt: Inserting a new node after a given node x in a singly linked list requires which order of pointer assignments to avoid losing the suffix?
answer: new.next=x.next, then x.next=new
questions.explanation: The new node must first retain the old successor. Then x can point to the new node; reversing the order creates a self-loop or loses the suffix.

questions.prompt: A singly linked list has head H and tail T. The only node is deleted. What must the resulting endpoints be?
options: head=null and tail remains old T
head remains old H and tail=null
answer: head=null and tail=null
questions.explanation: After deleting the sole node, the list is empty, so both endpoint pointers must be set to null to preserve the representation invariant.

questions.prompt: A queue is implemented by a singly linked list with head and tail pointers. Which operations are both O(1)?
options: Enqueue at tail and dequeue at head
Enqueue at head and dequeue at tail
Enqueue at tail without a tail pointer and dequeue at head
answer: Enqueue at tail and dequeue at head
questions.explanation: Appending via tail and removing via head each need constant pointer updates. Removing at tail from a singly linked representation would require finding its predecessor.

questions.prompt: A queue implemented with a singly linked list has 4 elements. After 11 enqueues and 8 dequeues, how many elements remain, assuming no underflow?
questions.explanation: The final length is 4+11-8=7, and the operation sequence never requires more than the available elements to be removed.

questions.prompt: For a circular singly linked list with a tail pointer, which operations can be O(1)?
options: Delete the rear node without a predecessor pointer
answer: Insert at the front
Insert at the rear
Delete the front node
questions.explanation: The tail.next identifies the head, allowing constant-time front and rear insertion and front deletion. Rear deletion needs the node before the tail, which requires a scan.

questions.prompt: A circular singly linked list stores only a tail pointer. Which expression gives the head?
answer: tail.next
questions.explanation: The tail's successor is defined as the head in a circular singly linked list.

questions.prompt: A circular singly linked list with tail pointer has one node x. After deleting the front node, what is the new tail?
answer: Null
questions.explanation: Deleting the sole node empties the structure, so tail must be set to null rather than retain a pointer into the removed cycle.

questions.prompt: A circular list has n=10 nodes and a pointer to its head. What is the minimum number of next links followed to reach the tail?
questions.explanation: The tail is the last node before returning to the head, so from zero-based head position 0 it is reached after n-1=9 links.

questions.prompt: A doubly linked list supports insertion before a node x. If x.prev is null, what additional pointer update is required after linking the new node?
options: Update head to the new node
Update tail to the new node
answer: Update head to the new node
questions.explanation: When x is the current head, its predecessor is absent. The new node becomes the list head; internal neighbor updates alone do not update the external endpoint.

questions.prompt: To delete the tail of a doubly linked list in O(1), which representation is sufficient?
options: A tail pointer and prev links
A head pointer only and next links
A tail pointer and next links only
answer: A tail pointer and prev links
questions.explanation: The tail pointer locates the node and its prev link locates the new tail directly. A head-only singly linked representation must scan for the predecessor.

questions.prompt: A doubly linked list has 15 nodes. How many prev fields contain null in a standard non-circular representation?
questions.explanation: Only the head has no predecessor, so exactly one prev field is null.

questions.prompt: Which statements about memory use of linked lists are generally true compared with a packed array of the same payload type?
options: Each node needs one or more pointer fields
Nodes may have allocation and alignment overhead
Sequential traversal may have poorer cache locality
A linked list always uses less memory
answer: Each node needs one or more pointer fields
Nodes may have allocation and alignment overhead
Sequential traversal may have poorer cache locality
questions.explanation: Pointer fields and allocator metadata add overhead, while pointer chasing harms locality. Arrays typically avoid per-element links and have contiguous storage.

questions.prompt: A singly linked list is represented by a pointer to its head. What is the space complexity of reversing it iteratively, excluding the list nodes themselves?
questions.explanation: The iterative algorithm uses a fixed number of pointers (prev, current, next) independent of list length, so its auxiliary space is constant.

questions.prompt: A linked list stores an integer at each node. Which pointer update is sufficient to insert x before the head in a singly linked list?
answer: x.next=head; head=x
questions.explanation: The new node must point to the old head and then become the new head. This works for both empty and nonempty lists if the empty-list tail is also updated when present.

questions.prompt: A singly linked list has head and tail pointers. A new node is inserted into an empty list. What should both pointers reference afterward?
options: head references new node, tail remains null
head remains null, tail references new node
answer: The new node
questions.explanation: A one-node list has the same node as both its first and last element; both endpoint pointers must refer to it.

questions.prompt: A linked list has 20 nodes. An algorithm repeatedly advances a pointer by 3 links while at least 3 links remain. How many advances occur before it stops?
questions.explanation: Six advances move 18 links. Only two links remain, insufficient for another three-link advance.

questions.prompt: Given only the head pointer of a singly linked list, what is the worst-case time to determine its length?
answer: Theta(n)
questions.explanation: Every node must be visited to count the list in the absence of a separately maintained length field, requiring linear time.

questions.prompt: A linked list stores a maintained size field. Which operation then becomes O(1) solely due to that field?
options: Access the node at index k
answer: Return the list length
questions.explanation: The size field directly stores the length. It does not provide links to a median, key, or arbitrary indexed node.

questions.prompt: For an unsorted singly linked list with distinct keys, which tasks require Theta(n) time in the worst case when only the head pointer is available?
options: Insert a new node at the head
answer: Find a particular key
Find the maximum key
Compute the number of nodes
questions.explanation: Searching, maximum computation, and counting need a scan. Head insertion is a constant number of pointer assignments.

questions.prompt: A singly linked list has an even number n of nodes. The goal is to return the first middle node. Which loop condition with slow=head and fast=head achieves this?
answer: while fast.next!=null and fast.next.next!=null
questions.explanation: This loop advances slow once while fast advances twice only when two fast steps are available. On even n, slow stops at index n/2-1, the first middle node.

questions.prompt: A list has 11 nodes. A slow/fast midpoint algorithm advances slow one node and fast two nodes per loop, with both starting at head. How many loop iterations occur before fast reaches the last node?
questions.explanation: Fast advances two positions per iteration. After five iterations it is at index 10, the last node of the 11-node list.

questions.prompt: Two singly linked lists intersect by sharing a suffix. Which property must hold from their first common node onward?
options: All subsequent node addresses are identical
The lists must have equal lengths
Their head pointers must be equal
answer: All subsequent node addresses are identical
questions.explanation: In an acyclic singly linked structure, once paths meet at a node, the shared node's single next pointer forces every later node to be shared too.

questions.prompt: Two acyclic singly linked lists with head pointers h1 and h2 are checked for intersection by aligning their lengths, then advancing both pointers together. Why does this work?
options: The pointers then have equal distance to any shared suffix
The lists must have equal lengths
The algorithm compares node values only
answer: The pointers then have equal distance to any shared suffix
questions.explanation: After alignment, each pointer has the same number of links remaining. If a suffix is shared, they arrive at its first node simultaneously; otherwise both reach null together.

questions.prompt: Two linked lists have lengths 14 and 9. By how many nodes should the longer list's pointer advance before simultaneous traversal to test intersection?
questions.explanation: Advancing the longer list by the length difference aligns the remaining path lengths, so 14-9=5 steps are needed.

questions.prompt: Which methods can detect whether two singly linked lists intersect by node identity in O(m+n) time and O(1) extra space?
options: Length alignment followed by simultaneous traversal
Switch each pointer to the other head after reaching null
Hash all node addresses in an auxiliary set
answer: Length alignment followed by simultaneous traversal
Switch each pointer to the other head after reaching null
questions.explanation: Length alignment and pointer switching exploit the shared-suffix property with constant extra storage. Hashing uses O(m+n) extra space; equal values do not establish shared identity.

questions.prompt: A list with n nodes is rotated right by k positions, where k may exceed n. Which normalized rotation count should be used?
answer: k mod n
questions.explanation: A rotation by n returns the original list, so only the remainder k modulo n changes the result. The empty-list case is handled separately.

questions.prompt: A list of 12 nodes is rotated right by 29 positions. How many positions is this equivalent to?
questions.explanation: 29 mod 12 equals 5, so a right rotation by 29 is equivalent to a right rotation by five.

questions.prompt: A singly linked list is rotated right by k, with 0<k<n. Which node becomes the new tail?
options: The node at zero-based index n-k-1
answer: The node at zero-based index n-k-1
questions.explanation: The last k nodes become the prefix. Therefore the node preceding that suffix, at index n-k-1, becomes the new tail.

questions.prompt: A singly linked list is partitioned around pivot x while preserving relative order within the less-than and greater-or-equal groups. What auxiliary structure can support a stable O(n) partition?
options: A stack of all nodes followed by sorting
answer: Two head-tail chains
questions.explanation: Appending each visited node to one of two tail-tracked chains preserves traversal order and performs constant work per node, resulting in a stable linear partition.

questions.prompt: A linked-list algorithm partitions nodes into two stable groups using tail pointers. Which implementation details prevent accidental cycles or stale links?
options: Detach each node from its old successor before appending it
Terminate both resulting tails with null
Maintain separate head and tail pointers for both groups
Append each node by scanning from each group's head
answer: Detach each node from its old successor before appending it
Terminate both resulting tails with null
Maintain separate head and tail pointers for both groups
questions.explanation: Detaching prevents retaining unintended old-chain links; null-terminating tails closes the output chains; endpoint pointers allow constant-time append. Repeated scans can make the algorithm quadratic.

questions.prompt: An algorithm removes all nodes with key x from a singly linked list in one pass. Why is a dummy head node useful?
options: It makes deletion of the original head use the same predecessor-link update
It makes key search constant time
It eliminates the need to examine node values
answer: It makes deletion of the original head use the same predecessor-link update
questions.explanation: With a dummy preceding the real head, every removable node has a predecessor, including the original head. The same bypass operation handles all positions.

questions.prompt: A list has 13 nodes, of which 4 contain key x. A one-pass filter removes all matches. How many nodes remain?
questions.explanation: The filter retains the 13-4=9 nodes whose keys differ from x.

questions.prompt: A singly linked list is deduplicated in one pass using a hash set of seen values. What are expected time and auxiliary space complexities?
options: O(n) expected time and O(n) space
O(n squared) time and O(1) space
O(log n) time and O(1) space
answer: O(n) expected time and O(n) space
questions.explanation: Each node's value is checked and inserted in expected constant time, while the set may store every distinct value, producing expected linear time and linear extra space.

questions.prompt: A linked list is represented by a pointer to its first node. To create a deep copy, which information must be reproduced?
options: Each node's payload and next-link structure
Only the values in reverse order
answer: Each node's payload and next-link structure
