questions.explanation: A deep copy creates distinct nodes with matching payloads and matching link relationships. Reusing original addresses would create aliases rather than a copy.

questions.prompt: A linked list has n nodes and is copied by repeatedly appending each copied node while maintaining a copy-tail pointer. What is the running time?
answer: Theta(n)
questions.explanation: Each original node is visited once, and each copied node is appended with a constant-time tail update, giving Theta(n) time.

questions.prompt: A linked list contains 18 nodes. A traversal to copy it performs one payload-copy operation per node. How many payload-copy operations occur?
questions.explanation: One distinct copied node is constructed for each of the 18 original nodes.

questions.prompt: In a singly linked list, an operation receives a pointer to node x and must insert a node immediately before x in O(1). Which extra information generally makes this possible?
options: A pointer to the tail only
answer: A pointer to x's predecessor
questions.explanation: The singly linked predecessor link points toward x, not from x to its predecessor. Having the predecessor directly allows constant-time rewiring.

questions.prompt: Which statements compare singly and doubly linked lists correctly?
options: Doubly linked nodes use extra pointer storage
A doubly linked list can delete a known node in O(1) with local updates
A singly linked list can be traversed backward from an arbitrary node in O(1)
A singly linked list uses less link storage per node
answer: Doubly linked nodes use extra pointer storage
A doubly linked list can delete a known node in O(1) with local updates
A singly linked list uses less link storage per node
questions.explanation: Prev links add storage and enable backward navigation and local known-node deletion. Singly linked nodes cannot directly follow a predecessor link.

questions.prompt: A doubly linked list is reversed in place by swapping next and prev at every node and exchanging head and tail. What is the time complexity?
answer: Theta(n)
questions.explanation: Every node's two links must be swapped once, so the operation takes linear time; exchanging endpoints is constant additional work.

questions.prompt: A doubly linked list has 8 nodes. An in-place reversal swaps next and prev once per node. How many nodes are processed?
questions.explanation: Each node must have its next and prev references exchanged, so all eight nodes are processed.

questions.prompt: A doubly linked list node x is inserted between nodes a and b. Which assignments establish the correct four neighbor relationships?
answer: x.prev=a; x.next=b; a.next=x; b.prev=x
questions.explanation: All four updates are needed: link x to both neighbors and link each neighbor back to x, preserving bidirectional consistency.

questions.prompt: A non-circular doubly linked list of n nodes is traversed forward from head. How many next links are followed?
questions.explanation: There is one next link between each adjacent pair, giving n-1 links; the final node has no next successor.

questions.prompt: Which invariants should hold in a non-circular doubly linked list with at least one node?
options: For every adjacent pair x,y, x.next=y implies y.prev=x
head.next is null for every list of size greater than one
answer: head.prev is null
tail.next is null
For every adjacent pair x,y, x.next=y implies y.prev=x
questions.explanation: The boundary links are null and each forward adjacency has a matching backward link. The head has a successor when there is more than one node.

questions.prompt: A linked list is used to implement a stack. Which endpoint choice gives O(1) push and pop with a singly linked list?
options: Use the head for both operations
Push at tail and pop at tail
Push at head and pop at tail
answer: Use the head for both operations
questions.explanation: Head insertion and removal are constant time. Tail removal in a singly linked list would require finding the predecessor by scanning.

questions.prompt: A stack implemented by head insertion contains 6 elements. It receives 9 pushes and 4 pops. What is the final number of elements?
questions.explanation: The size changes by +9 and -4, so 6+9-4=11.

questions.prompt: A linked-list queue uses a head pointer for dequeue and tail pointer for enqueue. What must be done on dequeue when the queue contains exactly one node?
options: Set both head and tail to null
answer: Set both head and tail to null
questions.explanation: Removing the sole node empties the queue. Both endpoint pointers must be cleared to avoid a stale tail pointer.

questions.prompt: A circular doubly linked list has sentinel node s. Which relationship holds in an empty list?
options: s.next points to a separate head node
answer: s.next=s and s.prev=s
questions.explanation: A sentinel-based circular representation points both links back to the sentinel when empty, simplifying boundary insertions and deletions.

questions.prompt: A circular doubly linked list with a sentinel has 5 data nodes. How many next-link traversals are needed from the sentinel to return to it after visiting all data nodes?
questions.explanation: The traversal follows sentinel-to-first, four internal links, and last-to-sentinel, for six next links total.

questions.prompt: In a sentinel-based doubly linked list, deleting a known data node x can use the same operation regardless of whether x is first or last because
options: the sentinel guarantees x has both a predecessor and a successor
the sentinel stores every node's key
answer: the sentinel guarantees x has both a predecessor and a successor
questions.explanation: The sentinel participates in the circular or boundary structure so endpoint nodes still have neighboring link targets, allowing uniform local bypass updates.

questions.prompt: Which benefits are commonly provided by sentinel nodes in linked-list implementations?
options: They eliminate null checks at list ends in a circular design
They make searching for a key O(1)
They may use one extra node of storage
answer: They can simplify boundary-case code
They eliminate null checks at list ends in a circular design
They may use one extra node of storage
questions.explanation: Sentinels unify endpoint handling and can eliminate null boundaries in circular layouts, at the cost of a dummy node. They do not accelerate value search.

questions.prompt: A singly linked list represents a polynomial by nodes (coefficient, exponent) sorted by decreasing exponent. To add two such polynomials, what is the time complexity for lists of m and n terms?
answer: O(m+n)
questions.explanation: A merge-style walk compares current exponents and emits or combines the larger/equal exponent terms. Each input term is consumed at most once.

questions.prompt: Two sparse polynomials have 8 and 6 terms, with exactly 3 matching exponents. If addition combines matching terms and retains all nonzero results, how many output terms are produced?
questions.explanation: The union of exponent sets has 8+6-3=11 exponents, and each yields one term under the no-zero-cancellation assumption.

questions.prompt: A linked list stores a sparse vector of dimension N with k nonzero entries. What is the storage order if each nonzero index and value is stored once?
answer: Theta(k)
questions.explanation: Only the k nonzero coordinates need nodes, so storage is proportional to k rather than the full dimension N.

questions.prompt: A sorted linked list stores n distinct keys. What is the worst-case time to determine the rank of a given key using only next links?
answer: Theta(n)
questions.explanation: The list must be traversed to count preceding keys or reach the target. Without random access or an auxiliary index, the scan is linear.

questions.prompt: A linked-list algorithm inserts n keys one by one at the correct position in an initially empty sorted singly linked list. What is the worst-case total time?
answer: Theta(n squared)
questions.explanation: Each insertion may scan a linear fraction of the current list to find its position. Summing 0+1+...+(n-1) gives Theta(n squared).

questions.prompt: A sorted list has 10 nodes. Inserting a new minimum key by scanning from the head and then linking it before the first node requires how many key comparisons?
questions.explanation: The first node is compared once and found greater than the new minimum, after which insertion occurs before it.

questions.prompt: A linked list is already sorted, and a new key is known to be greater than every existing key. With a tail pointer, what is the insertion time?
questions.explanation: Since the tail is directly available and the new key belongs after it, only a constant number of link and endpoint updates are required.

questions.prompt: Which linked-list operations can be supported in O(1) worst-case time by maintaining both head and tail pointers in a singly linked list?
answer: Insert at front
Insert at rear
Delete from front
questions.explanation: Head insertion, tail insertion, and head deletion need direct endpoint pointers. Tail deletion still requires locating the predecessor.

questions.prompt: A list node contains only a next pointer and payload. Which operation inherently cannot follow a link backward from a node to its predecessor?
answer: Move to predecessor in O(1)
questions.explanation: A singly linked node stores only a forward link, so its predecessor cannot be reached directly from that node.

questions.prompt: A list is traversed with a pointer that advances 4 nodes per iteration until fewer than 4 nodes remain. For 23 nodes, how many iterations occur?
questions.explanation: The pointer reaches positions 4, 8, 12, 16, and 20. Four nodes remain after that, so it performs five iterations and then stops if the condition requires at least four links before advancing.

questions.prompt: A program deletes a node x from a singly linked list by assigning x=x.next. Why does this not delete x from the list?
options: It changes only the local pointer and not the predecessor link
It changes the head in all cases
It is valid only for the tail
answer: It changes only the local pointer and not the predecessor link
questions.explanation: Removing x from a singly linked chain requires changing the predecessor's next field (or the head pointer). Reassigning a local pointer does not alter any incoming link.

questions.prompt: A singly linked list uses a dummy node before its first data node. What does the external head pointer typically reference?
answer: The dummy node
questions.explanation: In the common dummy-head representation, head refers to the sentinel, and the first data node is head.next. This makes front insertion and deletion uniform.

questions.prompt: A dummy-head list has 0 data nodes. If the sentinel is counted as an allocated node, how many nodes are allocated in total?
questions.explanation: The empty list still contains its single dummy sentinel node, so the allocated-node count is one.

questions.prompt: In a singly linked list, a node x has next=y and y has next=z. After deleting y by bypassing it, which assignment is needed?
answer: x.next=z
questions.explanation: The predecessor x must link directly to y's successor z. This removes y from the path traversed from the head.

questions.prompt: Which conditions are needed for an iterative singly linked-list reversal to work correctly without losing nodes?
options: Save the original next pointer before redirecting current.next
Advance current to the saved next pointer
Set every node's next to the original head
answer: Save the original next pointer before redirecting current.next
Advance current to the saved next pointer
Initialize prev to null
questions.explanation: Saving the suffix before overwriting a link preserves access to remaining nodes. prev starts null to make the new tail terminate; pointing every link to the old head is incorrect.

questions.prompt: A linked list contains a cycle. Why can a standard traversal that stops only when current becomes null fail to terminate?
options: No node in the cycle has a null next pointer
The head pointer becomes null immediately
Every cycle has a null link
The cycle makes next pointers undefined
answer: No node in the cycle has a null next pointer
questions.explanation: Once traversal enters a cycle, following next repeatedly revisits nodes and never reaches null, so a null-only termination test loops forever.

questions.prompt: A list has a noncyclic prefix of 4 nodes followed by a cycle of 6 nodes. What is the number of distinct nodes reachable from head?
questions.explanation: The reachable structure consists of four prefix nodes plus six distinct cycle nodes, totaling ten.

questions.prompt: Floyd cycle detection finds a meeting point. To locate the cycle entry, what is the standard next step?
options: Reset one pointer to head and move both one step at a time
Reset both pointers to head and move one two steps at a time
Keep moving fast twice as fast until null
answer: Reset one pointer to head and move both one step at a time
questions.explanation: After a meeting, one pointer returns to head. Advancing both at equal speed makes them meet at the cycle entry because of the distance relationship between prefix and cycle lengths.

questions.prompt: In a list with prefix length mu and cycle length lambda, how many distinct nodes are reachable before traversal repeats a node?
answer: mu+lambda
questions.explanation: The prefix nodes are visited once, then each of the lambda cycle nodes is visited once before the first repeated node is encountered.

questions.prompt: A cyclic list has prefix length 7 and cycle length 4. After how many next-pointer traversals from head is the first repeated node reached?
questions.explanation: The traversal visits seven distinct prefix nodes and then four distinct cycle nodes; after 11 links it returns to the cycle entry, the first repeated node.

questions.prompt: Two linked lists are structurally equal in values but have no shared node addresses. Do they intersect as data structures?
options: No, intersection is based on shared node identity
answer: No, intersection is based on shared node identity
questions.explanation: List intersection refers to shared node objects, not equal payloads. Structurally separate nodes with identical values do not constitute an intersection.

questions.prompt: Which are common applications where linked structures are useful?
options: Representing a dynamically growing sequence with frequent insertions
Implementing adjacency lists for sparse graphs
Providing O(1) arbitrary indexed access in a standard singly linked list
answer: Representing a dynamically growing sequence with frequent insertions
Implementing adjacency lists for sparse graphs
Implementing stacks and queues
questions.explanation: Linked structures support flexible insertion and are used for graph adjacency lists, stacks, and queues. Arbitrary indexed access requires traversal in a standard singly linked list.

questions.prompt: A singly linked list stores n nodes and is traversed to print each payload. What is the asymptotic running time and auxiliary space if output is streamed directly?
options: Theta(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space
Theta(n squared) time and O(n) space
Theta(log n) time and O(1) space
Theta(n) time and Theta(n) auxiliary space
answer: Theta(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space
questions.explanation: Each node is visited and emitted once. If output is streamed rather than accumulated in a separate collection, only a constant amount of extra state is needed.

questions.prompt: Let f(0)=0 and f(n)=n+f(n-1) for n>0. What is f(6)?
questions.explanation: Expanding the recurrence gives the sum 1+2+3+4+5+6, which equals 21.

questions.prompt: A function makes one recursive call on n-1 until n=0. What is the maximum recursion depth on input n?
answer: Theta(n)
questions.explanation: There is one active frame for n,n-1,...,0, so stack depth grows linearly with n.

questions.prompt: For T(n)=T(n-1)+1 with T(1)=1, what is the asymptotic running time?
answer: Theta(n)
questions.explanation: The recurrence decreases the argument by one and does constant work at each of n levels.

questions.prompt: A recursive factorial returns 1 at n=0 and n*f(n-1) otherwise. What does f(5) return?
questions.explanation: The recurrence multiplies 5*4*3*2*1*1, giving 120.

questions.prompt: For T(n)=2T(n/2)+1 with size-one leaves, how many leaves are in the recursion tree when n is a power of two?
answer: n
questions.explanation: Each level doubles subproblems. At depth log2(n), there are 2^log2(n)=n leaves.

questions.prompt: A recursive function makes one call on floor(n/3) until n<=1 and performs constant work per call. What is its maximum depth?
answer: Theta(log n)
questions.explanation: Each call reduces the input by a factor of three, so the nested call count grows logarithmically.

questions.prompt: For F(0)=0, F(1)=1, F(n)=F(n-1)+F(n-2), how many calls does naive evaluation of F(5) make including base calls?
questions.explanation: The call-count recurrence is C(n)=1+C(n-1)+C(n-2), C(0)=C(1)=1. Evaluating it gives C(5)=15.

questions.prompt: A recursive routine makes two calls on n-1 and constant work, with T(0)=1. What is its asymptotic call count?
answer: Theta(2^n)
questions.explanation: The recurrence T(n)=2T(n-1)+O(1) creates an exponentially growing binary call tree.

questions.prompt: A recursive traversal visits every node in a binary tree exactly once and performs constant work per node. What is the running time for n nodes?
answer: Theta(n)
questions.explanation: The function performs constant work at each of n nodes, yielding linear total time.

questions.prompt: What is the primary role of a reachable base case in recursion?
options: To stop further calls on sufficiently small inputs
To ensure every call branches twice
answer: To stop further calls on sufficiently small inputs
questions.explanation: A base case returns without another recursive call and prevents unbounded descent.

questions.prompt: A recursive factorial computes n*f(n-1) after the recursive call returns. Is this call in tail position?
options: No, multiplication remains after the call
Yes, every single recursive call is tail-recursive
No, because it has a base case
answer: No, multiplication remains after the call
questions.explanation: The caller still multiplies the returned value by n, so computation remains after the call; it is not tail-recursive.

questions.prompt: If recursion depth is d and each activation record uses O(1) words, what stack space is used?
answer: O(d)
questions.explanation: There are at most d simultaneously active constant-size activation records, giving O(d) stack space.

questions.prompt: For T(n)=T(n-1)+n with T(1)=1, what is the asymptotic running time?
answer: Theta(n^2)
questions.explanation: Expansion sums 1+2+...+n=n(n+1)/2, which is quadratic.

questions.prompt: A recursive function invokes itself on n-1 until n=1. How many recursive edges are followed from input n to the base call?
questions.explanation: The call sequence n,n-1,...,1 has n activations and n-1 transitions between them.

questions.prompt: A single-call recursive chain follows 12 recursive edges from the initial call to its base call. How many activations are in the chain?
questions.explanation: A path with 12 edges contains 13 vertices, corresponding to 13 calls including both endpoints.

questions.prompt: For T(n)=2T(n/2)+n with T(1)=1, what is the asymptotic running time?
answer: Theta(n log n)
questions.explanation: Each level of the recursion tree performs total work n, and there are logarithmically many levels.

questions.prompt: Why can naive recursive Fibonacci take exponential time?
options: It halves n at every call
It makes only one call per non-base case
It uses a memo table automatically
answer: It recomputes overlapping subproblems
questions.explanation: F(n) recursively evaluates F(n-1) and F(n-2), causing many smaller Fibonacci values to be recomputed along separate branches.

questions.prompt: What is the key time benefit of memoizing a recursive Fibonacci function?
options: Each distinct input value is computed once
answer: Each distinct input value is computed once
questions.explanation: Caching results avoids repeated evaluation of the same F(k). The number of distinct inputs from zero through n is linear.

questions.prompt: A depth-first recursive traversal visits a balanced binary tree with n nodes. What is the maximum number of simultaneously active calls?
answer: Theta(log n)
questions.explanation: The active calls follow one root-to-leaf path. A balanced tree has logarithmic height, which bounds the recursion depth.

questions.prompt: A depth-first recursive traversal visits a skewed binary tree with n nodes. What is the maximum recursion depth?
answer: Theta(n)
questions.explanation: A skewed tree is a chain of n nodes, so the traversal may retain one call frame per node.

questions.prompt: Let g(0)=1 and g(n)=2*g(n-1)+1 for n>0. What is g(4)?
questions.explanation: The values are g(1)=3, g(2)=7, g(3)=15, and g(4)=31.

questions.prompt: A full binary recursion tree has L leaves and each internal node has exactly two children. How many total nodes does it have?
questions.explanation: A full binary tree has L-1 internal nodes. Adding leaves and internal nodes gives 2L-1 total nodes.

questions.prompt: Define T(0)=0 and T(n)=T(n-1)+n. What is T(6)?
questions.explanation: Expanding the recurrence gives 1+2+3+4+5+6=21.

questions.prompt: A recursive routine calls itself on n-1 and performs no work after the call returns. What form is this?
answer: Tail recursion
questions.explanation: The recursive call is the final operation in the activation, so its result can be returned directly.

questions.prompt: Which statement about tail-call optimization in C is correct?
options: An implementation may perform it but is not required to
It is forbidden by the language
It is guaranteed only for void functions
answer: An implementation may perform it but is not required to
questions.explanation: Tail position can enable frame reuse, but the C standard does not mandate that optimization.

questions.prompt: A recursive procedure reduces n to floor(n/2) and makes one call per activation. How many non-base activations occur for n=32?
questions.explanation: The successive inputs are 32,16,8,4,2,1. Five calls process values greater than one before reaching the base case.

questions.prompt: A recursive function sums an array by adding its first value to the sum of the remaining n-1 values. What is its time complexity?
answer: Theta(n)
questions.explanation: It processes one element per activation and has n recursive levels, so the total work is linear.

questions.prompt: A recursive binary search on a sorted array of 64 elements can make at most how many midpoint comparisons before reaching a one-element interval?
questions.explanation: Each comparison halves the range. Six halvings reduce 64 candidates to one, so at most six midpoint comparisons are needed in this convention.

questions.prompt: A recurrence T(n)=T(n/2)+1 is expanded into a recursion tree. What does each root-to-leaf path contain asymptotically?
answer: Theta(log n) activations
questions.explanation: The input is halved at each level until one, which takes logarithmically many recursive activations.

questions.prompt: A recursive function makes two calls on n-1 and has constant base work. Which growth describes its call count?
answer: Exponential
questions.explanation: Both recursive branches have nearly the same input size, producing a recurrence with exponentially many leaves.

questions.prompt: For T(n)=2T(n/2)+n with constant base case, what is the asymptotic running time?
answer: Theta(n log n)
questions.explanation: Each recursion-tree level contributes total work n, and the tree has logarithmic height.

questions.prompt: For T(n)=T(n-1)+T(n-2)+1 with constant base cases, what is the asymptotic time?
answer: Exponential
questions.explanation: The recurrence branches into two overlapping subproblems and grows at a Fibonacci-like exponential rate.

questions.prompt: A full binary call tree has 8 leaves and every internal call has exactly two children. How many calls are in the entire tree?
questions.explanation: A full binary tree with L leaves has L-1 internal nodes. Total nodes are 2L-1, which is 15 for L=8.

questions.prompt: What is the main time benefit of memoizing recursive Fibonacci?
options: Each distinct input value is computed once
It changes the Fibonacci sequence values
answer: Each distinct input value is computed once
questions.explanation: Caching prevents recomputation of repeated F(k) subproblems, reducing evaluation count to O(n).

questions.prompt: If a recursive algorithm has depth d and each active frame stores constant-size state, what is its stack usage?
answer: Theta(d)
questions.explanation: There are d active frames along the deepest call chain, each using O(1) words.

questions.prompt: A recursive function f(n) makes exactly one call on n-1 until n=0. How many total activations occur on input 10?
questions.explanation: The activations are for n=10 down through n=0, giving eleven calls including the base case.

questions.prompt: A depth-first recursive traversal visits a balanced binary tree with n nodes. What is the maximum active call depth?
answer: Theta(log n)
questions.explanation: The calls follow one root-to-leaf path; the height of a balanced tree is logarithmic.

questions.prompt: A recurrence T(n)=4T(n/2)+n with constant base case has what asymptotic time?
answer: Theta(n^2)
questions.explanation: The critical exponent is n^(log2 4)=n^2. The linear toll is smaller, so the leaves dominate.

questions.prompt: Two functions call each other once while decreasing an integer argument by one until zero. What is the maximum call depth on input n?
answer: Theta(n)
questions.explanation: The function names alternate, but each activation decreases the argument by one and creates a single next call.

questions.prompt: In the recurrence T(n)=T(n/2)+1, how many recursive reductions occur for n=1024 before reaching 1?
questions.explanation: Repeated halving gives 1024,512,...,1. Ten reductions divide 1024 by 2^10 to reach one.

questions.prompt: Let f(0)=2 and f(n)=f(n-1)+2n for n>0. What is f(5)?
questions.explanation: The increments are 2,4,6,8,10. Adding their sum 30 to the base value 2 gives 32.

questions.prompt: A recursion tree has branching factor 2 and depth d, with the root at depth zero. How many leaves occur at depth d?
questions.explanation: Every level doubles its node count, so depth d contains 2^d nodes and leaves in a full tree.

questions.prompt: A recursive function calls itself on n-1 and performs n units of work at each activation. What is its total time?
answer: Theta(n^2)
questions.explanation: The total local work is n+(n-1)+...+1=n(n+1)/2, which is quadratic.

questions.prompt: A recursive procedure decrements n until n==0. What happens if it starts with a negative integer and keeps decrementing?
options: It does not reach the base case
It reaches zero after absolute-value-many calls
The compiler converts n to unsigned
answer: It does not reach the base case
questions.explanation: Decrementing a negative input moves it farther from zero, so the stated base condition is never reached.

questions.prompt: If each activation record occupies 24 bytes, approximately how much space do 1000 active recursive frames occupy?
answer: 24000 bytes
questions.explanation: The frames use about 1000*24=24000 bytes, excluding the base activation and other runtime overhead.

questions.prompt: While a recursive call waits for its child to return, what information must its activation preserve?
options: Return location and needed local state
answer: Return location and needed local state
questions.explanation: The caller resumes after the child, so it must preserve its return location and any local values needed afterward.

questions.prompt: A recursive list routine calls itself on the next node and immediately returns the child result. What form is this?
answer: Tail recursion
questions.explanation: No computation remains after the recursive call, so it is in tail position.

questions.prompt: Which statements about recursive call stacks are correct?
options: Each active call has its own local state
Peak stack use depends on maximum call depth
Total call count always equals peak stack depth
Depth-first traversal retains frames along its active path
answer: Each active call has its own local state
Peak stack use depends on maximum call depth
Depth-first traversal retains frames along its active path
questions.explanation: Total calls over completed branches do not all remain active simultaneously; active frames correspond to the current path.

questions.prompt: A recursive function f(n) has one call on n-1, constant work, and f(0)=0. What is f(7)?
questions.explanation: The recurrence adds one at each of seven steps starting from zero, giving f(7)=7.

questions.prompt: A memoized recurrence has n+1 possible integer states and O(1) work per state. What is the total time if each state is solved once?
answer: O(n)
questions.explanation: There are n+1 distinct states, each evaluated once with constant additional work.

questions.prompt: Which statements about naive recursive Fibonacci are correct?
options: The same subproblem can be recomputed in different branches
Memoization can reduce evaluation count to O(n)
Its stack depth is O(1) for every n
answer: The same subproblem can be recomputed in different branches
The call count grows exponentially
Memoization can reduce evaluation count to O(n)
questions.explanation: Overlapping subproblems create repeated work and exponential calls; caching each state once yields linear evaluations, though depth remains linear.

questions.prompt: A recursive maximum routine examines one element and recurses on the remaining n-1 elements. What is its running time?
answer: Theta(n)
questions.explanation: Every element is examined once, so the total amount of work grows linearly with n.

questions.prompt: For a one-call recursion with inputs n,n-1,...,0, how many activations occur when the initial input is 14?
questions.explanation: There are fourteen positive-input frames plus one base activation at zero.

questions.prompt: Which statements about recursion depth and total call count are correct?
options: A binary recursion can have exponentially many total calls
A depth-first execution can use stack space proportional to tree height
Total calls and peak active calls are always equal
A chain of n calls has Theta(n) stack depth
answer: A binary recursion can have exponentially many total calls
A depth-first execution can use stack space proportional to tree height
A chain of n calls has Theta(n) stack depth
questions.explanation: Total tree size determines work, while height determines the maximum simultaneous frames. A linear chain has linear height and stack use.

questions.prompt: A recursive function makes one call on n/2 until n<=1 and does constant local work. What is its auxiliary stack space?
answer: Theta(log n)
questions.explanation: The argument halves at each step, yielding logarithmically many simultaneously active calls.

questions.prompt: For T(n)=2T(n/2)+n/log n with T(1)=1, which asymptotic bound follows from a recursion tree?
answer: Theta(n log log n)
questions.explanation: At level i the aggregate nonrecursive work is n/(log n-i), while the tree has log n levels. Summing reciprocals gives a harmonic sum Theta(log log n), multiplied by n.

questions.prompt: A function makes three recursive calls on inputs of size n/2 and performs Theta(n) extra work. Its asymptotic running time is
answer: Theta(n^log2 3)
questions.explanation: The recurrence is T(n)=3T(n/2)+Theta(n). Since n^log2 3 grows faster than n, the leaf contribution dominates by the Master theorem.

questions.prompt: For T(n)=T(n-1)+2n with T(0)=0, give the exact value of T(5).
questions.explanation: Unrolling gives T(n)=2(1+2+...+n)=n(n+1). Substitution at n=5 gives 30.

questions.prompt: A recursive procedure calls itself on n-1 and n-2, doing constant work otherwise. What is its worst-case time?
answer: Theta(phi^n)
questions.explanation: The call-count recurrence is T(n)=T(n-1)+T(n-2)+Theta(1), whose characteristic roots include phi=(1+sqrt(5))/2, giving Theta(phi^n).

questions.prompt: Which recurrences have asymptotic solution Theta(n log n)?
answer: T(n)=4T(n/2)+n squared
questions.explanation: For the first, every level costs Theta(n), and there are logarithmically many levels. The fourth has Theta(n squared) aggregate cost per level, hence Theta(n squared log n). The second sums geometrically to Theta(n), and the third is Theta(n).

questions.prompt: Consider recursive binary search on a sorted array of n distinct elements. The maximum number of comparisons for n=31 is
questions.explanation: Each comparison halves the candidate interval. At most ceil(log2(n+1)) comparisons are required; for n=31 this is 5.

questions.prompt: A recurrence is T(n)=T(n/3)+T(2n/3)+n. Which bound is correct?
answer: Theta(n log n)
questions.explanation: At each recursion depth the subproblem sizes sum to n, so work per level is Theta(n). The longest root-to-leaf path has Theta(log n) levels, yielding Theta(n log n).

questions.prompt: A recursive algorithm satisfies T(n)=2T(n/2)+1 for n a power of two, with T(1)=1. Find T(16).
questions.explanation: A full binary recursion tree with 16 leaves has 15 internal nodes. Each node contributes one, and each leaf contributes one, so the total is 31.

questions.prompt: For T(n)=T(n/2)+T(n/4)+n, which asymptotic order is correct?
answer: Theta(n)
questions.explanation: The total subproblem size at each depth shrinks by a factor at most 3/4. Summed work over levels is bounded by n times a convergent geometric series, so T(n)=Theta(n).

questions.prompt: A recursive function has recurrence T(n)=T(n-1)+Theta(log n). What is T(n)?
answer: Theta(n log n)
questions.explanation: Unrolling sums logarithms from 1 through n. The sum is Theta(n log n), as follows from integral bounds or grouping the upper half of terms.

questions.prompt: Which statements about recursion are true?
options: A base case must be reachable for every permitted input
A recursive call must always use a smaller numeric argument
Mutual recursion may terminate even if each function calls another function
Tail recursion guarantees O(1) stack space in every programming language
answer: A base case must be reachable for every permitted input
Mutual recursion may terminate even if each function calls another function
questions.explanation: A base case must be reachable, and mutual recursion can terminate when the calls collectively make progress. Progress need not mean a smaller numeric argument, and tail-call stack elimination depends on the implementation.

questions.prompt: For T(n)=8T(n/2)+n squared, the solution is
answer: Theta(n^3)
questions.explanation: Here n^log2 8=n^3 dominates f(n)=n^2, so the recursion tree is dominated by its leaves and T(n)=Theta(n^3).

questions.prompt: A recursive algorithm creates 2 subproblems of half-size until size 1. For n=64, how many leaves are in its recursion tree?
questions.explanation: Every root-to-leaf path has six halvings and the branching factor is two, so the leaf count is 2^6=64.

questions.prompt: A procedure makes one recursive call on n-1 and then scans n items. Its running time is
answer: Theta(n squared)
questions.explanation: The recurrence T(n)=T(n-1)+Theta(n) sums 1+2+...+n, which is Theta(n squared).

questions.prompt: In a recursive tree traversal of a binary tree with n nodes, each node is processed once and makes calls on its children. The time is
answer: Theta(n)
questions.explanation: There is constant work per node and one call per child edge plus null-child calls. The total number of calls is linear in the number of nodes.

questions.prompt: For T(n)=T(n/2)+T(n/4)+n, with T(1)=1, which is the tight asymptotic bound?
answer: Theta(n)
questions.explanation: The sum of child input sizes is at most 3n/4. Thus nonrecursive work n dominates the geometrically shrinking total work across successive levels, giving Theta(n).

questions.prompt: For T(n)=2T(n/2)+n and T(1)=1, where n is a power of two, find T(8).
questions.explanation: At each internal level the total cost is n, across three internal levels giving 24; the eight leaves cost 8, totaling 32.

questions.prompt: In the preceding recurrence T(n)=2T(n/2)+n with unit leaf cost, the closed form for n=2^k is
answer: n log2 n+n
questions.explanation: There are k internal levels each contributing n, plus n leaves of cost one, hence nk+n.

questions.prompt: A recursive algorithm solves one subproblem of size n-1 and one of size n-2 with constant overhead. Which statement best describes its time?
answer: Exponential in n
questions.explanation: The recurrence has Fibonacci growth. Its characteristic equation has a root greater than one, so the number of calls grows exponentially.

questions.prompt: For a divide-and-conquer algorithm with recurrence T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n), which conditions are sufficient to apply the standard Master theorem directly?
options: a is at least 1 and b is greater than 1
The subproblem sizes are all exactly n/b
The input size is a positive integer
answer: a is at least 1 and b is greater than 1
f(n) is asymptotically nonnegative
The subproblem sizes are all exactly n/b
questions.explanation: The standard form assumes a>=1, b>1, equally sized subproblems n/b, and asymptotically nonnegative f. The positive integer input convention is not the relevant structural restriction.

questions.prompt: A recursive routine calls itself on n/2 until n=1, with Theta(n) work at every call. Its running time is
answer: Theta(n)
questions.explanation: The work sums n+n/2+n/4+... which is a geometric series bounded above and below by constant multiples of n.

questions.prompt: A full ternary recursion tree has height 3 edges, with root at depth 0. How many leaves does it have?
questions.explanation: Each level triples the number of nodes; at depth 3 the number of leaves is 3^3=27.

questions.prompt: For T(n)=T(n-1)+1 and T(0)=0, how many non-base recursive calls occur on input n?
answer: n
questions.explanation: The argument decreases once per call from n to zero, giving exactly n calls that perform the recurrence step.

questions.prompt: A recursive algorithm has recurrence T(n)=4T(n/2)+n. The tight bound is
answer: Theta(n squared)
questions.explanation: The critical exponent is log2 4=2, while f(n)=n is polynomially smaller. Thus T(n)=Theta(n^2).

questions.prompt: For T(n)=T(n-1)+n with T(0)=0, find T(4).
questions.explanation: The recurrence sums the increments 1+2+3+4=10.

questions.prompt: Which recurrence-solving methods can establish a bound without guessing a closed form first?
options: Master theorem when its conditions apply
Treating every recurrence as a geometric series
answer: Recursion-tree expansion
Substitution with an induction hypothesis
Master theorem when its conditions apply
questions.explanation: Recursion trees, induction by substitution, and the Master theorem under its conditions are valid methods. Not every recurrence has geometric level costs.

questions.prompt: A recursive function computes F(n)=F(n-1)+F(n-1)+1 with F(0)=0. What is F(4)?
questions.explanation: The values satisfy F(n)=2F(n-1)+1, yielding F(n)=2^n-1 by induction; at n=4 the value is 15.

questions.prompt: A recursive algorithm makes two calls of size n/2 and performs constant work. Its running time is
answer: Theta(n)
questions.explanation: The recurrence is T(n)=2T(n/2)+Theta(1); the leaf count is n, and constant work at internal nodes adds only O(n), so the total is Theta(n).

questions.prompt: For a binary recursive algorithm that branches twice and stops at size 1, with n=32, how many total nodes are in a full recursion tree?
questions.explanation: A full binary tree with 32 leaves has 31 internal nodes, for 63 total nodes.

questions.prompt: In recursive merge sort, merging subarrays of total length n costs Theta(n). The recurrence and bound are
answer: T(n)=2T(n/2)+Theta(n), Theta(n log n)
questions.explanation: There are two half-size recursive calls and a linear merge. Each of log n levels costs Theta(n), yielding Theta(n log n).

questions.prompt: A recursive routine makes one call on n/2 and does constant work per call. For n a power of two, its time is
answer: Theta(log n)
questions.explanation: There is one call at each halved size until one, so the recursion depth and total constant work are Theta(log n).

questions.prompt: For T(n)=T(n/2)+3 with T(1)=2 and n=16, find T(n).
questions.explanation: There are four recursive halvings from 16 to 1, adding 3 at each level to the base value 2. Hence T(16)=2+4*3=14.

questions.prompt: A routine recursively processes n-1 elements, then performs a constant-time operation. What is its maximum recursion depth?
answer: Theta(n)
questions.explanation: Each call reduces the input by one, so starting from n requires n-O(1) nested calls before the base case.

questions.prompt: For T(n)=2T(n/2)+n, with n a power of two, which statements are true?
options: The recursion tree has log2 n internal levels
Each internal level contributes total cost n
The number of leaves is n
The total cost is Theta(n squared)
answer: The recursion tree has log2 n internal levels
Each internal level contributes total cost n
The number of leaves is n
questions.explanation: There are log2 n internal levels, each with aggregate cost n, and n leaves. The total is Theta(n log n), so the final n-squared statement is false.

questions.prompt: A recursive algorithm reduces n to n-1 and performs n squared work at each call. Its running time is
answer: Theta(n cubed)
questions.explanation: Summing the per-call work gives n^2+(n-1)^2+...+1, which is Theta(n^3) by comparison with the sum of squares.

questions.prompt: A binary recursion tree has 16 leaves and is full. How many internal nodes does it have?
questions.explanation: In a full binary tree every internal node has two children, giving leaves=internal nodes+1. Therefore there are 15 internal nodes.

questions.prompt: For T(n)=3T(n/2)+n, which term dominates the asymptotic solution?
options: Every level equally, giving Theta(n log n)
The recurrence is exponential in n
answer: The leaves, giving Theta(n^log2 3)
questions.explanation: The critical exponent log2 3 is greater than one, so n^log2 3 grows faster than the linear nonrecursive work and dominates.

questions.prompt: A recurrence T(n)=T(n/2)+T(n/2)+n/log n is given for n>2, with constant base values. Its order is
answer: Theta(n log log n)
questions.explanation: At level i, total work is n/(log n-i). Summing over levels gives n times a harmonic sum of order log log n, hence Theta(n log log n).

questions.prompt: A recursive routine calls itself on n/2 twice and spends n squared extra work. Its running time is
answer: Theta(n squared)
questions.explanation: At each level the aggregate extra work is proportional to n squared divided by 2^i, a geometric series dominated by the root. The leaves contribute only O(n), so total time is Theta(n^2).

questions.prompt: A binary recursive procedure makes two calls of size n/2 until size 1. For n=128, how many leaves are there?
questions.explanation: Seven halvings produce depth 7; with branching factor two this gives 2^7=128 leaves.

questions.prompt: Which are valid ways to prove a proposed asymptotic bound for a recurrence?
options: Use induction after substituting the proposed bound
Expand a recursion tree and sum level costs
Compare with a recurrence having a known bound
Assume the largest subproblem alone determines total work
answer: Use induction after substituting the proposed bound
Expand a recursion tree and sum level costs
Compare with a recurrence having a known bound
questions.explanation: Induction, recursion-tree summation, and comparison with a known recurrence can prove bounds. Considering only the largest subproblem omits the work of the remaining branches.

questions.prompt: For T(n)=T(n-1)+log n, T(1)=1, the tight order is
answer: Theta(n log n)
questions.explanation: Unrolling gives a sum of logarithms. Its upper bound is n log n and the last n/2 terms are each Theta(log n), giving a matching lower bound.

questions.prompt: For T(n)=2T(n/2)+1, T(1)=1, with n=4, find T(n).
questions.explanation: The recurrence gives T(2)=2*1+1=3 and T(4)=2*3+1=7.

questions.prompt: A recursive algorithm has T(n)=T(n/3)+Theta(1). Its time complexity is
answer: Theta(log n)
questions.explanation: Each call reduces the input by a constant factor, so there are Theta(log_3 n) calls, each with constant overhead.

questions.prompt: A function computes both f(n-1) and f(n-1) independently, with constant work and f(0)=1. How many base-case calls occur for input n?
questions.explanation: Each recursive level doubles the number of calls and all paths reach zero after n levels, yielding 2^n leaves/base calls.

questions.prompt: A stack initially empty receives push(4), push(7), pop(), push(9), push(2), pop(). What is the top element afterward?
questions.explanation: The first pop removes 7, leaving 4. After pushing 9 and 2, the final pop removes 2, so 9 is on top.

questions.prompt: An empty stack receives 12 pushes and 5 pops. How many elements remain?
questions.explanation: Each push adds one and each pop removes one, so the resulting size is 12-5=7.

questions.prompt: Which structure is required to evaluate a postfix expression in one left-to-right scan?
answer: Stack
questions.explanation: Operands are pushed; an operator pops its operands and pushes the result. This last-in-first-out behavior is implemented naturally by a stack.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the postfix expression 8 2 3 * +. What is the result?
questions.explanation: The multiplication is evaluated first: 2*3=6. Then 8+6=14.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the postfix expression 5 1 2 + 4 * + 3 -. Give the result.
questions.explanation: Compute 1+2=3, then 3*4=12, then 5+12=17, and finally 17-3=14.

questions.prompt: When evaluating postfix expression a b -, which operand is popped first and what is computed?
options: Pop b, then a, and compute a-b
Pop a, then b, and compute a-b
Pop b, then a, and compute b-a
The order is irrelevant for subtraction
answer: Pop b, then a, and compute a-b
questions.explanation: The top operand b is popped first as the right operand; the next popped value a is the left operand. The result must preserve the original subtraction order.

questions.prompt: Which expressions can be evaluated using a stack in one scan without operator precedence parsing?
options: A prefix expression scanned from right to left
An infix expression with arbitrary precedence and no parentheses or precedence rules
answer: A postfix expression
A prefix expression scanned from right to left
Balanced-parentheses matching
questions.explanation: Postfix and reverse-scanned prefix are directly stack-evaluable. Parenthesis matching uses a stack; arbitrary infix still needs precedence/associativity rules.

questions.prompt: For an array-based stack with capacity C, which condition indicates overflow before a push when top is the index of the current top and initially -1?
answer: top=C-1
questions.explanation: With zero-based storage, the last valid position is C-1. A push overflows when that position is already occupied.

questions.prompt: An array stack has capacity 10 and top=-1 initially. After 7 successful pushes and 3 successful pops, what is top?
questions.explanation: Seven pushes leave top at index 6. Three pops reduce it to index 3, corresponding to four remaining elements.

questions.prompt: A queue is implemented by a circular array of capacity C with one slot left unused to distinguish full from empty. Which full condition is used?
answer: (rear+1) mod C = front
questions.explanation: With one reserved slot, the queue is full when advancing rear by one modulo C would collide with front.

questions.prompt: In a circular queue of capacity 8 using all slots and an explicit size field, rear is at index 7. Where is the next enqueued element stored?
answer: Index 0
questions.explanation: Circular indexing wraps modulo capacity. The next position after index 7 in an array of length 8 is index 0.

questions.prompt: A circular queue has capacity 9 and front index 6. What index follows front after one dequeue, using modulo indexing?
questions.explanation: A dequeue advances front to (6+1) mod 9, which is 7.

questions.prompt: A queue implemented by a singly linked list maintains both head and tail pointers. What is the worst-case time for enqueue and dequeue respectively?
questions.explanation: Enqueue links the new node at tail in constant time, while dequeue removes head in constant time and updates tail when the queue becomes empty.

questions.prompt: Which statements about stacks and queues are true?
options: A deque supports insertion and deletion at both ends
A standard queue permits deletion at both ends
answer: A stack is LIFO
A queue is FIFO
A deque supports insertion and deletion at both ends
questions.explanation: Stacks remove the most recently inserted item; queues remove the earliest inserted item. A deque supports both ends, unlike a standard queue.

questions.prompt: A sequence of push and pop operations on an initially empty stack is valid only if
options: Every pop has a preceding unmatched push
The number of pushes equals the number of pops in every prefix
The final operation is a pop
Every push is immediately followed by a pop
answer: Every pop has a preceding unmatched push
questions.explanation: At every prefix, the number of pops cannot exceed the number of preceding pushes. A valid sequence may end with elements still on the stack.

questions.prompt: Consider operations push A, push B, pop, push C, pop, pop on an empty stack. What sequence of items is returned by the three pops, from first to last?
answer: B, C, A
questions.explanation: The first pop returns B. After pushing C, the next pop returns C, and the final pop returns A; the sequence is B, C, A.

questions.prompt: Which data structure can implement a stack with amortized O(1) push using a dynamically resized array?
options: Dynamic array that doubles when full
answer: Dynamic array that doubles when full
questions.explanation: When full, doubling capacity copies O(n) elements but occurs infrequently. Across a sequence of pushes, total copying is O(n), yielding amortized constant push time.

questions.prompt: A dynamic array stack doubles capacity when full. Starting with capacity 1, how many element copies occur during 8 pushes, assuming each resize copies all existing elements?
questions.explanation: Resizes occur before pushes 2, 3, 5, and 9. During eight pushes, copied counts are 1, 2, and 4, totaling seven.

questions.prompt: Which claims about amortized analysis of a doubling stack are correct?
options: A single push may take Theta(n) due to resizing
A sequence of n pushes takes O(n) total time
Every push has worst-case O(1) time
The amortized cost per push is O(1)
answer: A single push may take Theta(n) due to resizing
A sequence of n pushes takes O(n) total time
The amortized cost per push is O(1)
questions.explanation: A resizing push can copy all existing items, so its individual worst-case is linear. The geometric sum of copies is linear overall, giving constant amortized cost.

questions.prompt: A queue is implemented using two stacks: enqueue pushes onto S1; dequeue pops from S2, transferring all S1 items to S2 only when S2 is empty. What is the amortized cost per operation?
questions.explanation: Each element is pushed onto S1 once, transferred and pushed onto S2 at most once, then popped once. Total stack operations are linear over the sequence, giving constant amortized cost.

questions.prompt: An initially empty queue supports enqueue and dequeue. Which output sequence results from enqueue(1), enqueue(2), dequeue(), enqueue(3), dequeue(), dequeue()?
questions.explanation: A queue removes in insertion order: the first dequeue returns 1, then 2, and the final dequeue returns 3.

questions.prompt: A queue initially contains 4 elements. It receives 13 enqueues and 9 dequeues, with no underflow. How many elements remain?
questions.explanation: The queue size changes by 13-9=4; adding its initial size yields 8.

questions.prompt: A circular queue uses front as the index of the first element and size as the number of elements in a capacity-C array. What is the rear index when size>0?
answer: (front+size-1) mod C
questions.explanation: Starting from front, the size occupied positions end at offset size-1. Modulo C wraps the resulting rear index around the array.

questions.prompt: A circular queue has capacity 11, front=8, and size=5. What is the rear index?
questions.explanation: The rear is (8+5-1) mod 11 = 12 mod 11 = 1.

questions.prompt: A circular queue of capacity C leaves one array slot unused. If front=rear, the queue is
answer: empty
questions.explanation: With one-slot-empty encoding, front equals rear for empty. Full is distinguished by the next rear position equaling front.

questions.prompt: In a one-slot-empty circular queue of capacity 10, front=4 and rear=3. What is the queue state?
options: Invalid because rear is less than front
answer: Full
questions.explanation: The next position after rear is (3+1) mod 10=4, equal to front, satisfying the full condition.

questions.prompt: Which techniques can distinguish full from empty in a circular array queue?
options: Compare front and rear alone while using every slot
answer: Maintain an explicit element count
Leave one array slot unused
Maintain a separate full flag
questions.explanation: A count or a full flag provides extra state. Leaving one slot unused makes pointer equality uniquely indicate empty; pointers alone with all slots used are ambiguous.

questions.prompt: A deque is stored in a circular array. Which operation pair can be supported in O(1) time at both ends?
options: Insert and delete at either front or rear
Search by value at either end
answer: Insert and delete at either front or rear
questions.explanation: A deque (double-ended queue) supports constant-time endpoint operations in a circular array, subject to available capacity or resize behavior.

questions.prompt: A monotonic deque is used to compute sliding-window maxima. Which property should its stored values satisfy from front to rear?
answer: Nonincreasing order
questions.explanation: For maxima, values are kept in nonincreasing order. Smaller values at the rear are removed when a larger new value arrives because they cannot be future maxima.

questions.prompt: For a sliding window of width 3 over values 2, 5, 1, 4, 3, how many window maxima are produced?
questions.explanation: There are 5-3+1=3 complete windows, each producing one maximum.

questions.prompt: When processing a new value x for sliding-window maximum, why may smaller values at the deque's rear be removed?
options: They are dominated by x for every future window containing x
They have already been output as maxima
They occur before the current window
answer: They are dominated by x for every future window containing x
questions.explanation: The newer x is larger and remains in future windows at least as long as earlier values. Any smaller earlier candidate cannot become the maximum before x expires.

questions.prompt: A stack is used to check balanced parentheses. On reading a closing delimiter, what should the algorithm do?
options: Check that the stack top is the matching opening delimiter, then pop
Ignore its type and increment a counter
answer: Check that the stack top is the matching opening delimiter, then pop
questions.explanation: Matching types and nesting require checking the most recent unmatched opener. A counter alone cannot distinguish bracket types or proper nesting.

questions.prompt: Which delimiter strings are balanced under standard properly nested parentheses/brackets rules?
questions.explanation: Balanced strings close the most recently opened delimiter of the matching type. The first and third strings obey nesting; the others do not.

questions.prompt: For an input string of length n, what are the time and auxiliary-space complexities of stack-based balanced-parenthesis checking?
options: O(n squared) time and O(1) space
O(log n) time and O(n) space
answer: O(n) time and O(n) space
questions.explanation: Each character is examined once and at most O(n) opening delimiters may be stored on the stack.

questions.prompt: While scanning the prefix '(([]', how many unmatched opening delimiters are on the stack after the final character?
questions.explanation: The two parentheses and one bracket have been opened; the closing bracket matches only the most recent bracket, leaving two parentheses and the opening bracket? Actually sequence '(' '(' '[' ']' leaves two unmatched opening parentheses.

questions.prompt: In infix-to-postfix conversion, when a left-associative operator of precedence p is read, which stacked operators should generally be popped first?
options: Operators of greater or equal precedence
No operators before the next operand
answer: Operators of greater or equal precedence
questions.explanation: For a left-associative incoming operator, prior operators of equal or higher precedence must be emitted first so the postfix evaluation preserves grouping and associativity.

questions.prompt: The infix expression a-b-c is evaluated with subtraction left-associative. Its postfix form is
answer: a b - c -
questions.explanation: Left associativity groups it as (a-b)-c. The corresponding postfix sequence performs the first subtraction before the second.

questions.prompt: How many operators are present in the postfix expression 4 5 + 6 2 - *?
questions.explanation: The expression contains addition, subtraction, and multiplication, for three operator tokens.

questions.prompt: A postfix expression contains n operands and b binary operators and is a single valid expression. What relation must hold between n and b?
answer: n=b+1
questions.explanation: Each binary operator combines two existing expression components into one, reducing the component count by one. Starting with n operands and ending with one requires b=n-1.

questions.prompt: During evaluation of a valid postfix expression containing only binary operators, which invariants hold after each token is processed?
options: The stack contains values of completed subexpressions
An operator requires at least two stack values
Applying a binary operator reduces stack size by one
The stack size always equals the number of operands seen
answer: The stack contains values of completed subexpressions
An operator requires at least two stack values
Applying a binary operator reduces stack size by one
questions.explanation: Operands add one stack value and binary operators consume two and add one. Thus the size depends on operators too, and every operator needs two values.

questions.prompt: A stack supports push, pop, and an auxiliary operation that returns the minimum element. Which approach gives O(1) worst-case time for all three?
options: Maintain a second stack of minima
Scan all stack elements on each query
Keep the stack sorted in an array
answer: Maintain a second stack of minima
questions.explanation: A parallel min-stack records the minimum at each depth, so the current minimum is available at its top and updates track push and pop.

questions.prompt: When pushing x onto a stack with a min-stack, what should be pushed onto the min-stack if it stores one minimum per main-stack depth?
answer: min(x,current minimum)
questions.explanation: The new minimum at that depth is the smaller of x and the previous minimum. This allows the minimum to be retrieved in constant time and restored after pop.

questions.prompt: A stack's contents from bottom to top are 8, 3, 6, 2. If a min-stack stores one prefix minimum per element, what is the current minimum?
questions.explanation: The minimum of the prefix ending at the top is min(8,3,6,2)=2.

questions.prompt: Which operations can be implemented in O(1) worst-case time using an auxiliary stack alongside a standard stack?
answer: Return the current minimum
Return the current maximum
Return the top element
questions.explanation: A second stack can track minima and another can track maxima. The median generally requires more elaborate order information; top is directly available from the main stack.

questions.prompt: A stack is implemented by a singly linked list with the top at head. What is the time for push and pop?
answer: O(1) each
questions.explanation: Inserting and removing the head node each require constant pointer updates, independent of stack size.

questions.prompt: A stack is implemented by a singly linked list with the top at tail and no predecessor link. What is the worst-case time for pop?
answer: O(n)
questions.explanation: Removing the tail requires locating its predecessor by traversing from the head, which takes linear time.

questions.prompt: A stack receives pushes of values 1 through 5, then two pops, then pushes 6 and 7, then one pop. What is the top value?
questions.explanation: After pushing 1..5, popping twice leaves 3 on top. Push 6 then 7, and pop removes 7, leaving 6 on top.

questions.prompt: Which permutation can be produced by a stack from input sequence 1,2,3, with pushes in input order and arbitrary pops?
questions.explanation: Push 1 and 2, pop 2 then 1, then push and pop 3; this yields 2,1,3.

questions.prompt: For a stack permutation, input items arrive in increasing order 1,2,3,4. Can output 3,1,2,4 be produced?
options: No, after outputting 3, item 2 remains above item 1
Yes, push all four then pop in order
Yes, because every item appears once
answer: No, after outputting 3, item 2 remains above item 1
questions.explanation: To output 3, the stack must have 1,2,3 with 3 on top. After popping 3, 2 is above 1, so 1 cannot be next.

questions.prompt: Which output sequences are possible from input 1,2,3,4 using a single stack and preserving input push order?
questions.explanation: Each feasible output can be obtained by pushing the needed prefix and popping in LIFO order. Sequence 3,1,2 is impossible because 2 blocks 1 after 3 is popped.

questions.prompt: A queue is implemented using two stacks with the transfer-on-empty rule. An element enqueued most recently can be dequeued immediately only if
options: All older elements have already been dequeued
The element is also pushed onto S2
answer: All older elements have already been dequeued
questions.explanation: FIFO order requires every earlier enqueued element to leave first. The two-stack implementation preserves that order through its transfer process.

questions.prompt: A two-stack queue receives enqueue(A), enqueue(B), enqueue(C), dequeue(), enqueue(D), dequeue(). Which item is returned by the second dequeue?
answer: B
questions.explanation: The first dequeue returns A after transfer. B remains at the top of the output stack, so the second dequeue returns B.

questions.prompt: A priority queue differs from a FIFO queue because it
options: Removes an element according to its priority key
Supports only insertion at the rear
answer: Removes an element according to its priority key
questions.explanation: A priority queue selects the highest- or lowest-priority item according to its ordering rule, rather than insertion chronology.

questions.prompt: Which applications naturally use a queue or deque rather than a stack as the primary ordering discipline?
answer: Breadth-first graph traversal
Round-robin scheduling
Level-order tree traversal
questions.explanation: BFS, round-robin scheduling, and level-order traversal process items in arrival order. Iterative DFS typically uses a stack.

questions.prompt: Breadth-first search uses a queue. In an unweighted graph, what does first discovery of a vertex from source s establish?
options: A shortest path in number of edges from s
That the vertex has no alternate path
answer: A shortest path in number of edges from s
questions.explanation: BFS explores vertices in nondecreasing distance from the source, so the first discovery uses the fewest edges in an unweighted graph.

questions.prompt: A tree has 1 root, 3 nodes at depth 1, and 5 nodes at depth 2. During level-order traversal, how many nodes are dequeued?
questions.explanation: Every node is enqueued and dequeued exactly once; the total number is 1+3+5=9.

questions.prompt: A queue is used for BFS on a graph with V vertices and E edges represented by adjacency lists. What is the total time complexity?
answer: O(V+E)
questions.explanation: Each vertex is enqueued and dequeued once, and every adjacency-list edge is examined once, giving O(V+E).

questions.prompt: In an array-based circular queue, why is modulo arithmetic used to update indices?
options: To wrap an index from the last array position back to zero
answer: To wrap an index from the last array position back to zero
questions.explanation: Modulo capacity maps an incremented endpoint back into the valid index range when it passes the last slot.

questions.prompt: A circular buffer has capacity 13. If rear is at index 11, what is the index after advancing rear by 5 positions modulo capacity?
questions.explanation: Advance rear five steps with wraparound: (11+5) mod 13 equals 16 mod 13, which is index 3.

questions.prompt: A bounded queue receives an enqueue when it is full. Which policy is not determined by the queue abstraction itself?
options: Reject, block, or overwrite according to the implementation contract
Remove the front item in every implementation
answer: Reject, block, or overwrite according to the implementation contract
questions.explanation: The abstract queue specifies FIFO ordering, while overflow handling depends on design: reject, block, resize, or overwrite may be chosen.

questions.prompt: A recursive procedure uses a stack of activation records. For recursion depth d, what is the maximum number of simultaneously active records?
answer: Theta(d)
questions.explanation: Each call remains active until its recursive work returns, so a chain of d nested calls has d activation records simultaneously on the call stack.

questions.prompt: A recursive function makes one nested call per decrement from n=12 to the base case n=0. What is the maximum number of active non-base calls?
questions.explanation: The calls for arguments 12 down through 1 are active before the base call returns, totaling 12 non-base activation records.

questions.prompt: Tail recursion can be converted to iteration by
options: Replacing the recursive call with a loop update when no work remains after the call
Storing all return values in a queue
answer: Replacing the recursive call with a loop update when no work remains after the call
questions.explanation: In tail recursion, the recursive call is the final action. A loop can update parameters and repeat without preserving a pending computation for return.

questions.prompt: Which statements about recursive versus iterative DFS are correct?
options: Recursive DFS uses the language call stack
Iterative DFS commonly uses an explicit stack
Both can run in O(V+E) with adjacency lists
BFS and DFS always visit vertices in identical order
answer: Recursive DFS uses the language call stack
Iterative DFS commonly uses an explicit stack
Both can run in O(V+E) with adjacency lists
questions.explanation: Both DFS versions can mark vertices and examine each edge once, taking O(V+E) with adjacency lists. They may produce differing traversal orders, and BFS uses a queue.

questions.prompt: An iterative algorithm simulates recursive preorder tree traversal. When should a node be output to match preorder?
options: When the node is first popped/entered, before its children
Only when it is pushed twice
At the end of the traversal
answer: When the node is first popped/entered, before its children
questions.explanation: Preorder visits root before left and right subtrees. In an iterative simulation the node is processed upon entry, with child push order chosen appropriately.

questions.prompt: A binary tree has 31 nodes. A stack-based DFS pushes each node once and pops each node once. How many total push and pop operations occur?
questions.explanation: Each of 31 nodes is pushed once and popped once, for 31+31=62 operations.

questions.prompt: To simulate recursive inorder traversal iteratively, which action occurs after descending to the leftmost node?
options: Pop a node, visit it, then move to its right subtree
Move to the left child after popping and never revisit
answer: Pop a node, visit it, then move to its right subtree
questions.explanation: The stack stores deferred ancestors. Once no left child remains, the top node is visited, then traversal proceeds into its right subtree.

questions.prompt: An expression tree is traversed in postorder to produce postfix notation. What is the visit order?
answer: Left subtree, right subtree, root
questions.explanation: Postorder visits both operand subtrees before the operator at the root, producing operands before their operation in postfix notation.

questions.prompt: Which traversals of an expression tree with binary operators produce standard notation forms?
options: Level order always produces an equivalent unparenthesized infix expression
answer: Preorder produces prefix
Inorder with parentheses produces infix
Postorder produces postfix
questions.explanation: Root-left-right yields prefix; left-root-right yields infix when grouping is represented; left-right-root yields postfix. Level order does not generally encode expression structure as infix.

questions.prompt: A full binary expression tree has 7 leaves and only binary internal operators. How many operator nodes does it have?
questions.explanation: For a full binary tree, leaves equal internal nodes plus one. Thus 7 leaves imply 6 internal operator nodes.

questions.prompt: A stack is used to reverse a sequence of n items. How many push and pop operations are required in total?
answer: 2n
questions.explanation: Each item is pushed once and popped once, resulting in 2n stack operations.

questions.prompt: A queue receives n=17 elements and then drains completely. How many enqueue and dequeue operations are performed altogether?
questions.explanation: There are 17 enqueues and 17 dequeues, giving 34 operations.

questions.prompt: A circular queue has capacity 6, uses one unused slot, and currently has front=2 and rear=5. How many elements are stored?
questions.explanation: The occupied positions after front through rear are 3, 4, and 5, giving three elements; equivalently (rear-front+6) mod 6=3.

questions.prompt: A circular queue of capacity 7 with one slot unused has front=5 and rear=2. How many elements are stored?
questions.explanation: (2-5+7) mod 7=4 elements are stored in the wrapped interval after front through rear.

questions.prompt: A circular queue is empty when front=rear. On the first enqueue in a representation that stores front as the first occupied index and rear as the next free index, which pointer relationship holds afterward?
answer: rear=(front+1) mod C
questions.explanation: One item occupies the front position, so rear advances once to the next free slot modulo capacity.

questions.prompt: Which are valid implementation strategies for a queue using an array?
options: Shift all elements after each dequeue
Use a dynamically resized circular buffer
answer: Shift all elements after each dequeue
Use circular indices
Use a dynamically resized circular buffer
Use two stacks
questions.explanation: Shifting is valid but makes dequeue O(n); circular indices and a dynamic circular buffer are common direct implementations. Two stacks also implement a queue while preserving FIFO behavior.

questions.prompt: A queue implementation shifts all remaining array elements left after every dequeue. What is the worst-case dequeue time?
answer: O(n)
questions.explanation: Removing the front by shifting requires moving up to n-1 elements, so worst-case time is linear.

questions.prompt: An array queue contains 9 elements. It performs 6 dequeues, shifting each remaining element once per dequeue. How many element moves are made in total?
questions.explanation: The moves are 8+7+6+5+4+3=33 after successive removals.

questions.prompt: A circular queue avoids shifting after dequeue by
options: Advancing the front index modulo the array capacity
Copying every element to index zero
answer: Advancing the front index modulo the array capacity
questions.explanation: Advancing front marks the next occupied array position without moving stored elements. Modulo arithmetic handles wraparound.

questions.prompt: A queue is implemented as a circular singly linked list with only a tail pointer. Where is the front element found?
answer: tail.next
questions.explanation: The tail's next link points to the front of the circular list, making both enqueue at rear and dequeue at front constant time.

questions.prompt: A circular singly linked list with tail pointer is used as a queue. After enqueueing x into an empty queue, what should tail and tail.next reference?
options: tail references null and tail.next references x
tail references x.next and tail.next references null
answer: Both reference x
questions.explanation: A one-node circular queue has its sole node as both rear and front. Its next link points to itself, so tail and tail.next both identify x.

questions.prompt: In a circular linked queue with tail pointer, enqueue y into a nonempty queue whose old tail is t. Which updates are correct?
answer: y.next=t.next; t.next=y; tail=y
questions.explanation: The old tail's successor is the front. The new node must point to that front, the old tail must point to the new node, and the new node becomes tail.

questions.prompt: A circular linked queue currently has 6 nodes. After 10 enqueues and 12 dequeues, assuming dequeues are valid, how many nodes remain?
questions.explanation: The count changes from six by +10-12, resulting in four nodes; the stated sequence is feasible since the maximum occupancy is 16 before removals.

questions.prompt: A queue stores tasks with arrival times and service durations. Which discipline guarantees service in arrival order regardless of duration?
answer: FIFO queue
questions.explanation: A FIFO queue removes tasks in the order they arrived. Priority queues keyed by duration may reorder tasks, and a stack reverses arrival order.

questions.prompt: Which data structures support O(1) amortized insertion and removal at both ends?
options: Deque implemented by a circular dynamic array
Doubly linked list with endpoint pointers
Singly linked list with only a head pointer
answer: Deque implemented by a circular dynamic array
Doubly linked list with endpoint pointers
questions.explanation: A circular dynamic array and a doubly linked list can support both endpoint operations in constant amortized or worst-case time. A singly linked head-only list cannot remove the tail in constant time.

questions.prompt: An input-restricted deque permits insertion at one end but deletion at both ends. A deletion at the rear is
answer: Allowed
questions.explanation: The restriction applies to insertion: it is permitted at only one end. Deletion remains permitted at either end.

questions.prompt: A queue receives items A,B,C,D. Two dequeues occur, followed by enqueue E and dequeue. Which item is returned by the third dequeue?
answer: C
questions.explanation: The first two dequeues remove A and B. E is added after D, so the next dequeue removes C.

questions.prompt: A deque initially contains 4 items. It performs 7 insertions and 5 deletions, all valid. What is its final size?
questions.explanation: The deque begins with four items. Seven insertions and five valid deletions change the size by a net increase of two, giving six.

questions.prompt: A stack can be implemented using two queues by making push costly. Which operation sequence maintains the newest item at the front of the primary queue?
options: On push, enqueue new item in auxiliary queue, move all primary items behind it, then swap queues
On pop, move all primary items into the auxiliary queue
Always dequeue the primary queue for pop
Sort both queues after every operation
answer: On push, enqueue new item in auxiliary queue, move all primary items behind it, then swap queues
questions.explanation: Enqueueing the new value first in the auxiliary queue and transferring old values behind it makes the new value the front. Swapping roles then allows O(1) pop from the primary queue.

questions.prompt: Which statements about implementing one ADT using another are correct?
options: A queue can be implemented using two stacks
A stack can be implemented using two queues
A queue can be implemented using a single ordinary stack with no recursion or extra state
The implementation may trade cost between operations while preserving behavior
answer: A queue can be implemented using two stacks
A stack can be implemented using two queues
The implementation may trade cost between operations while preserving behavior
questions.explanation: Two stacks can provide FIFO and two queues can provide LIFO. A single stack alone cannot generally reorder to FIFO without extra mechanisms; operation costs can be shifted.

questions.prompt: A bounded circular queue of capacity C uses a count variable. Which count values correspond to empty and full?
answer: 0 and C
questions.explanation: The explicit count ranges from zero elements to C elements inclusive. This distinguishes empty from full even when front equals rear in both states.

questions.prompt: A circular queue has capacity 12 and count=9. How many additional elements can be enqueued before it becomes full?
questions.explanation: The remaining capacity is C-count=12-9=3.

questions.prompt: A stack's push and pop operations are used to reverse a string. If the input is A,B,C,D in that order, what is the output when characters are popped?
answer: D,C,B,A
questions.explanation: The last character pushed is the first popped, so the output is the reverse order.

questions.prompt: A string of 7 distinct characters is pushed one by one onto a stack and then fully popped. How many inversions relative to the original order does the output have?
questions.explanation: The reversal places every pair in opposite order, giving n(n-1)/2=7*6/2=21 inversions.

questions.prompt: A queue is used to perform level-order traversal of a tree. When processing a node, when are its children enqueued?
options: After the node is dequeued, in left-to-right order
Only after all nodes at every level are processed
At the front of the queue
answer: After the node is dequeued, in left-to-right order
questions.explanation: The current node is removed, then its children are appended at the rear. Enqueueing left before right yields left-to-right traversal within each level.

questions.prompt: A tree has maximum branching factor b and height h. What is the worst-case auxiliary queue space for level-order traversal?
answer: O(b^h) in the broadest level
questions.explanation: The queue may hold an entire widest level. A full b-ary tree's last level can contain Theta(b^h) nodes, so queue space is proportional to maximum width.

questions.prompt: Which properties of a queue make it suitable for breadth-first search?
options: It processes vertices in order of discovery
It ensures vertices at distance d are processed before those at distance d+1
It selects the smallest numeric vertex label first
answer: It processes vertices in order of discovery
