questions.explanation: Each hexadecimal digit represents four bits. A 48-bit address therefore has 48/4=12 hexadecimal digits.

questions.prompt: A 48-bit MAC address is written using two hexadecimal digits per byte. How many bytes are represented?
questions.explanation: There are eight bits per byte, so 48/8=6 bytes. Each byte is shown by two hexadecimal digits.

questions.prompt: Which fields are commonly present in an Ethernet II frame?
options: An Ethernet II frame uses a hop-count field in place of the Type field
answer: Destination MAC address
Source MAC address
Type field
questions.explanation: Ethernet II includes destination and source MAC addresses and a Type field indicating the upper-layer protocol. TCP acknowledgment numbers reside in the transport header.

questions.prompt: A switch receives a frame whose destination MAC is unknown in its forwarding table. What does a learning Ethernet switch commonly do?
options: Flood it out other ports in the same VLAN except the incoming port
Route it using the destination IP
Send it only to the oldest learned port
answer: Flood it out other ports in the same VLAN except the incoming port
questions.explanation: For an unknown unicast destination, a switch floods the frame within the broadcast domain, excluding the port on which it arrived.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Ethernet switch learning are correct?
options: The source MAC and incoming port can be learned from a frame
The forwarding database maps MAC addresses to ports
A switch learns the destination port solely from the destination address of an incoming frame
answer: The source MAC and incoming port can be learned from a frame
The forwarding database maps MAC addresses to ports
Aging can remove stale entries
questions.explanation: A switch learns from source MAC addresses and records the associated input port. Dynamic entries age out; ordinary Ethernet switching is based on MAC rather than physical-layer signal interpretation or IP routing.

questions.prompt: A stop-and-wait link sends 2000-bit frames at 2 Mb/s. RTT excluding data transmission is 18 ms, ACK transmission negligible. Find utilization percentage.
questions.explanation: Transmission time is 1 ms. Cycle time is 1+18=19 ms, so utilization is 1/19≈0.05263=5.26%.

questions.prompt: One-way propagation delay is 5 ms and frame transmission time is 1 ms. A sliding window has 11 frames. Under the standard window-filling condition, is this sufficient to keep the sender busy?
options: No; at least 5 frames are needed
No; at least 21 frames are needed
No window can overcome propagation delay
answer: Yes; W=1+2a/Tt=11
questions.explanation: With a=5 ms and Tt=1 ms, the required window is 1+2a/Tt=1+10=11 frames. The stated window exactly meets the idealized condition.

questions.prompt: Which outcomes follow when a sender window is smaller than the number of frames needed to cover the bandwidth-delay product?
options: The sender may become idle while waiting for acknowledgments
The link can be underutilized despite available capacity
Increasing the window can improve utilization up to the path limit
A smaller sender window always increases link utilization
answer: The sender may become idle while waiting for acknowledgments
The link can be underutilized despite available capacity
Increasing the window can improve utilization up to the path limit
questions.explanation: An undersized window cannot keep enough data in flight to cover the feedback delay. Increasing it can raise utilization until the link or another bottleneck is saturated.

questions.prompt: Which statements about ARQ sequence-number spaces are correct?
options: Sequence numbers wrap modulo the field's value range
Window constraints prevent old and new frames from becoming ambiguous
Selective Repeat needs a smaller maximum window than the full sequence space
Selective Repeat can use a window of the entire sequence-number space without ambiguity
answer: Sequence numbers wrap modulo the field's value range
Window constraints prevent old and new frames from becoming ambiguous
Selective Repeat needs a smaller maximum window than the full sequence space
questions.explanation: An m-bit sequence number has 2^m values and wraps modulo that space. Window limits ensure the receiver can distinguish delayed duplicates from new transmissions.

questions.prompt: A two-bit Go-Back-N protocol uses sequence numbers modulo 4. Frames 2, 3, and 0 are sent. A cumulative ACK says the next expected frame is 0. How many of these frames remain unacknowledged?
questions.explanation: The ACK for next expected 0 confirms receipt of frames 2 and 3. Frame 0 is still outstanding, so one remains unacknowledged.

questions.prompt: Why is a Selective Repeat window limited to at most half of the sequence-number space?
options: To prevent an old delayed frame from being mistaken for a new frame after wraparound
To make the link rate exactly twice the RTT
To force the sender to retransmit all frames
answer: To prevent an old delayed frame from being mistaken for a new frame after wraparound
questions.explanation: If sender and receiver windows overlap across sequence-number wraparound, an old duplicate may appear to be a new frame. Keeping each window at most half the space avoids this ambiguity.

questions.prompt: Which events are handled differently by Go-Back-N and Selective Repeat?
options: Go-Back-N retransmits the missing frame and later outstanding frames
Selective Repeat can retransmit only the missing frame
Selective Repeat buffers out-of-order data frames
Go-Back-N buffers and individually acknowledges every out-of-order frame
answer: Go-Back-N retransmits the missing frame and later outstanding frames
Selective Repeat can retransmit only the missing frame
Selective Repeat buffers out-of-order data frames
questions.explanation: Go-Back-N recovers by resending the suffix beginning at the missing frame. Selective Repeat buffers later frames and selectively retransmits the missing one.

questions.prompt: An ACK in Go-Back-N states that the receiver expects sequence number 7. What does this cumulative ACK normally imply?
options: All frames before 7 have been received in order
Frames 7 and later have been delivered
answer: All frames before 7 have been received in order
questions.explanation: A cumulative ACK for the next expected number indicates that the receiver has accepted every preceding frame in sequence.

questions.prompt: A sender transmits 4-bit Go-Back-N frames with sequence numbers 0 through 15. If the next expected sequence is 14, what sequence number follows 15?
questions.explanation: Sequence numbers wrap modulo 16. After 15, the next value is 0.

questions.prompt: Which statements about acknowledgments and retransmissions are correct?
options: A duplicate ACK can indicate a missing earlier frame
Sequence numbers help suppress duplicate delivery
A duplicate ACK proves that the reverse path has no packet loss
answer: A duplicate ACK can indicate a missing earlier frame
Timeouts can trigger retransmission
Sequence numbers help suppress duplicate delivery
questions.explanation: Repeated cumulative acknowledgments often signal a gap; timers recover when feedback is absent. Sequence numbers let receivers recognize duplicate frames, while ACKs are separate control messages.

questions.prompt: In a link protocol with bit errors, why is a checksum or CRC added to each frame?
options: To detect corruption before accepting the frame
To guarantee the frame is delivered
answer: To detect corruption before accepting the frame
questions.explanation: Error-detection bits allow the receiver to identify many corrupted frames. Detection alone does not guarantee delivery; ARQ may be used for recovery.

questions.prompt: A 1200-byte payload has a 4-byte CRC field and a 6-byte framing header. What is the total frame length?
questions.explanation: The frame consists of 1200 payload bytes plus 4 CRC bytes and 6 header bytes: 1210 bytes.

questions.prompt: Which statements about checksums and CRCs are correct?
options: They add redundancy for error detection
They can detect but not necessarily correct errors
CRC operates on polynomial representations over GF(2)
A CRC can always reconstruct the original corrupted bits without retransmission
answer: They add redundancy for error detection
They can detect but not necessarily correct errors
CRC operates on polynomial representations over GF(2)
questions.explanation: Checksums and CRCs detect corruption by adding check bits; correction needs additional coding or retransmission. Some error patterns can yield a valid check value, so passing is not absolute proof.

questions.prompt: Which error patterns are guaranteed to be detected by a degree-r CRC generator?
options: Every nonzero burst error of length at most r
Every burst error of length r+1
Every error pattern containing an even number of bit flips
Only burst errors whose length is exactly r
answer: Every nonzero burst error of length at most r
questions.explanation: A degree-r generator guarantees detection of all nonzero burst errors up to length r. Some longer error polynomials are multiples of the generator and can be undetected.

questions.prompt: A received CRC codeword has a nonzero remainder under the agreed generator. What is the correct interpretation?
options: The sender used an even number of bits
answer: The receiver detected an error
questions.explanation: A nonzero remainder means the received polynomial is not divisible by the agreed generator, so the CRC check detects corruption.

questions.prompt: Which statements about error-detecting codes are correct?
options: A valid codeword is selected from a subset of all bit strings
Redundancy can make some corrupted strings invalid
Some error patterns can transform one valid codeword into another
Every possible bit string is a valid codeword when redundancy is added
answer: A valid codeword is selected from a subset of all bit strings
Redundancy can make some corrupted strings invalid
Some error patterns can transform one valid codeword into another
questions.explanation: Coding redundancy separates valid codewords, enabling detection or correction within distance limits. A corruption may land on another codeword, and detection alone does not correct it.

questions.prompt: A code's minimum distance is 4. Which pair of guarantees is valid?
answer: Detect 3 errors and correct 1
questions.explanation: Detection is guaranteed through d−1=3 errors, and correction through floor((4−1)/2)=1 error.

questions.prompt: A parity code adds one bit to 7 data bits. What is the resulting codeword length?
questions.explanation: One parity bit is appended to the seven data bits, producing an 8-bit codeword.

questions.prompt: Which statements about a single parity bit are correct?
options: It detects every odd number of flipped bits
It can fail to detect two flipped bits
It adds one bit of redundancy
A single parity bit detects every pattern with an even number of flips
answer: It detects every odd number of flipped bits
It can fail to detect two flipped bits
It adds one bit of redundancy
questions.explanation: Parity checks only whether the total number of 1s has the required parity. It detects odd-weight errors but gives no location information, and two flips preserve parity.

questions.prompt: In Ethernet CSMA/CD, why does the jam signal follow collision detection?
options: To ensure all stations on the collision domain recognize the collision
answer: To ensure all stations on the collision domain recognize the collision
questions.explanation: The jam sequence makes the collision event sufficiently noticeable across the shared medium before stations enter backoff.

questions.prompt: A shared Ethernet has a slot time of 51.2 microseconds. At 100 Mb/s, how many bits are transmitted during one slot?
questions.explanation: 100,000,000×51.2×10^−6=5,120 bits are transmitted in one slot interval.

questions.prompt: Which properties are associated with switched full-duplex Ethernet?
options: A dedicated point-to-point link can carry simultaneous send and receive traffic
Collisions are not expected on a full-duplex link
Full-duplex switched links use collision backoff independently in both directions
answer: A dedicated point-to-point link can carry simultaneous send and receive traffic
Collisions are not expected on a full-duplex link
CSMA/CD is unnecessary
questions.explanation: Full-duplex switched links separate transmit and receive paths between a host and switch. They do not use the shared-medium collision mechanism.

questions.prompt: A station has experienced several consecutive collisions. What effect does binary exponential backoff have?
options: It expands the random backoff window as collisions accumulate
It forces immediate retransmission every time
It reduces the frame's CRC length
answer: It expands the random backoff window as collisions accumulate
questions.explanation: Increasing the contention window after repeated collisions reduces the chance that the same stations retransmit simultaneously again.

questions.prompt: Which statements about ALOHA protocols are correct?
options: Pure ALOHA allows transmission at arbitrary times
Slotted ALOHA restricts transmissions to slot boundaries
Slotted ALOHA has a shorter vulnerable period than pure ALOHA
Pure ALOHA has half the vulnerable period of slotted ALOHA
answer: Pure ALOHA allows transmission at arbitrary times
Slotted ALOHA restricts transmissions to slot boundaries
Slotted ALOHA has a shorter vulnerable period than pure ALOHA
questions.explanation: Slotted operation aligns frame starts and reduces the vulnerable period from two frame times to one. Both remain random-access protocols and can collide.

questions.prompt: Classic Ethernet operates at 100 Mb/s. The maximum one-way propagation delay is 25.6 microseconds. What minimum frame size in bytes is needed to ensure a sender is still transmitting when a worst-case collision returns? Ignore jam bits.
questions.explanation: The round-trip propagation time is 51.2 microseconds. At 100 Mb/s, 5120 bits can be transmitted during that interval, which is 640 bytes.

questions.prompt: For pure ALOHA, the vulnerable period for a frame of duration T is
answer: 2T
questions.explanation: A frame can collide with another that starts up to T before or T after its start. The total vulnerable interval is 2T.

questions.prompt: Which statements about CSMA persistence strategies are correct?
options: 1-persistent transmits immediately when the medium becomes idle
Nonpersistent waits a random time after sensing busy
p-persistent applies probabilistic transmission at slot boundaries
Nonpersistent CSMA transmits continuously while the channel is busy
answer: 1-persistent transmits immediately when the medium becomes idle
Nonpersistent waits a random time after sensing busy
p-persistent applies probabilistic transmission at slot boundaries
questions.explanation: The variants define how a station behaves when it senses a busy or idle channel. Propagation can still cause collisions, so none eliminates them entirely.

questions.prompt: A link's one-way propagation delay is 4 microseconds and rate is 25 Mb/s. What frame size in bits has transmission time equal to the round-trip propagation time?
questions.explanation: Round-trip propagation is 8 microseconds. Multiply by 25×10^6 bits/s to get 200 bits.

questions.prompt: An Ethernet collision domain has round-trip propagation time 40 microseconds at 10 Mb/s. What minimum frame size satisfies the collision-detection timing condition?
answer: 400 bits
questions.explanation: The minimum frame transmission time must cover the 40-microsecond round trip. At 10 Mb/s, that is 10,000,000×40×10^−6=400 bits.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Ethernet framing and collision handling are correct?
options: The frame check sequence detects many transmission errors
The minimum frame size supports collision detection in classic Ethernet
Backoff randomizes retransmission timing after collision
Ethernet backoff guarantees that a collision never occurs again
answer: The frame check sequence detects many transmission errors
The minimum frame size supports collision detection in classic Ethernet
Backoff randomizes retransmission timing after collision
questions.explanation: Ethernet uses an FCS for error detection, a minimum frame size related to collision timing, and backoff after collisions. The interframe gap is timing, not an address field.

questions.prompt: A 1500-byte Ethernet payload is sent in a frame with 18 bytes of header and trailer overhead. How many total bytes are carried, ignoring preamble and interframe gap?
questions.explanation: Add the payload and stated overhead: 1500+18=1518 bytes.

questions.prompt: A receiver gets a frame with a CRC remainder that is nonzero. What should it conclude?
options: An error has been detected and the frame should not be accepted as valid
The sender has received an ACK
answer: An error has been detected and the frame should not be accepted as valid
questions.explanation: A nonzero syndrome indicates that the received bit sequence fails the CRC check. The receiver treats it as corrupted and discards it or requests retransmission per protocol.

questions.prompt: A 4-bit CRC remainder is appended to a 100-bit dataword. What is the resulting codeword length?
questions.explanation: The codeword includes the original 100 data bits plus 4 CRC bits, totaling 104 bits.

questions.prompt: Which statements about a sliding-window link protocol are correct?
options: It can keep multiple frames in flight
It can improve utilization on a long-RTT link
It requires sequence numbers to identify frames
A sliding window permits only one unacknowledged frame at a time
answer: It can keep multiple frames in flight
It can improve utilization on a long-RTT link
It requires sequence numbers to identify frames
questions.explanation: Sliding windows pipeline frames and use sequence numbers to track outstanding data. Reliable ARQ still uses acknowledgments or equivalent feedback.

questions.prompt: A 5-bit sequence number field is used. What is the sequence-number space size?
questions.explanation: An m-bit field represents 2^m values. For m=5, there are 32 sequence numbers.

questions.prompt: A Go-Back-N receiver expects frame 7 in a modulo-8 sequence space, but receives frame 0 before frame 7. What does it normally do?
options: Discard frame 0 and repeat the ACK for frame 7
Buffer frame 0 and deliver it immediately
answer: Discard frame 0 and repeat the ACK for frame 7
questions.explanation: Go-Back-N accepts only the next in-order frame. Since 7 is missing, frame 0 is out of order and is discarded; the receiver indicates that 7 is still expected.

questions.prompt: A Selective Repeat receiver has an in-window frame 0 arrive before missing frame 7, with sequence numbers modulo 8. What can it do?
options: Buffer and acknowledge frame 0 while waiting for frame 7
Discard frame 0 because every protocol is Go-Back-N
Deliver frame 0 before all preceding data
answer: Buffer and acknowledge frame 0 while waiting for frame 7
questions.explanation: Selective Repeat can accept an in-window out-of-order frame, store it, and acknowledge it individually. Ordered delivery can resume after frame 7 fills the gap.

questions.prompt: Which statements about error detection versus error correction are correct?
options: Detection can indicate corruption without identifying the original bits
Correction requires enough redundancy to infer the intended codeword
ARQ can recover by retransmission after detecting an error
Error detection always identifies the exact positions of all corrupted bits
answer: Detection can indicate corruption without identifying the original bits
Correction requires enough redundancy to infer the intended codeword
ARQ can recover by retransmission after detecting an error
questions.explanation: Detection flags invalid data; correction needs sufficient code distance to identify the transmitted codeword. One parity bit detects a single-bit error but cannot locate which bit flipped.

questions.prompt: An even-parity receiver sees data plus parity containing an odd number of 1s. What can it conclude?
options: The exact error location is known
answer: A parity error is detected
questions.explanation: An odd count violates the even-parity rule, so an error is detected. Parity alone cannot determine the error location or number of flipped bits.

questions.prompt: A codeword is changed by flipping exactly one bit. Which additional property is needed to guarantee that the receiver can identify and correct the flipped bit?
options: A code with minimum distance at least 3
answer: A code with minimum distance at least 3
questions.explanation: Correcting one error requires disjoint radius-one decoding neighborhoods, which needs minimum distance 2t+1=3. A parity bit can detect a single error but cannot locate it.

questions.prompt: Which statements summarize reliable data-link communication?
options: Frames can be protected with error-detection bits
Retransmissions can recover from loss or detected corruption
Acknowledgments eliminate the need for sequence numbers and duplicate suppression
answer: Frames can be protected with error-detection bits
Acknowledgments provide receiver feedback
Retransmissions can recover from loss or detected corruption
questions.explanation: Reliable link protocols combine detection and feedback with retransmission. They can recover from many errors but cannot ensure the physical medium never produces errors.

questions.prompt: The Domain Name System primarily maps
options: domain names to resource records such as IP addresses
MAC addresses to Ethernet frame checksums
answer: domain names to resource records such as IP addresses
questions.explanation: DNS is a distributed naming system that stores diverse resource records, including address records that map names to IP addresses.

questions.prompt: A DNS resolver commonly queries which port?
questions.explanation: DNS traditionally uses port 53 for both UDP and TCP transport.

questions.prompt: Which transports can DNS use on port 53?
answer: UDP
TCP
questions.explanation: DNS commonly uses UDP for ordinary queries and TCP for zone transfers or responses that require reliable stream transport; both use port 53.

questions.prompt: A DNS stub resolver sends a recursive query when it asks the resolver to
options: return the final answer or an error after performing necessary lookups
return only a list of root servers
refuse to contact other DNS servers
translate an IP address to a MAC address
answer: return the final answer or an error after performing necessary lookups
questions.explanation: With recursion desired, the contacted resolver performs the lookup process on behalf of the client and returns a final result or failure.

questions.prompt: In iterative DNS resolution, a server that lacks the answer may return
options: the final answer in every case
answer: a referral to another server
questions.explanation: An iterative server can refer the resolver to another authoritative server closer to the answer rather than performing the remaining lookup itself.

questions.prompt: How many root DNS server identifier letters are commonly named, from A through M?
questions.explanation: The root server system has 13 named identifiers A through M, each implemented by many anycast instances worldwide.

questions.prompt: A DNS resolver commonly begins an iterative lookup by querying a
answer: root server
questions.explanation: The resolver starts at the DNS root, which refers it to the appropriate top-level domain servers.

questions.prompt: A root DNS server typically returns a referral to
options: the final A record for every domain
the authoritative server for every hostname directly
answer: a TLD name server
questions.explanation: The root zone delegates top-level domains such as .com or .org to their TLD name servers; it usually does not hold individual host records.

questions.prompt: Which are common DNS record types and their purposes?
options: A maps a name to an IPv4 address
AAAA maps a name to an IPv6 address
CNAME stores a TCP port number
answer: A maps a name to an IPv4 address
AAAA maps a name to an IPv6 address
MX identifies mail exchangers
questions.explanation: A, AAAA, and MX are standard record types. CNAME creates an alias to another DNS name, not a TCP port mapping.

questions.prompt: An AAAA DNS record stores
answer: an IPv6 address
questions.explanation: AAAA records map a DNS name to an IPv6 address; A records carry IPv4 addresses.

questions.prompt: A CNAME record represents
options: an alias from one DNS name to another DNS name
answer: an alias from one DNS name to another DNS name
questions.explanation: CNAME specifies that an owner name is an alias whose canonical target is another domain name.

questions.prompt: How many IPv4 addresses does one A resource record contain?
questions.explanation: An individual A record holds one IPv4 address; a name may have multiple A records.

questions.prompt: The MX record's preference value is used to
options: order mail exchangers, with lower values preferred
specify the mail server's TCP port
answer: order mail exchangers, with lower values preferred
questions.explanation: Lower MX preference numbers indicate more preferred mail exchangers; multiple records provide fallback choices.

questions.prompt: Two MX records have preferences 10 and 20. Which preference is tried first? Give the number.
questions.explanation: The smaller MX preference value has higher priority, so preference 10 is preferred over 20.

questions.prompt: A PTR record is primarily used for
options: reverse lookup from an IP address to a name
mapping a name to an IPv4 address
answer: reverse lookup from an IP address to a name
questions.explanation: PTR records provide reverse DNS mappings, typically under in-addr.arpa for IPv4 or ip6.arpa for IPv6.

questions.prompt: The reverse DNS name for IPv4 address 192.0.2.7 is formed under
answer: 7.2.0.192.in-addr.arpa
questions.explanation: IPv4 reverse lookup reverses the octets and appends in-addr.arpa, giving 7.2.0.192.in-addr.arpa.

questions.prompt: How many octets are reversed to form an IPv4 in-addr.arpa name?
questions.explanation: An IPv4 address has four octets, all reversed in the reverse DNS name.

questions.prompt: The DNS hierarchy has root at the top, followed by
options: top-level domains, second-level domains, and lower labels
IP subnets, MAC addresses, then hostnames
answer: top-level domains, second-level domains, and lower labels
questions.explanation: Below the root are TLDs, then delegated domains and subdomains represented by labels in the name.

questions.prompt: In DNS, the fully qualified domain name www.example.com. includes a final dot representing
answer: the DNS root
questions.explanation: The trailing dot denotes the root label, making the name absolute and fully qualified rather than relative to a search suffix.

questions.prompt: How many labels appear in www.example.com. if the root label is included?
questions.explanation: The labels are www, example, com, and the root label, totaling four.

questions.prompt: A DNS resolver returns a cached answer only while
options: the answer contains an IPv4 address
answer: its TTL has not expired
questions.explanation: Caching obeys each resource record's TTL; after it expires, the resolver should obtain fresh data before answering from cache.

questions.prompt: A DNS record has TTL 3600 seconds. How many minutes is this?
questions.explanation: There are 60 seconds per minute; 3600 seconds equals 60 minutes.

questions.prompt: A DNS TTL of zero generally means
options: the record should not be cached for future use
answer: the record should not be cached for future use
questions.explanation: A zero TTL indicates that a resolver should not retain the answer in cache beyond the immediate response.

questions.prompt: Which DNS message fields or sections are present in a typical DNS response format?
answer: Header
Question section
Answer section
Authority/additional sections
questions.explanation: DNS messages contain a header and question, answer, authority, and additional sections; some sections may be empty depending on the response.

questions.prompt: The DNS transaction ID is used to
options: match a response to its outstanding query
answer: match a response to its outstanding query
questions.explanation: The transaction identifier lets a requester correlate a reply with the query that initiated it, especially when multiple queries are pending.

questions.prompt: A DNS message uses a 16-bit transaction ID. How many distinct identifiers can it represent?
questions.explanation: A 16-bit field has 2^16 possible values, equal to 65,536.

questions.prompt: The DNS recursion desired (RD) bit is set by a client to
options: request recursive service from the contacted resolver
indicate that the answer is cached
answer: request recursive service from the contacted resolver
questions.explanation: RD asks the contacted DNS server to perform recursion and return a final result, if it offers that service.

questions.prompt: The DNS recursion available (RA) bit indicates
options: whether the query asked for an AAAA record
answer: whether the server supports recursion
questions.explanation: RA reports whether recursive service is available from the responding server.

questions.prompt: A DNS response has the TC (truncated) bit set. Is it truncated? Use 1 for yes and 0 for no.
questions.explanation: TC stands for truncated and indicates that the response was shortened, often prompting a retry over TCP.

questions.prompt: When a UDP DNS response is too large for the permitted message size, a client may
answer: retry using TCP
questions.explanation: A response with truncation set can lead the resolver to retry over TCP, which supports larger reliable DNS messages.

questions.prompt: DNS zone transfers commonly use
answer: TCP
questions.explanation: AXFR/IXFR zone transfers use TCP for reliable transfer of potentially large zone data, though ordinary DNS queries commonly use UDP.

questions.prompt: An authoritative DNS server is one that
options: serves records from zones for which it has authority
translates names directly to Ethernet addresses
answer: serves records from zones for which it has authority
questions.explanation: An authoritative server holds or serves zone data for its delegated namespace and provides authoritative answers for those records.

questions.prompt: Which statements about authoritative and recursive DNS servers are true?
options: A recursive resolver follows referrals on behalf of a client
An authoritative server answers from its zones
One server can provide both roles
A root server is authoritative for every hostname
answer: A recursive resolver follows referrals on behalf of a client
An authoritative server answers from its zones
One server can provide both roles
questions.explanation: Recursive resolvers follow referrals for clients; authoritative servers answer from their zones; and one server can implement both roles. Root servers are authoritative for the root zone, not every hostname.

questions.prompt: The AA bit in a DNS response indicates
options: the responding server's answer is authoritative
answer: the responding server's answer is authoritative
questions.explanation: AA means authoritative answer for the queried name, signaling that the response comes from an authoritative source.

questions.prompt: A resolver receives a DNS response with AA=1. Is the authoritative-answer bit set? Use 1 for yes and 0 for no.
questions.explanation: The AA flag value one indicates the response is marked authoritative.

questions.prompt: A DNS NXDOMAIN response indicates
options: the queried domain name does not exist
the name exists but has no A record only
answer: the queried domain name does not exist
questions.explanation: NXDOMAIN is the negative response code indicating the queried name does not exist in the DNS namespace.

questions.prompt: A NODATA response generally means
options: the name exists but lacks the requested record type
the domain name itself does not exist
the resolver cannot reach any server
answer: the name exists but lacks the requested record type
questions.explanation: NODATA indicates that the name exists but no record of the requested type is available at that name.

questions.prompt: A DNS lookup returns three A records for one name. How many IPv4 addresses were returned?
questions.explanation: Each A record contains one IPv4 address; three A records return three addresses.

questions.prompt: DNS round-robin can distribute clients by
options: returning multiple address records in varying order
assigning a different top-level domain per query
answer: returning multiple address records in varying order
questions.explanation: A DNS server or resolver can vary the ordering of multiple A/AAAA records, spreading client selections across addresses, though it is not full load balancing.

questions.prompt: DNS caching improves performance primarily by
options: reducing repeated queries to authoritative servers
answer: reducing repeated queries to authoritative servers
questions.explanation: Cached answers are served locally until TTL expiry, reducing lookup latency and upstream query load.

questions.prompt: A DNS zone is
options: a portion of the namespace administered as a unit
answer: a portion of the namespace administered as a unit
questions.explanation: A zone is an administratively managed part of the DNS namespace, served by authoritative name servers and defined by zone data.

questions.prompt: The SOA record contains information such as
options: zone authority, serial number, and timers
answer: zone authority, serial number, and timers
questions.explanation: The Start of Authority record identifies zone metadata including primary server, responsible party, serial, and refresh/retry/expiry timers.

questions.prompt: A DNS SOA serial number is 32 bits. How many bits wide is it?
questions.explanation: The SOA serial field is a 32-bit unsigned integer used to track zone versions for transfers and synchronization.

questions.prompt: Which values are commonly specified in an SOA record?
answer: Serial number
Refresh and retry intervals
Expire interval
questions.explanation: SOA metadata includes serial, refresh, retry, and expire timers (as well as minimum TTL-related information). TCP congestion state is unrelated.

questions.prompt: A secondary authoritative DNS server obtains zone data from a primary using
answer: zone transfer
questions.explanation: Secondaries synchronize authoritative zone copies from a primary through AXFR or IXFR zone transfer mechanisms.

questions.prompt: An NS record identifies
options: name servers authoritative for a zone or delegated domain
the IPv4 address of a host
the canonical name of an alias
answer: name servers authoritative for a zone or delegated domain
questions.explanation: NS records list the authoritative name servers for a zone or delegation; glue A/AAAA records may accompany them.

questions.prompt: Glue records are used to
options: provide address records for in-bailiwick name servers needed to reach the delegation
answer: provide address records for in-bailiwick name servers needed to reach the delegation
questions.explanation: When a delegated name server is inside the delegated domain, glue provides its address to avoid a circular dependency during resolution.

questions.prompt: A DNS name has two NS records. How many listed name-server hostnames does it have?
questions.explanation: Each NS record names one server; two NS records list two name-server hostnames.

questions.prompt: A DNS resolver detects a delegation referral when a response provides
options: NS records for a child zone
answer: NS records for a child zone
questions.explanation: A delegation is represented by NS records identifying the child zone's authoritative name servers, often accompanied by glue.

questions.prompt: Which statements about DNS delegation are true?
options: A parent zone can delegate a child zone using NS records
The child zone's authoritative servers serve its zone data
Glue may help resolve in-bailiwick name-server addresses
Delegation transfers the entire root zone to the child
answer: A parent zone can delegate a child zone using NS records
The child zone's authoritative servers serve its zone data
Glue may help resolve in-bailiwick name-server addresses
questions.explanation: A parent zone delegates a child through NS records. Child authoritative servers serve that child records, and glue may supply addresses for in-bailiwick nameservers. Delegation does not transfer the root zone.

questions.prompt: DNSSEC primarily provides
options: data origin authentication and integrity for DNS data
answer: data origin authentication and integrity for DNS data
questions.explanation: DNSSEC adds cryptographic signatures and chain-of-trust validation for authenticity and integrity; it does not encrypt queries or allocate addresses.

questions.prompt: DNSSEC signatures are carried in which record type?
answer: RRSIG
questions.explanation: RRSIG records contain digital signatures covering DNS resource record sets.

questions.prompt: If a DNSSEC-signed RRset has 4 records and a signature record is included separately, how many records are counted in the RRset itself?
questions.explanation: The RRSIG signs the RRset but is a separate DNS record; the RRset still contains its four data records.

questions.prompt: A DNSSEC DS record in a parent zone helps
options: authenticate a child's DNSKEY during chain validation
specify a recursive resolver's cache size
answer: authenticate a child's DNSKEY during chain validation
questions.explanation: A Delegation Signer record stores a digest of a child's DNSKEY, linking the parent's trust chain to the child zone.

questions.prompt: A validating resolver that cannot validate a required DNSSEC chain may
options: return a validation failure such as SERVFAIL
answer: return a validation failure such as SERVFAIL
questions.explanation: If validation is required and signatures or chain data fail checks, the resolver typically reports a failure rather than treating the data as secure.

questions.prompt: Which statements about DNSSEC are true?
options: It provides integrity and origin authentication
It encrypts the queried domain name by itself
Trust is established through a chain from a trust anchor
answer: It signs RRsets
It provides integrity and origin authentication
Trust is established through a chain from a trust anchor
questions.explanation: DNSSEC signs RRsets and provides data integrity and origin authentication through a chain from a trust anchor. It does not encrypt query names; encrypted DNS transport is separate.

questions.prompt: DNS over TLS conventionally uses
answer: TCP port 853
questions.explanation: DNS over TLS conventionally uses TCP port 853 to protect DNS traffic with TLS.

questions.prompt: DNS over HTTPS carries DNS messages inside
answer: HTTPS requests
questions.explanation: DoH encapsulates DNS queries and responses in HTTPS, typically over port 443.

questions.prompt: If a DNS query is carried over HTTPS on the conventional service port, what port number is used?
questions.explanation: HTTPS conventionally uses TCP port 443 for DNS over HTTPS deployments.

questions.prompt: Encrypted DNS transport such as DoT or DoH primarily protects
options: the truth of every DNS answer without validation
the destination web server from all attacks
answer: DNS query confidentiality in transit
questions.explanation: TLS encryption hides DNS message contents from passive observers on the path but does not itself prove that answers are authentic or correct.

questions.prompt: The DNS message opcode identifies
options: the kind of query or operation requested
answer: the kind of query or operation requested
questions.explanation: Opcode identifies the DNS operation, such as a standard query, status request, or update.

questions.prompt: The DNS response code NXDOMAIN is an example of
answer: a negative response code
questions.explanation: NXDOMAIN is a DNS response code indicating that the queried name does not exist.

questions.prompt: A DNS label can contain at most how many octets?
questions.explanation: DNS wire-format labels are limited to 63 octets each.

questions.prompt: The maximum wire-format DNS name length is
answer: 255 octets
questions.explanation: A full DNS name is limited to 255 octets in wire format, including length fields and the terminating root label.

questions.prompt: A DNS query for example.com with type A requests
answer: IPv4 address records
questions.explanation: The A query type asks for IPv4 address resource records associated with the owner name.

questions.prompt: How many bits are in an IPv6 address returned in an AAAA record?
questions.explanation: An IPv6 address has 128 bits; AAAA records contain such addresses.

questions.prompt: Which DNS query types commonly return address information?
answer: A
AAAA
questions.explanation: A returns IPv4 addresses and AAAA returns IPv6 addresses. PTR provides reverse names and MX mail exchange information.

questions.prompt: DNS name comparison is generally
options: based on the server's local timezone
performed after converting to an IP address
answer: case-insensitive for ASCII letters
questions.explanation: DNS domain names are case-insensitive in ASCII, although case may be preserved in presentation.

questions.prompt: The owner name in a DNS resource record identifies
options: the domain name to which the record pertains
the number of bytes in the answer
answer: the domain name to which the record pertains
questions.explanation: The owner name specifies the DNS name associated with the record's type and data.

questions.prompt: A DNS response's answer section contains 5 resource records. How many answer records are present?
questions.explanation: The answer count is five, matching the five records in the response answer section.

questions.prompt: A recursive resolver uses a negative cache to
options: temporarily remember that a name or record type was not found
store only successful A records forever
answer: temporarily remember that a name or record type was not found
questions.explanation: Negative caching stores authoritative denial information for a limited period, reducing repeated queries for nonexistent names or absent types.

questions.prompt: DNS cache poisoning attempts to
options: insert false DNS data into a resolver's cache
increase the TTL of every valid record
change an Ethernet switch's MAC table
answer: insert false DNS data into a resolver's cache
questions.explanation: Cache poisoning seeks to cause a resolver to cache forged name-to-data mappings, redirecting users to incorrect destinations.

questions.prompt: Which practices help reduce DNS cache-poisoning risk?
options: Use unpredictable query identifiers and source ports
Validate DNSSEC when available and required
Accept unsolicited replies from any source
answer: Use unpredictable query identifiers and source ports
Validate DNSSEC when available and required
Match responses to outstanding queries
questions.explanation: Unpredictability and strict response matching make forgery harder; DNSSEC validation authenticates signed data. Unsolicited replies should not be accepted.

questions.prompt: A DNS resolver should match a response to a query using
answer: transaction ID and query/endpoint context
questions.explanation: Matching transaction identifiers, question data, and transport endpoint context helps reject unrelated or forged responses.

questions.prompt: A DNS cache entry has a remaining TTL of 45 seconds. After 20 seconds, what TTL remains if no refresh occurs?
questions.explanation: TTL counts down with elapsed cache time; 45-20=25 seconds remain.

questions.prompt: When a DNS TTL expires in a recursive resolver, the resolver generally
options: must refresh the data before using it as a valid cached answer
answer: must refresh the data before using it as a valid cached answer
questions.explanation: Once TTL expires, the cached record is stale and should not be served as an ordinary valid cache answer without refresh or a specific stale-answer policy.

questions.prompt: A DNS alias chain A CNAME B, B CNAME C, and C A-record 192.0.2.8 resolves A to
questions.explanation: The resolver follows CNAME targets until it reaches the terminal A record at C, yielding address 192.0.2.8 for the alias chain.

questions.prompt: A CNAME chain contains 3 alias links before an A record. How many CNAME records are followed?
questions.explanation: Each alias link corresponds to one CNAME record, so three links require following three CNAMEs.

questions.prompt: A CNAME owner name generally cannot coexist with
options: other data records at that same owner name, except DNSSEC-related records
an A record at its target
an MX record at its target
answer: other data records at that same owner name, except DNSSEC-related records
questions.explanation: A CNAME makes the owner an alias, so it generally cannot have other data types at that same name, subject to protocol-defined exceptions such as DNSSEC records.

questions.prompt: A wildcard DNS record can synthesize an answer when
options: no closer explicit name exists and the query matches the wildcard rules
every query is sent to the root
the name is an IP address
answer: no closer explicit name exists and the query matches the wildcard rules
questions.explanation: Wildcard synthesis applies to otherwise nonexistent names under the relevant zone node; closer explicit names or delegations affect the result.

questions.prompt: An MX record points to
options: a mail server hostname, which is resolved separately
answer: a mail server hostname, which is resolved separately
questions.explanation: MX RDATA names a mail exchanger host and preference; the mail server's A or AAAA records are looked up separately.

questions.prompt: A domain publishes an MX record pointing to mail.example.com but no address record for that host. The mail exchanger may be
options: unreachable by name until address data is provided
automatically assigned the domain's A record
converted to a CNAME by the resolver
answer: unreachable by name until address data is provided
questions.explanation: The MX target must ultimately resolve to an address; without an A/AAAA record or another valid resolution path, clients cannot connect to it.

questions.prompt: A DNS response contains 2 MX records and 3 A records. How many resource records are in these two sets combined?
questions.explanation: The response has two MX records and three A records, totaling five records across the sets.

questions.prompt: Which statements about DNS CNAME records are true?
options: The target is another domain name
Aliases may require additional queries or records to reach an address
A CNAME is itself an IP address
A CNAME owner generally cannot also have unrelated data records
answer: The target is another domain name
Aliases may require additional queries or records to reach an address
A CNAME owner generally cannot also have unrelated data records
questions.explanation: A CNAME points to a canonical DNS name, not an address. Resolution follows the target, and CNAME owners generally cannot coexist with other ordinary data.

questions.prompt: DNS uses a distributed hierarchy primarily to
options: ensure every query reaches one central server
answer: scale naming and delegate administration
questions.explanation: The hierarchy and delegation distribute responsibility and load across root, TLD, and authoritative servers rather than relying on one global database.

questions.prompt: A recursive resolver's cache may contain
options: answers from many domains with remaining TTLs
only records from the root zone
the entire global DNS database permanently
answer: answers from many domains with remaining TTLs
questions.explanation: Resolvers cache records learned from different authorities until their TTLs expire; cache contents vary and are not permanent or complete.

questions.prompt: A cached DNS record starts with TTL 300 seconds. After 2 minutes, how many seconds remain?
questions.explanation: Two minutes is 120 seconds; 300-120=180 seconds remain.

questions.prompt: A resolver can answer from cache without contacting authoritative servers if
options: a usable unexpired cached answer is present
the query is for an A record only
the client sets RD to zero
answer: a usable unexpired cached answer is present
questions.explanation: An unexpired cached record matching the query can be returned directly, avoiding an upstream lookup.

questions.prompt: If the answer is absent from cache, a recursive resolver may contact
options: root, TLD, and authoritative servers through referrals
answer: root, TLD, and authoritative servers through referrals
questions.explanation: The resolver follows the DNS hierarchy from root to TLD to the authoritative zone, using referrals until it obtains the answer.

questions.prompt: Which may be returned in the additional section of a DNS response?
options: Glue A/AAAA records for name servers
A records related to an MX target
Records that help avoid extra lookups
answer: Glue A/AAAA records for name servers
A records related to an MX target
Records that help avoid extra lookups
questions.explanation: The additional section can include useful address data such as glue or mail-server addresses. It contains DNS resource records, not arbitrary application payload.

questions.prompt: Glue data is called glue because it
options: helps connect a delegation to the address of an in-bailiwick name server
answer: helps connect a delegation to the address of an in-bailiwick name server
questions.explanation: Glue supplies the address needed to contact a delegated nameserver whose name itself lies within the delegated namespace.

questions.prompt: A DNS answer has TTL 7200 seconds. Express it in hours.
questions.explanation: There are 3600 seconds in an hour, so 7200 seconds equals two hours.

questions.prompt: Which DNS record type maps a domain to a mail exchanger?
answer: MX
questions.explanation: MX records specify mail exchange hosts and preference values for a domain.

questions.prompt: Which record type identifies a zone's authoritative name servers?
answer: NS
questions.explanation: NS records list the authoritative name servers associated with a zone or delegation.

questions.prompt: Which DNS records can contain textual metadata or service information rather than simple host address mappings?
answer: TXT
SRV
SOA
questions.explanation: TXT stores text, SRV identifies service endpoints and ports, and SOA contains zone metadata. AAAA stores an IPv6 address.

questions.prompt: An SRV record includes a port number because it identifies
options: the transport endpoint for a named service
the TTL of an A record
answer: the transport endpoint for a named service
questions.explanation: SRV records publish service target, port, priority, and weight information for locating a service endpoint.

questions.prompt: An SRV record specifies service port 8443. What numeric port does it advertise?
questions.explanation: The port field directly identifies TCP or UDP port 8443 for the target service.

questions.prompt: A TXT record is commonly used to
options: publish arbitrary textual data such as verification or email-policy data
map directly to an IPv4 address
answer: publish arbitrary textual data such as verification or email-policy data
questions.explanation: TXT records carry textual strings used by many applications and policies, including domain verification and email authentication frameworks.

questions.prompt: DNSSEC's RRSIG validity period is relevant because
options: signatures are valid only within their inception and expiration times
it is the same as a record TTL
answer: signatures are valid only within their inception and expiration times
questions.explanation: RRSIG records specify inception and expiration times; validators reject signatures used outside their validity interval.

questions.prompt: A DNSSEC validating resolver checks the chain of trust from
options: a configured trust anchor through signed delegations to the answer
the client's MAC address to the root server
the TCP source port to the MX record
the answer TTL to the default route
answer: a configured trust anchor through signed delegations to the answer
questions.explanation: Validation follows DNSKEY and DS relationships from a trust anchor, verifying signatures along delegations to the target RRset.

questions.prompt: HTTP is primarily an
options: application-layer protocol for transferring web resources
answer: application-layer protocol for transferring web resources
questions.explanation: HTTP defines request and response semantics for web resources at the application layer; it typically runs over TCP or QUIC-based transport.

questions.prompt: A standard HTTP request contains a
answer: request line, headers, optional body
questions.explanation: An HTTP/1.1 request begins with method, target, and version, followed by headers, a blank line, and an optional message body.

questions.prompt: In an HTTP request line, GET is the
answer: method
questions.explanation: The method token specifies the action requested, such as GET, POST, PUT, or DELETE.

questions.prompt: How many decimal digits are in the HTTP status code 404?
questions.explanation: HTTP status codes are three-digit numeric codes; 404 has three digits.

questions.prompt: The HTTP status code 200 belongs to which class?
answer: 2xx success
questions.explanation: Status codes 200-299 indicate successful handling of the request; 200 specifically means OK.

questions.prompt: Which are HTTP method names?
answer: GET
POST
PUT
questions.explanation: GET, POST, and PUT are methods. HTML is a markup language, not an HTTP method.

questions.prompt: A GET request is intended primarily to
options: retrieve a representation of a resource
submit an entity for processing only
answer: retrieve a representation of a resource
questions.explanation: GET requests a representation of a resource and is defined as a safe method in normal HTTP semantics.

questions.prompt: The HTTP method POST is commonly used to
options: submit data for processing or resource-specific actions
answer: submit data for processing or resource-specific actions
questions.explanation: POST asks the target resource to process the enclosed representation according to resource-specific semantics.

questions.prompt: An HTTP response begins with a
answer: status line
questions.explanation: An HTTP/1.1 response begins with a status line containing the version, status code, and reason phrase, followed by headers and optional body.

questions.prompt: How many standard status-code classes exist in HTTP, labeled 1xx through 5xx?
questions.explanation: HTTP status codes are grouped into five classes: informational, success, redirection, client error, and server error.

questions.prompt: The HTTP status code 301 indicates
answer: permanent redirection
questions.explanation: 301 Moved Permanently indicates that the target resource has a new permanent URI; clients may update stored links according to semantics.

questions.prompt: The HTTP status code 302 is in the
answer: 3xx redirection class
questions.explanation: Status 302 Found is a redirection response, belonging to the 3xx class.

questions.prompt: What is the numeric HTTP status code for Not Found?
questions.explanation: HTTP 404 is the standard Not Found response indicating that no current representation was found for the target resource.

questions.prompt: HTTP 400 indicates
options: a client error due to a malformed or invalid request
answer: a client error due to a malformed or invalid request
questions.explanation: 400 Bad Request is a 4xx response indicating that the server cannot process the request due to perceived client error.

questions.prompt: HTTP 401 generally indicates
options: authentication is required or has failed
the server encountered an internal error
the request succeeded with no content
answer: authentication is required or has failed
questions.explanation: 401 Unauthorized indicates that valid authentication credentials are required or were not accepted.

questions.prompt: HTTP 403 differs from 401 because 403 generally means
options: the server understood the request but refuses authorization
the client must always send a password
the server is redirecting the client
answer: the server understood the request but refuses authorization
questions.explanation: 403 Forbidden indicates refusal to fulfill the request, while 401 is associated with an authentication challenge or missing/invalid credentials.

questions.prompt: What does an HTTP Internal Server Error response indicate?
answer: an internal server error
questions.explanation: 500 Internal Server Error is a generic server-side failure response.

questions.prompt: Which status code represents Service Unavailable?
questions.explanation: HTTP 503 indicates that the server is temporarily unable to handle the request, often due to overload or maintenance.

questions.prompt: HTTP status 204 means
options: the request succeeded and there is no response content
answer: the request succeeded and there is no response content
questions.explanation: 204 No Content indicates successful processing with no response body to return.

questions.prompt: HTTP headers are used to
options: carry metadata about the request or response
answer: carry metadata about the request or response
questions.explanation: Headers convey metadata such as content type, caching directives, authentication, and connection behavior.

questions.prompt: HTTP is stateless at the protocol level because
options: each request can be understood independently without built-in per-client session state
answer: each request can be understood independently without built-in per-client session state
questions.explanation: HTTP semantics do not inherently maintain a session across requests; applications add state using cookies, tokens, or other mechanisms.

questions.prompt: HTTP cookies are commonly used to
options: carry state identifiers between client requests
answer: carry state identifiers between client requests
questions.explanation: Cookies let a server associate subsequent requests with state such as a session, while HTTP itself remains stateless at the protocol level.

questions.prompt: A cookie expires 86400 seconds after creation. How many hours is that?
questions.explanation: There are 3600 seconds per hour, and 86400/3600=24 hours.

questions.prompt: Which statements about HTTP cookies are true?
options: A server can send Set-Cookie in a response
A browser can send Cookie in later requests
Cookies can help maintain application sessions
Cookies are stored by DNS root servers
answer: A server can send Set-Cookie in a response
A browser can send Cookie in later requests
Cookies can help maintain application sessions
questions.explanation: Set-Cookie instructs the client to store cookie state; later Cookie headers return it to the server. DNS servers are unrelated.

questions.prompt: HTTPS is HTTP carried over
options: TLS-protected transport, conventionally TCP for HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2
answer: TLS-protected transport, conventionally TCP for HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2
questions.explanation: HTTPS protects HTTP communication using TLS; HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 conventionally use TCP, while HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP.

questions.prompt: TLS server authentication in HTTPS commonly uses
options: a certificate validated against a trust store
answer: a certificate validated against a trust store
questions.explanation: The server presents a certificate binding its identity to a public key, which the client validates through a trusted certification chain and hostname checks.

questions.prompt: How many bytes are in a standard TLS record header?
questions.explanation: A TLS record header is five bytes in common TLS record framing.

questions.prompt: HTTP/1.1 persistent connections allow
options: multiple request-response exchanges over one TCP connection
a client to skip DNS permanently
responses to be sent without ordering in all cases
answer: multiple request-response exchanges over one TCP connection
questions.explanation: Persistent connections reuse a TCP connection for multiple exchanges, reducing connection setup overhead.

questions.prompt: HTTP/1.1 pipelining permits a client to
options: send multiple requests without waiting for each response
use multiple DNS names in one packet
answer: send multiple requests without waiting for each response
questions.explanation: Pipelining sends several requests on one connection before receiving prior responses, though response ordering and head-of-line issues limit it.

questions.prompt: HTTP/2 multiplexing improves over HTTP/1.1 pipelining by
options: interleaving multiple streams on one connection
using one TCP connection per header
changing every HTTP request into UDP
answer: interleaving multiple streams on one connection
questions.explanation: HTTP/2 multiplexes independent streams over one connection, allowing frames from different streams to interleave, though TCP loss can still block all streams.

questions.prompt: Which are features of HTTP/2?
options: One TCP connection per request is mandatory
answer: Binary framing layer
Multiplexed streams
Header compression using HPACK
questions.explanation: HTTP/2 uses binary frames, multiplexes streams, and compresses headers with HPACK. It commonly reuses a connection rather than requiring one per request.

questions.prompt: HTTP/2 server push was designed to
options: allow a server to send resources associated with a response before explicit requests
answer: allow a server to send resources associated with a response before explicit requests
questions.explanation: Server push allowed a server to proactively send resources it anticipated the client would need, although browser support and usage have been limited.

questions.prompt: HTTP/3 uses which transport protocol?
answer: QUIC
questions.explanation: HTTP/3 maps HTTP semantics to QUIC, which runs over UDP and provides streams, reliability, and TLS 1.3 integration.

questions.prompt: How many independent bidirectional streams can HTTP/3 use within one QUIC connection, in principle?
options: Many independent streams, subject to negotiated limits
answer: Many independent streams, subject to negotiated limits
questions.explanation: QUIC supports many independently multiplexed streams in one connection. The protocol permits large stream counts, while practical limits are negotiated by endpoints.

questions.prompt: QUIC can reduce transport head-of-line blocking compared with HTTP/2 over TCP because
options: loss in one stream need not block delivery of data in other streams
answer: loss in one stream need not block delivery of data in other streams
questions.explanation: QUIC streams are independently ordered, so a lost packet containing data for one stream need not block delivery of other streams' already received data.

questions.prompt: HTTP message framing in HTTP/1.1 can use Content-Length to
options: state the body length in octets
answer: state the body length in octets
questions.explanation: Content-Length gives the number of octets in the message body, allowing the receiver to identify its end when applicable.

questions.prompt: An HTTP response body has Content-Length 4096. How many body octets are specified?
questions.explanation: Content-Length is measured in octets; the value 4096 specifies a 4096-octet body.

questions.prompt: Chunked transfer coding in HTTP/1.1 allows
options: a message body to be sent in chunks when its full length is not known in advance
the TCP stream to be reordered
headers to be encrypted without TLS
answer: a message body to be sent in chunks when its full length is not known in advance
questions.explanation: Chunked transfer coding frames the body in size-labelled chunks and terminates with a zero-size chunk, supporting streaming without a known upfront length.

questions.prompt: The HTTP Host header is important in HTTP/1.1 because
options: multiple hostnames can share one server IP address
it carries the client's MAC address
it specifies the TCP congestion window
answer: multiple hostnames can share one server IP address
questions.explanation: Host identifies the target authority, enabling name-based virtual hosting when many domains share one IP address.

questions.prompt: An HTTP request includes Host: www.example.com. How many domain-name labels are present, excluding any trailing root dot?
questions.explanation: The labels are www, example, and com, totaling three.

questions.prompt: An HTTP cache can reuse a stored response when
options: the response's caching directives permit reuse and it is fresh or successfully revalidated
answer: the response's caching directives permit reuse and it is fresh or successfully revalidated
questions.explanation: HTTP caching follows freshness and validation rules expressed through directives such as Cache-Control, Expires, and validators.

questions.prompt: The Cache-Control directive max-age=60 means a response is fresh for up to
answer: 60 seconds
questions.explanation: max-age is expressed in seconds, so 60 sets a freshness lifetime of one minute.

questions.prompt: An HTTP response has max-age=1800 seconds. How many minutes is this?
questions.explanation: 1800 seconds divided by 60 seconds per minute equals 30 minutes.

questions.prompt: Which HTTP headers can participate in cache validation?
answer: ETag
Last-Modified
If-None-Match
questions.explanation: ETag and Last-Modified are validators; If-None-Match carries an ETag condition for validation. Content-Length describes body size, not freshness validation.

questions.prompt: An ETag is used as
options: a validator identifying a particular representation version
answer: a validator identifying a particular representation version
questions.explanation: ETag is an opaque validator for a selected representation; clients can use it in conditional requests to check whether the representation changed.

questions.prompt: A client sends If-None-Match and the representation is unchanged. The server can respond with
answer: 304 Not Modified
questions.explanation: 304 indicates that the selected representation has not changed relative to the supplied validator, allowing the client to reuse its cached body.

questions.prompt: How many digits are in HTTP status code 304?
questions.explanation: HTTP status codes use three decimal digits; 304 has three digits.

questions.prompt: A conditional GET with If-Modified-Since can reduce transfer by receiving
options: 304 Not Modified when the representation has not changed
answer: 304 Not Modified when the representation has not changed
questions.explanation: If the resource has not changed since the supplied date, the server may return 304 without retransmitting the representation body.

questions.prompt: The HTTP Cache-Control directive no-store tells caches to
options: not store the request or response
answer: not store the request or response
questions.explanation: no-store prohibits caches from storing the request or response, subject to the directive's defined semantics.

questions.prompt: The Cache-Control directive no-cache means a cache
options: must validate with the origin before reusing the response
should use UDP instead of TCP
answer: must validate with the origin before reusing the response
questions.explanation: no-cache permits storage but requires successful validation before reuse; no-store is the directive that prohibits storage.

questions.prompt: Which are HTTP conditional request headers?
answer: If-Modified-Since
If-None-Match
If-Match
questions.explanation: If-Modified-Since and If-None-Match are common validators; If-Match is also a precondition. Accept-Language negotiates representation language.

questions.prompt: The HTTP Vary header tells a cache that
options: the response may differ based on specified request headers
the client must use a new TCP port
answer: the response may differ based on specified request headers
questions.explanation: Vary identifies request-header fields that influenced representation selection, so caches maintain separate variants accordingly.

questions.prompt: If a response includes Vary: Accept-Encoding, a cache should distinguish variants based on
answer: the request's Accept-Encoding value
questions.explanation: The response representation may depend on whether the client accepts gzip, br, or identity encoding, so the cache key must account for Accept-Encoding.

questions.prompt: A cache stores 4 variants for a resource based on Vary dimensions. How many stored variants are there?
questions.explanation: The stated cache contains four distinct representation variants, one for each relevant request-header combination.

questions.prompt: The HTTP Content-Type header specifies
options: the media type of the representation
answer: the media type of the representation
questions.explanation: Content-Type identifies the media type, such as text/html or application/json, and may include parameters like charset.

questions.prompt: The Content-Encoding header describes
options: a coding applied to the representation, such as gzip
answer: a coding applied to the representation, such as gzip
questions.explanation: Content-Encoding indicates a representation coding applied to the body, such as gzip, which the recipient decodes.

questions.prompt: Accept-Language is an example of
answer: content negotiation metadata
questions.explanation: Clients use Accept-Language to express language preferences; servers may select a representation and describe it with Content-Language.

questions.prompt: A request lists three language preferences in Accept-Language. How many preference entries are specified?
questions.explanation: The header lists three language ranges, so it expresses three preference entries.

questions.prompt: HTTP content negotiation can select a representation based on
options: media type, language, or content coding preferences
answer: media type, language, or content coding preferences
questions.explanation: Negotiation may consider Accept, Accept-Language, and Accept-Encoding to choose an appropriate representation variant.

questions.prompt: A 406 Not Acceptable response indicates
options: the server cannot provide a representation matching the request's stated preferences
the request body is too large
answer: the server cannot provide a representation matching the request's stated preferences
questions.explanation: 406 is a client-error response used when acceptable representations cannot be supplied according to negotiation preferences.

questions.prompt: An HTTP request using the HEAD method asks the server to
options: return headers that would accompany a GET response, without the response body
answer: return headers that would accompany a GET response, without the response body
questions.explanation: HEAD is like GET but asks for response metadata without transferring the representation content.

questions.prompt: The HTTP method OPTIONS is commonly used to
options: ask about communication options supported by a target resource
answer: ask about communication options supported by a target resource
questions.explanation: OPTIONS requests information about communication options for the target, including methods or cross-origin policy details in some contexts.

questions.prompt: How many letters are in the HTTP method name PATCH?
questions.explanation: PATCH consists of the five letters P-A-T-C-H.

questions.prompt: HTTP method semantics classify GET as safe because it
options: is intended not to change server state
answer: is intended not to change server state
questions.explanation: A safe method is intended to be read-only in terms of requested semantics, though servers may still log or perform incidental actions.

questions.prompt: Which HTTP methods are idempotent by their defined semantics?
answer: GET
PUT
DELETE
questions.explanation: GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent: repeating the same request has the same intended effect as one request. POST is not generally idempotent.

questions.prompt: HTTP idempotence means that
options: repeating the same request has the same intended effect as performing it once
the response is always identical byte-for-byte
answer: repeating the same request has the same intended effect as performing it once
questions.explanation: Idempotence concerns intended effect on server state; response status or incidental effects may differ across repetitions.

questions.prompt: The HTTP method PUT commonly means
options: create or replace the target resource representation
retrieve a resource without side effects
answer: create or replace the target resource representation
questions.explanation: PUT requests creation or replacement of the target resource's state with the enclosed representation, according to target semantics.

questions.prompt: A 201 Created response commonly indicates
options: the request created one or more resources
the response has no body by definition
answer: the request created one or more resources
questions.explanation: 201 indicates successful creation; a Location header may identify the newly created resource.

questions.prompt: How many digits are in status code 201?
questions.explanation: 201 contains three decimal digits, as do standard HTTP status codes.

questions.prompt: A 429 Too Many Requests response indicates
options: the client sent too many requests in a given time
answer: the client sent too many requests in a given time
questions.explanation: 429 is a rate-limiting response; a Retry-After header may indicate when to retry.

questions.prompt: A 503 response may include Retry-After to
options: suggest when the client should retry
answer: suggest when the client should retry
questions.explanation: Retry-After communicates a suggested delay or date before retrying after temporary unavailability.

questions.prompt: Which are HTTP response status codes in the 5xx server-error class?
questions.explanation: 500, 502, and 503 are 5xx server errors. 404 is a 4xx client-error response.

questions.prompt: 502 Bad Gateway indicates
options: a gateway or proxy received an invalid response from an upstream server
answer: a gateway or proxy received an invalid response from an upstream server
questions.explanation: 502 indicates that a server acting as gateway or proxy received an invalid response from an upstream server while fulfilling the request.

questions.prompt: What is the numeric status code for Gateway Timeout?
questions.explanation: HTTP 504 Gateway Timeout is a 5xx response indicating an upstream server did not respond in time.

questions.prompt: A 304 Not Modified response normally has
options: a TCP FIN as its body
answer: no message body
questions.explanation: 304 is a cache validation response and does not include the selected representation content; the client uses its stored copy.

questions.prompt: A 206 Partial Content response is associated with
answer: a range request
questions.explanation: 206 indicates that the server is returning a requested range of a representation, often with Content-Range metadata.

questions.prompt: An HTTP byte range is bytes 0-99 inclusive. How many bytes are requested?
questions.explanation: The inclusive range contains 99-0+1=100 bytes.

questions.prompt: The HTTP Range header allows a client to
options: request a selected portion of a representation
set the server's TCP receive window
answer: request a selected portion of a representation
questions.explanation: Range requests let clients request portions, useful for resumable downloads or media seeking when supported.

questions.prompt: A 416 response indicates
options: the requested range is not satisfiable
the request is accepted for processing
answer: the requested range is not satisfiable
questions.explanation: 416 Range Not Satisfiable indicates that the requested byte range cannot be served, for example because it lies beyond the current representation length.

questions.prompt: The Location header is commonly used with
answer: redirection responses or resource creation
questions.explanation: Location supplies a URI reference, often for a redirect target or the newly created resource in a 201 response.

questions.prompt: The HTTP Authorization header is used to
options: carry credentials or authorization information from the client
answer: carry credentials or authorization information from the client
questions.explanation: Authorization carries credentials or a token that the server can use to authenticate or authorize the request.

questions.prompt: The WWW-Authenticate response header is commonly associated with
answer: 401 Unauthorized
questions.explanation: A 401 response commonly includes WWW-Authenticate challenges describing authentication schemes the client can use.

questions.prompt: An HTTP Basic authorization credential is encoded using Base64. Is Base64 itself encryption? Use 1 for yes and 0 for no.
questions.explanation: Base64 is a reversible encoding, not encryption; HTTPS is needed to protect credentials in transit.

questions.prompt: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) is enforced primarily by
options: web browsers using HTTP response headers to control cross-origin script access
answer: web browsers using HTTP response headers to control cross-origin script access
questions.explanation: CORS is a browser security mechanism. Servers declare allowed origins and related policy through response headers, which browsers enforce for scripts.

questions.prompt: A CORS preflight request uses the HTTP method
answer: OPTIONS
questions.explanation: Browsers send an OPTIONS preflight to ask whether a cross-origin method and headers are permitted before the actual request when required.

questions.prompt: Which headers may appear in a CORS preflight exchange?
answer: Origin
Access-Control-Request-Method
Access-Control-Request-Headers
questions.explanation: The browser identifies the requesting origin, intended method, and non-simple headers. TCP window scaling is unrelated to CORS.

questions.prompt: The Same-Origin Policy compares origin components including
answer: scheme, host, and port
questions.explanation: An origin is the tuple of scheme, host, and port; differing any of these generally makes a different origin.

questions.prompt: A reverse proxy can
options: receive client HTTP requests and forward them to backend servers
guarantee an origin server never fails
answer: receive client HTTP requests and forward them to backend servers
questions.explanation: A reverse proxy stands in front of backend servers, forwarding requests and often handling TLS, caching, routing, or load balancing.

questions.prompt: A load balancer distributes requests evenly across 4 servers. If 20 requests are divided equally, how many go to each server?
questions.explanation: Equal distribution gives 20/4=5 requests per server.

questions.prompt: HTTP keep-alive reduces latency by
options: reusing an existing connection for multiple exchanges
forcing each response to use UDP
answer: reusing an existing connection for multiple exchanges
questions.explanation: Connection reuse avoids repeated transport handshakes and can reduce setup latency for multiple requests to the same origin.

questions.prompt: HTTP request smuggling can arise from
options: front-end and back-end disagreement about message framing
a DNS TTL that is too short
answer: front-end and back-end disagreement about message framing
