answer: It does not consume a stored signal and waits if its predicate is false
questions.explanation: Condition variables are not counting permits. Correct code checks a shared predicate under its mutex; a prior signal alone does not satisfy it.

questions.prompt: A thread waits on a condition variable in an if statement rather than a while loop. Why can this be incorrect?
options: Wakeups can be spurious or the predicate can become false before reacquisition
The condition variable always wakes every process
answer: Wakeups can be spurious or the predicate can become false before reacquisition
questions.explanation: A wakeup is only a prompt to recheck state. Spurious wakeups and competing threads mean the predicate may not hold when the waiter runs.

questions.prompt: Two locks are always acquired in the global order A then B. Which deadlock condition does this policy prevent?
answer: Circular wait
questions.explanation: A consistent global acquisition order prevents cycles in the wait-for graph, breaking circular wait. It does not remove the other conditions in every system.

questions.prompt: A process holds one resource while requesting another unavailable resource. Which deadlock condition is present?
answer: Hold and wait
questions.explanation: Holding an allocated resource while waiting for an additional one is hold-and-wait. A cycle is not implied by this fact alone.

questions.prompt: Resources are allocated so that an allocated resource cannot be forcibly taken from its owner. Which deadlock condition is this?
answer: No preemption
questions.explanation: No preemption means resources are released voluntarily rather than forcibly removed. It is one of the necessary conditions for deadlock.

questions.prompt: A wait-for graph contains a cycle. When does this prove deadlock?
options: When each resource type has a single instance
For every resource system regardless of instances
Only when there are no processes
Only when all resources are free
answer: When each resource type has a single instance
questions.explanation: With one instance per resource type, a cycle in the wait-for graph is both necessary and sufficient for deadlock. Multiple instances complicate the criterion.

questions.prompt: A system has multiple instances of some resource types. A cycle appears in the resource-allocation graph. What can be concluded?
options: Deadlock is possible but not guaranteed
Deadlock is certain in every case
answer: Deadlock is possible but not guaranteed
questions.explanation: With multiple instances, a cycle is necessary for deadlock but not sufficient; another instance may satisfy a waiting process and break the cycle.

questions.prompt: A system avoids deadlock by granting a request only if the resulting state is safe. This is:
answer: deadlock avoidance
questions.explanation: Avoidance evaluates the post-grant state and denies requests that could lead to an unsafe state. Detection instead allows allocation and later searches for deadlock.

questions.prompt: In Banker?s algorithm, Need is computed as:
answer: Max minus Allocation
questions.explanation: For each process and resource type, Need = Max ? Allocation, the additional units the process may still request.

questions.prompt: A state is safe if:
options: There exists an order in which each process can finish with available plus released resources
Every process has all its maximum resources now
The allocation graph has no edges
answer: There exists an order in which each process can finish with available plus released resources
questions.explanation: Safety means a safe sequence exists: each process can obtain its remaining need in sequence using currently available resources plus releases from earlier completions.

questions.prompt: A safe state and an unsafe state differ because:
options: An unsafe state has no guaranteed completion sequence, though deadlock may not yet exist
Unsafe means deadlock is already certain
Safe means all resources are free
Unsafe means no process can run
answer: An unsafe state has no guaranteed completion sequence, though deadlock may not yet exist
questions.explanation: Unsafe means the system cannot guarantee a safe sequence under worst-case claims. It may still complete; deadlock is not necessarily already present.

questions.prompt: A process requests resources that are currently unavailable. In deadlock avoidance, the request should generally be:
options: Made to wait until it can be considered safely
answer: Made to wait until it can be considered safely
questions.explanation: The request cannot be granted immediately if resources are unavailable. If available, the algorithm still checks whether tentative allocation leaves a safe state.

questions.prompt: A lock-free algorithm guarantees system-wide progress but an individual thread can starve. It is:
answer: lock-free but not wait-free
questions.explanation: Lock-free guarantees that some operation completes in finite steps, not that every particular thread does. Wait-free algorithms provide per-thread progress bounds.

questions.prompt: A spinlock waiter repeatedly checks a lock variable. What is its main cost while waiting?
options: CPU cycles are consumed by polling
The lock owner is forcibly terminated
answer: CPU cycles are consumed by polling
questions.explanation: Spinning consumes processor time and may create cache-coherence traffic. It is useful mainly when waits are expected to be very short.

questions.prompt: A semaphore implements a producer-consumer buffer. The consumer acquires the buffer mutex and then waits on empty-buffer condition while holding the mutex. Why can this deadlock?
options: The producer needs the mutex to insert the item that would wake the consumer
The consumer releases the mutex automatically
The semaphore count grows without bound
answer: The producer needs the mutex to insert the item that would wake the consumer
questions.explanation: If the consumer sleeps while retaining the mutex, the producer cannot enter to add data and signal availability. The consumer waits for an event that cannot occur.

questions.prompt: A monitor provides mutual exclusion for its procedures. What is a condition variable used for inside the monitor?
options: Waiting for a condition while temporarily releasing the monitor lock
Making a process ready without a scheduler
answer: Waiting for a condition while temporarily releasing the monitor lock
questions.explanation: Condition variables let a thread wait for a monitor predicate. Waiting releases the monitor lock and reacquires it before returning.

questions.prompt: A reader-writer lock allows multiple readers or one writer. Which access pattern is permitted?
options: Several readers concurrently, with no writer active
A reader and writer always concurrently
answer: Several readers concurrently, with no writer active
questions.explanation: The lock?s defining rule permits concurrent readers but excludes writers while readers hold the lock, and vice versa.

questions.prompt: A reader-preference reader-writer lock allows new readers to enter while a writer waits. What problem may occur?
options: Deadlock is impossible and guaranteed fairness
answer: Writer starvation
questions.explanation: An ongoing stream of readers can repeatedly delay the waiting writer, potentially starving it unless fairness is enforced.

questions.prompt: A dining-philosophers solution lets every philosopher pick up the left fork first. What can happen if all do so simultaneously?
options: Each can wait forever for the right fork, forming deadlock
answer: Each can wait forever for the right fork, forming deadlock
questions.explanation: Each philosopher holds one fork and waits for the next, creating a circular wait. Breaking the acquisition symmetry or limiting entry prevents this cycle.

questions.prompt: A binary semaphore starts at 0 and receives two signals before any wait. What is a correct concern?
options: If it is a true binary semaphore, extra signals may not accumulate as two permits
It must become a count of two
The two signals guarantee two waiters proceed
answer: If it is a true binary semaphore, extra signals may not accumulate as two permits
questions.explanation: A binary semaphore?s state is capped at available/unavailable; unlike a counting semaphore it does not necessarily preserve multiple signals as multiple permits.

questions.prompt: A thread unlocks a mutex before writing shared data. Is the write protected by the mutex?
options: No, because it occurs after the critical section ends
Yes, until another thread locks it
Yes, if the write is one machine instruction
Only if the process has one CPU
answer: No, because it occurs after the critical section ends
questions.explanation: The mutex protects only operations performed while held. Once unlocked, another thread can access the data concurrently with the write.

questions.prompt: A deadlock detection algorithm finds a cycle and terminates one process. Which approach is this?
answer: deadlock recovery by process termination
questions.explanation: Terminating a process to release its resources is a recovery strategy applied after detecting deadlock. It is not avoidance.

questions.prompt: A system periodically runs a deadlock detection algorithm and reclaims resources by rolling back a process. Which phase is rollback part of?
answer: recovery
questions.explanation: Rollback is a recovery action used after deadlock has been detected. It can release resources and allow remaining processes to proceed.

questions.prompt: A process waits indefinitely because the scheduler continually favors others, though no resource cycle exists. This is:
answer: starvation
questions.explanation: Starvation is indefinite postponement of a process, often due to unfair scheduling or resource allocation. It does not require a deadlock cycle.

questions.prompt: A counting semaphore has value 5. Three waits complete, then one signal occurs. What is the resulting value?
questions.explanation: Three waits reduce the count from five to two. A signal increments it once, resulting in three.

questions.prompt: A semaphore starts at 2. Five threads each wait once, with no signals. How many threads are blocked after all requests are made?
questions.explanation: Two wait calls consume the available permits. The remaining three cannot proceed and block.

questions.prompt: A process holds resource R1 and waits for R2. Another holds R2 and waits for R1. What is the minimum conclusion?
options: A circular wait exists and the processes are deadlocked if both resources are single-instance
answer: A circular wait exists and the processes are deadlocked if both resources are single-instance
questions.explanation: Each process waits for a resource held by the other, forming a cycle. With single-instance resources and no preemption, neither can proceed, so this is deadlock.

questions.prompt: A system has 3 instances of resource R. Process P holds one and requests one more; two instances are free. Can P?s request be satisfied immediately?
options: Yes, assuming no other constraints, one free instance exists
No, because P already holds an instance
No, multiple instances cannot be allocated
answer: Yes, assuming no other constraints, one free instance exists
questions.explanation: At least one unit is currently available, so the request can be granted if allocation rules and safety analysis permit it. Holding one does not forbid another.

questions.prompt: In Banker?s algorithm, Available = (3,2), Allocation for P = (1,1), and Max = (4,2). What is P?s Need vector?
questions.explanation: Need = Max ? Allocation componentwise: (4?1, 2?1) = (3,1).

questions.prompt: A system has Available=(2,1). P0 needs (1,1) to finish and then releases (2,0); P1 needs (3,0). Is the sequence P0 then P1 safe?
options: No, because P1 cannot finish first
No, because P0 needs more than total resources
Cannot determine without CPU burst times
answer: Yes
questions.explanation: P0?s need (1,1) fits Available (2,1). After P0 finishes it releases (2,0), making Available (4,1), which covers P1?s need (3,0).

questions.prompt: Available=(1,1), P0 Need=(2,0), P1 Need=(1,1). Which process can be selected first in a safety check?
answer: P1 only
questions.explanation: A process can finish when its Need is componentwise no greater than Available. P1?s (1,1) fits; P0?s need of two units of the first resource does not.

questions.prompt: A resource-allocation graph has one instance of each resource type. What does a directed cycle imply?
answer: Deadlock
questions.explanation: With one instance of each resource type, a cycle in the allocation graph is sufficient to establish deadlock.

questions.prompt: A resource-allocation graph has multiple instances of resource types and contains a cycle. What is the strongest valid conclusion?
options: The state may be deadlocked; the cycle alone is insufficient
All requests can be granted safely
answer: The state may be deadlocked; the cycle alone is insufficient
questions.explanation: With multiple instances, a cycle does not prove deadlock because another available instance can potentially satisfy a request and allow progress.

questions.prompt: A thread is awakened after a mutex becomes available, but another thread acquires it first. What should the awakened thread do?
options: Retry acquisition and wait if necessary
answer: Retry acquisition and wait if necessary
questions.explanation: Wakeup does not necessarily reserve ownership. The thread must compete for and successfully acquire the mutex before entering its critical section.

questions.prompt: An atomic test-and-set lock uses a busy loop. What correctness property does test-and-set help provide?
answer: Atomic acquisition decision
questions.explanation: An atomic test-and-set ensures only one thread can observe and set the lock as free in the same acquisition race. It does not ensure fairness or avoid spinning.

questions.prompt: A spinlock is used on a uniprocessor, and the lock holder is preempted by a spinning waiter of higher priority. What risk exists?
options: Priority inversion can prevent the owner from running to release the lock
The lock holder is automatically resumed immediately
The waiter enters the critical section
The lock changes to a counting semaphore
answer: Priority inversion can prevent the owner from running to release the lock
questions.explanation: The high-priority spinner consumes the CPU while the lower-priority owner cannot run. Priority inheritance or avoiding such spinning can address this inversion.

questions.prompt: A mutex supports priority inheritance. A high-priority thread waits on a mutex held by a low-priority thread. What may the kernel do?
answer: Temporarily raise the owner?s priority
questions.explanation: Priority inheritance raises the lock owner?s effective priority so it can run and release the mutex sooner, reducing medium-priority interference.

questions.prompt: A lock is reentrant. What does that mean?
options: The owning thread can acquire it recursively without self-deadlock
Multiple threads can own it simultaneously
answer: The owning thread can acquire it recursively without self-deadlock
questions.explanation: A reentrant or recursive lock tracks ownership depth, allowing its owner to acquire it again and release matching times without deadlocking itself.

questions.prompt: A thread enters a critical section and is interrupted by a timer. Another thread runs and attempts the same mutex. What should happen?
options: The second thread cannot enter until the first releases the mutex
The first thread automatically releases the lock on preemption
Both enter because they are in different time slices
The timer interrupt destroys the mutex
answer: The second thread cannot enter until the first releases the mutex
questions.explanation: Preemption does not change mutex ownership. The second thread must wait until the original owner resumes and unlocks.

questions.prompt: A monitor condition wait releases its lock while waiting, then reacquires it before return. Why is reacquisition required?
options: To preserve monitor mutual exclusion when the thread resumes
To guarantee the predicate is true forever
To stop all other threads permanently
To convert the condition into a semaphore
answer: To preserve monitor mutual exclusion when the thread resumes
questions.explanation: The waiting thread must re-enter the monitor under mutual exclusion before inspecting shared state. It still must recheck the predicate.

questions.prompt: A reader-writer lock gives priority to writers. What may happen to new readers while a writer waits?
options: They can be blocked to prevent writer starvation
The writer is converted into a reader
answer: They can be blocked to prevent writer starvation
questions.explanation: Writer preference typically prevents new readers from extending the reader phase, allowing the waiting writer eventually to acquire the lock after current readers exit.

questions.prompt: A philosopher solution allows at most four of five philosophers to attempt to acquire forks simultaneously. What deadlock condition can this break?
answer: Circular wait
questions.explanation: Limiting contenders prevents all five from each holding one fork in a full cycle, breaking circular wait for the dining-philosophers configuration.

questions.prompt: A deadlock prevention policy requests all resources at once before a process begins. Which necessary condition does it eliminate?
answer: Hold and wait
questions.explanation: If processes request their full resource set before proceeding, they do not hold some resources while waiting for additional ones, eliminating hold-and-wait.

questions.prompt: A system allows resources to be forcibly taken from a process when needed. Which deadlock condition is weakened?
answer: No preemption
questions.explanation: Permitting preemption removes the condition that resources cannot be forcibly reclaimed. This can prevent some deadlocks, though not all resources are safely preemptible.

questions.prompt: A policy assigns a total order to resource types and requires acquisition only in increasing order. What is the effect?
options: It detects deadlock after it occurs
answer: It prevents circular wait
questions.explanation: A cycle would require moving strictly upward in order and eventually returning to a lower resource, which is impossible. Thus circular wait is eliminated.

questions.prompt: A deadlock recovery policy terminates the process holding the fewest resources. What tradeoff must be considered?
options: Victim selection may affect lost work and starvation
The policy prevents deadlock before allocation
It guarantees the victim has no side effects
It always releases all resources instantly
answer: Victim selection may affect lost work and starvation
questions.explanation: Choosing a victim balances recovery cost, lost computation, and repeated selection risk. The process may have performed substantial non-rollbackable work.

questions.prompt: A process is repeatedly chosen as the deadlock victim and restarted. What problem may arise?
answer: Starvation of that process
questions.explanation: Repeatedly selecting the same victim can prevent it from completing, which is starvation. Recovery policies can track victim cost or age.

questions.prompt: A system detects deadlock only when CPU utilization falls below a threshold. What is a limitation?
options: Deadlock can occur without a unique or immediate utilization signature
Utilization always becomes zero in deadlock
The system cannot have blocked processes
The detection has no runtime cost
answer: Deadlock can occur without a unique or immediate utilization signature
questions.explanation: Processes may retain partial CPU use or unrelated work may continue; low utilization is only a heuristic and cannot reliably establish deadlock.

questions.prompt: A lock-free stack guarantees at least one operation completes under contention. What does this not guarantee?
options: That each particular thread completes within a bounded number of steps
That the system makes any progress
answer: That each particular thread completes within a bounded number of steps
questions.explanation: Lock-free progress is system-wide. A particular thread can repeatedly lose races, so per-thread bounded completion (wait-freedom) is not implied.

questions.prompt: A wait-free queue guarantees each operation completes in a bounded number of its own steps. What progress property is provided?
answer: Per-thread progress
questions.explanation: Wait-freedom gives each individual operation a bounded completion guarantee independent of other threads? behavior, assuming its steps continue.

questions.prompt: A thread holds mutex A and waits for B. Another holds B and waits for A. Which change directly breaks this particular cycle?
options: Make all threads acquire A before B
Allow each thread to acquire locks in any order
Add a condition variable without changing lock order
answer: Make all threads acquire A before B
questions.explanation: A consistent global order removes the inversion that creates the cycle. Priority changes and unrelated condition variables do not resolve the circular dependency.

questions.prompt: A lock protects a counter. One thread increments under the lock while another reads without acquiring it. Is the read synchronized with the increment?
options: Yes, because one writer used the lock
Yes, if the read is aligned
answer: No
questions.explanation: Synchronization must be observed by both sides using the same lock or an equivalent atomic protocol. An unlocked read can race with the write.

questions.prompt: A semaphore is initialized to 1 and used for mutual exclusion. Two threads both call signal after their critical sections, though only one acquired it. What can go wrong?
options: The count can exceed 1 and allow concurrent entry later
No issue; signals are ignored when count is positive
answer: The count can exceed 1 and allow concurrent entry later
questions.explanation: An extra signal can create an additional permit. Later, multiple waiters may pass, violating the intended binary mutual-exclusion invariant.

questions.prompt: A thread waits on a condition while holding mutex M, then another thread signals without locking M after changing the predicate. Why is this unsafe?
options: The predicate update and notification can race with the waiter?s check-and-sleep sequence
The mutex is automatically acquired by the signaler
answer: The predicate update and notification can race with the waiter?s check-and-sleep sequence
questions.explanation: Changing and signaling without the associated mutex can create a missed wakeup between predicate check and wait. The condition protocol should coordinate both under M.

questions.prompt: A semaphore begins at 7. Ten wait operations occur and no signals occur. How many wait calls block?
questions.explanation: Seven waits consume the initial permits. The remaining 10 ? 7 = 3 calls block.

questions.prompt: A semaphore begins at 4. Six signals and five waits complete. What is its final count?
questions.explanation: Signals add six and waits consume five: 4 + 6 ? 5 = 5 permits remain.

questions.prompt: A system has 5 resource instances. P0 holds 2 and requests 1. P1 holds 1 and requests 2. How many instances are currently available?
questions.explanation: Allocated instances total 2 + 1 = 3. With five total, Available = 5 ? 3 = 2.

questions.prompt: Available=(3,2), Need=(2,1), and a process releases Allocation=(1,2). What is the first component of Available after it finishes?
questions.explanation: The process can complete because its need fits; it releases one unit of the first resource, making that component 4.

questions.prompt: A lock acquisition costs 20 ns, and unlock costs 15 ns. Ignoring work inside, what is the combined lock/unlock overhead in ns?
questions.explanation: The stated operations cost 20 ns and 15 ns. Their combined overhead is 20 + 15 = 35 ns.

questions.prompt: A critical section takes 8 microseconds and is executed by 25 threads sequentially under one mutex. Ignoring overhead, what is the total serialized time in microseconds?
questions.explanation: Mutual exclusion serializes the 25 executions: 25 ? 8 = 200 microseconds.

questions.prompt: A producer-consumer buffer has capacity 18 with 11 occupied slots. What should the empty-slot semaphore count be?
questions.explanation: There are 18 total slots and 11 are occupied, leaving 18 ? 11 = 7 empty permits.

questions.prompt: A buffer has 9 items. Two consumers remove one item each, then a producer inserts 4. What is the final occupancy?
questions.explanation: Occupancy changes from 9 to 7 after two removals, then to 11 after four insertions.

questions.prompt: A wait-for graph has a single cycle containing 4 processes, with one instance per resource type. How many processes are in the deadlocked cycle?
questions.explanation: With single-instance resources, a wait-for cycle indicates deadlock. The cycle explicitly contains four processes, so all four are in it.

questions.prompt: A counting semaphore has value 12. Eight waits and three signals occur. What is the final value?
questions.explanation: Each wait decrements and each signal increments, giving 12 ? 8 + 3 = 7.

questions.prompt: A barrier requires 9 threads to arrive. Seven have arrived. How many more arrivals are required?
questions.explanation: The barrier threshold is nine; 9 ? 7 = 2 participants remain.

questions.prompt: A reader-writer lock allows 6 readers to hold it. One reader exits, and no writer is waiting. How many readers may continue to hold it?
questions.explanation: One of the six current readers exits, leaving five active readers. With no writer waiting, additional readers may also be admitted depending on policy.

questions.prompt: A process requests 3 units of a resource when 2 are available. How many units short is the current availability?
questions.explanation: The request exceeds availability by 3 ? 2 = 1 unit. The request cannot be fully granted now.

questions.prompt: There are 10 identical resources. P0 holds 4, P1 holds 3, and P2 holds 1. How many are available?
questions.explanation: Allocated total is 4 + 3 + 1 = 8. Of ten units, two remain available.

questions.prompt: A semaphore value is 0. Four signals occur, followed by six successful waits, with two additional waits blocking. What is its value after those operations?
questions.explanation: Four permits are created and four waits consume them. The remaining two waiters block without consuming available permits, leaving the value zero.

questions.prompt: Which are necessary conditions for deadlock in the classical Coffman characterization?
answer: Mutual exclusion
Hold and wait
No preemption
Circular wait
questions.explanation: All four conditions must hold simultaneously for a classical deadlock. Prevention strategies work by ensuring at least one condition cannot hold.

questions.prompt: Which statements about safe states are correct?
options: A safe sequence provides a possible completion order
A safe state is not currently deadlocked
An unsafe state is not necessarily already deadlocked
A safe state requires every process to hold its maximum claim
answer: A safe sequence provides a possible completion order
A safe state is not currently deadlocked
An unsafe state is not necessarily already deadlocked
questions.explanation: Safety means some sequence exists that can complete all processes. Unsafe states lack that guarantee but need not yet be deadlocked; maximum claims need not already be allocated.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Banker?s algorithm are correct?
options: A tentative grant must leave a safe state
A safe sequence can be found by repeatedly selecting a satisfiable Need
answer: Need equals Max minus Allocation
A tentative grant must leave a safe state
Available represents currently unallocated resources
A safe sequence can be found by repeatedly selecting a satisfiable Need
questions.explanation: These are the core quantities and safety-test steps: compute remaining need, tentatively grant, then find a completion order using available resources and releases.

questions.prompt: Which policies can prevent circular wait?
options: Impose a total order on resource types
Require acquisition only in increasing order
answer: Impose a total order on resource types
Require acquisition only in increasing order
Use a consistent lock hierarchy
questions.explanation: A total ordering or lock hierarchy prevents cycles by constraining acquisition direction. Arbitrary acquisition order preserves the possibility of circular wait.

questions.prompt: Which are deadlock recovery actions after detection?
options: Roll back a process to a checkpoint
Deny all future requests before checking safety
answer: Terminate one or more processes
Preempt resources where safe
Roll back a process to a checkpoint
questions.explanation: Termination, safe resource preemption, and rollback are recovery options. Denying requests based on safety is avoidance, not recovery after detection.

questions.prompt: Which statements about semaphores are correct?
options: Signal increases availability or wakes a waiter
A counting semaphore can represent multiple units
A semaphore used as a mutex should not be signaled by a non-owner accidentally
answer: Wait decrements an available permit
Signal increases availability or wakes a waiter
A counting semaphore can represent multiple units
A semaphore used as a mutex should not be signaled by a non-owner accidentally
questions.explanation: Semaphores coordinate permits. For mutex-like use, preserving the intended ownership and count invariant is essential; extra signals can break exclusion.

questions.prompt: Which statements about condition variables are correct?
options: They should be paired with a predicate
Wait atomically releases the mutex and sleeps
The waiter reacquires the mutex before returning
A signal is a persistent permit for future waiters
answer: They should be paired with a predicate
Wait atomically releases the mutex and sleeps
The waiter reacquires the mutex before returning
questions.explanation: Correct condition protocols protect predicates with a mutex. Wait releases and later reacquires it; notifications generally are not stored as future permits.

questions.prompt: Which claims about starvation are correct?
options: A process can starve without deadlock
Unfair lock acquisition can cause starvation
A deadlock cycle requires every process in the cycle to wait
Starvation means every process is blocked in a cycle
answer: A process can starve without deadlock
Unfair lock acquisition can cause starvation
A deadlock cycle requires every process in the cycle to wait
questions.explanation: Starvation is indefinite postponement and can affect one process while others progress. A deadlock cycle involves cyclic waiting, unlike starvation in general.

questions.prompt: Which statements about spinlocks are correct?
options: They can be useful for very short waits
They can waste CPU for long waits
answer: They busy-wait while unavailable
They can be useful for very short waits
They can waste CPU for long waits
questions.explanation: Spinning polls the lock and can be efficient for short holds, but wastes cycles for long waits. FIFO fairness requires a specific lock design.

questions.prompt: Which conditions can support a lost wakeup bug?
options: Predicate checked without the associated mutex
Signaler updates predicate outside the synchronization protocol
Wait begins after a notification that was not retained
Using a counting semaphore with a stored permit
answer: Predicate checked without the associated mutex
Signaler updates predicate outside the synchronization protocol
Wait begins after a notification that was not retained
questions.explanation: If checking, updating, and sleeping are not coordinated, a notification can occur just before the waiter sleeps. A semaphore retains permits and avoids that exact lost-notification issue.

questions.prompt: Which statements about reader-writer locks are correct?
options: Multiple readers may hold a read lock together
A reader-writer lock guarantees higher throughput for every workload
answer: Multiple readers may hold a read lock together
A writer requires exclusive access
Reader preference can starve writers
questions.explanation: Concurrent reads and exclusive writes define the lock. Reader-heavy workloads may benefit, but overhead or contention can make it slower for other workloads.

questions.prompt: Which changes can break a dining-philosophers deadlock cycle?
options: Allow at most N?1 philosophers to compete
Make one philosopher acquire forks in reverse order
Require all philosophers to acquire forks in one global order
Let every philosopher take left then right simultaneously
answer: Allow at most N?1 philosophers to compete
Make one philosopher acquire forks in reverse order
Require all philosophers to acquire forks in one global order
questions.explanation: Limiting contenders or imposing an ordering breaks the circular wait. Symmetric simultaneous left-first acquisition preserves the cycle.

questions.prompt: Which statements about atomic operations are correct?
options: Atomicity of one operation does not make a multi-step protocol atomic
Memory ordering can matter for publishing data
An atomic counter prevents all deadlocks
answer: They can implement synchronization primitives
Atomicity of one operation does not make a multi-step protocol atomic
Memory ordering can matter for publishing data
questions.explanation: Atomics underpin locks and counters, but compound logic still needs protocol design and visibility ordering. They do not prevent unrelated deadlocks.

questions.prompt: Which are examples of progress guarantees?
options: Lock-free: some operation completes in finite system-wide steps
Wait-free: each operation completes in bounded own steps
Blocking mutex: a stalled owner may prevent others from progressing
Mutual exclusion: guarantees every waiter eventually enters
answer: Lock-free: some operation completes in finite system-wide steps
Wait-free: each operation completes in bounded own steps
Blocking mutex: a stalled owner may prevent others from progressing
questions.explanation: Lock-free and wait-free define progress properties; a blocking lock can depend on its owner. Mutual exclusion alone does not imply fairness or eventual entry.

questions.prompt: Which practices reduce lock-order deadlocks?
options: Release a lock before acquiring another where safe
Acquire multiple locks in arbitrary order
Use try-lock and back off on failure
answer: Document a global acquisition order
Release a lock before acquiring another where safe
Use try-lock and back off on failure
questions.explanation: Consistent order, reducing nested ownership, or retrying after failed try-lock can avoid cycles. Arbitrary order enables lock-order inversion.

questions.prompt: Which statements about priority inversion are correct?
options: A high-priority thread can wait for a low-priority lock owner
Medium-priority work can delay the low-priority owner
Priority inheritance can mitigate the delay
It is the same as a deadlock cycle
answer: A high-priority thread can wait for a low-priority lock owner
Medium-priority work can delay the low-priority owner
Priority inheritance can mitigate the delay
questions.explanation: Priority inversion describes indirect priority blocking; priority inheritance boosts the owner so it can release the lock. It need not be deadlock.

questions.prompt: Which statements about mutex ownership are typically correct?
options: Only the owner should unlock a normal mutex
A mutex may remain locked if its owner dies
answer: Only the owner should unlock a normal mutex
Preemption does not release ownership
A mutex may remain locked if its owner dies
questions.explanation: Mutex ownership persists across preemption and may be stranded if an owner dies. Robust recovery is an optional feature, not universal.

questions.prompt: Which conditions should a safety-check algorithm compare componentwise?
options: Request with Available before tentative allocation
Allocation with Max to derive Need
answer: Need with Available
Request with Available before tentative allocation
Allocation with Max to derive Need
questions.explanation: Resource vectors are compared componentwise to decide whether requests can be met and processes can finish. Process identifiers are not resource quantities.

questions.prompt: Which claims about deadlock detection are correct?
options: It can be run periodically or on demand
It allows allocations that may later deadlock
Recovery is needed if deadlock is found
answer: It can be run periodically or on demand
It allows allocations that may later deadlock
Recovery is needed if deadlock is found
questions.explanation: Detection permits the system to enter deadlock and searches for it later; recovery follows. It does not prevent deadlock from occurring.

questions.prompt: Which actions may release resources held by a deadlocked process?
options: Roll it back to a state before allocation
answer: Terminate that process
Roll it back to a state before allocation
Preempt a safely preemptible resource
questions.explanation: Termination, rollback, and safe preemption can free resources. Raising priority alone does not release resources or resolve a wait cycle.

questions.prompt: Available=(2,1). P0 needs (1,1) and will release (2,0) on completion; P1 needs (3,0). Is P0?P1 a safe sequence?
answer: Yes
questions.explanation: P0?s need fits the available vector. After completion, availability becomes (4,1), which satisfies P1?s remaining need, so the sequence is safe.

questions.prompt: A binary semaphore has value 1. Two threads call wait, and the first later calls signal twice. What is the most important risk?
options: The second signal can leave an extra permit and break mutual exclusion
The first thread becomes a zombie
The second thread is guaranteed to starve
answer: The second signal can leave an extra permit and break mutual exclusion
questions.explanation: A mutex-like binary semaphore should represent one ownership permit. Extra signaling can create an additional available permit and allow overlapping entry.

questions.prompt: A process waits for a condition variable while holding a mutex, but the wait implementation does not release the mutex. What happens if the producer needs that mutex to make the condition true?
answer: Deadlock
questions.explanation: The waiter sleeps while holding the only lock the producer needs to update and signal the predicate. Neither can proceed.

questions.prompt: A system with multiple instances of resource R has a wait-for cycle. One unused instance of R is available. What does this suggest?
options: The cycle may be resolved by granting the available instance
Deadlock is certain despite the free instance
The system must terminate every process
answer: The cycle may be resolved by granting the available instance
questions.explanation: A free instance may satisfy a pending request and let a process complete, so a cycle alone does not prove deadlock when resource types have multiple instances.

questions.prompt: A fair mutex guarantees that a thread waiting longest is eventually served. Which problem does this property primarily address?
answer: Starvation
questions.explanation: Fair service reduces indefinite postponement of an individual waiter, addressing starvation. It does not by itself eliminate lock cycles or change mutual exclusion.

questions.prompt: Two processes arrive at time 0 with bursts P1=4 and P2=2. Under FCFS in that order, what is the average waiting time?
questions.explanation: P1 waits zero and P2 waits four units. Their average waiting time is (0 + 4)/2 = 2.

questions.prompt: Two processes arrive at time 0 with bursts P1=4 and P2=2. Under FCFS, what is the average turnaround time?
questions.explanation: Completion times are 4 and 6; both arrive at zero, so average turnaround is (4 + 6)/2 = 5.

questions.prompt: Two processes arrive together with bursts 4 and 2. Under non-preemptive SJF, what is the average waiting time?
questions.explanation: SJF runs the 2-unit burst first, then the 4-unit burst. Waiting times are 0 and 2, averaging 1.

questions.prompt: A CPU scheduler selects the process with the smallest predicted next CPU burst. Which algorithm is this?
answer: Shortest Job First
questions.explanation: SJF chooses the shortest estimated next CPU burst. Round Robin uses a quantum; FCFS follows arrival; feedback queues use dynamic class movement.

questions.prompt: A preemptive scheduler always runs the ready process with the least remaining CPU time. This is:
answer: Shortest Remaining Time First
questions.explanation: SRTF is the preemptive form of SJF: a newly arriving job can preempt the current one if its remaining time is smaller.

questions.prompt: A process arrives with a shorter remaining burst than the currently running process under SRTF. What happens?
options: The new process waits until the current burst ends
Both run simultaneously on one CPU
answer: The running process is preempted
questions.explanation: SRTF selects the minimum remaining time among ready processes. The arriving shorter job preempts the current process.

questions.prompt: Round Robin uses quantum q. A process has CPU burst 10 and q=4, with no context-switch cost. How many times does it receive CPU before completion?
questions.explanation: It runs for 4, then 4, then the remaining 2 units. Thus it receives three CPU turns.

questions.prompt: Round Robin with q=2 has one process of burst 5 and no competitors. Ignoring overhead, what is its completion time?
questions.explanation: The process uses two full quanta and a final one-unit turn. With no competitors or overhead, elapsed CPU time is exactly its burst: 5.

questions.prompt: Round Robin uses a very large quantum. Which behavior does it approach?
answer: FCFS
questions.explanation: If the quantum exceeds every burst, no process is preempted by the timer. Processes run in queue order, approximating FCFS.

questions.prompt: Round Robin uses an extremely small quantum. Which cost tends to increase?
answer: Context-switch overhead
questions.explanation: A smaller quantum causes more frequent preemption and dispatch, increasing context-switch overhead relative to useful CPU work.

questions.prompt: A priority scheduler always chooses the highest-priority ready process, and low numeric value means higher priority. Which process runs among priorities 3, 1, and 2?
answer: Priority 1
questions.explanation: The convention states lower numbers represent higher priority, so priority 1 is selected.

questions.prompt: A low-priority process waits indefinitely because higher-priority jobs continually arrive. This is:
answer: starvation
questions.explanation: Strict priority scheduling can indefinitely postpone low-priority work, which is starvation. Aging can raise its priority over time.

questions.prompt: Aging in priority scheduling is used primarily to:
options: reduce starvation by increasing waiting processes? priorities
answer: reduce starvation by increasing waiting processes? priorities
questions.explanation: Aging gradually improves the priority of processes that wait, eventually allowing them to run despite a stream of higher-priority arrivals.

questions.prompt: A convoy effect is most associated with:
options: short processes waiting behind a long CPU-bound process
a high quantum causing no preemption
answer: short processes waiting behind a long CPU-bound process
questions.explanation: In FCFS, a long CPU-bound process can hold the CPU while many short or I/O-bound jobs queue behind it, creating a convoy.

questions.prompt: Which scheduling criterion measures completed processes per unit time?
answer: Throughput
questions.explanation: Throughput is the number of completed jobs per unit time. Turnaround, response, and waiting measure per-process delays.

questions.prompt: A user submits an interactive request at time 8; it first receives CPU at time 11. What is its response time?
questions.explanation: Response time is first CPU service minus arrival time: 11 ? 8 = 3 time units.

questions.prompt: A process arrives at 2 and completes at 17. What is its turnaround time?
questions.explanation: Turnaround time is completion minus arrival: 17 ? 2 = 15.

questions.prompt: A process has turnaround time 20 and CPU burst 7, with no other service counted. What is its waiting time?
questions.explanation: Turnaround consists of waiting plus CPU burst time. Waiting is 20 ? 7 = 13.

questions.prompt: A CPU burst prediction uses exponential averaging ?(n+1)=?t(n)+(1??)?(n), with ?=0.5, prior estimate 8, and last burst 4. What is the new estimate?
questions.explanation: The next estimate is 0.5?4 + 0.5?8 = 6 units.

questions.prompt: With exponential averaging, ?=1. Which information determines the next burst estimate?
options: Only the most recent actual burst
answer: Only the most recent actual burst
questions.explanation: When ?=1, the previous estimate receives zero weight, so the new estimate equals the latest actual burst.

questions.prompt: A process spends most of its time waiting for I/O with short CPU bursts. It is:
answer: I/O-bound
questions.explanation: I/O-bound processes have short CPU bursts relative to their time spent waiting for I/O. CPU-bound processes have long bursts.

questions.prompt: A preemptive scheduler uses priorities. A low-priority process is executing when a higher-priority process becomes ready. What happens under strict preemption?
options: The new process waits for the current burst to finish
Both processes share the same CPU instantaneously
answer: The low-priority process is preempted
questions.explanation: A strict preemptive priority scheduler immediately gives the CPU to the higher-priority ready process, returning the former process to ready.

questions.prompt: A multilevel queue scheduler assigns foreground jobs to RR and background jobs to FCFS. What distinguishes this from a feedback queue?
options: Processes do not move between queues based on observed behavior
It must use SRTF in all queues
The foreground jobs are never scheduled
Background jobs have no CPU bursts
answer: Processes do not move between queues based on observed behavior
questions.explanation: A multilevel queue has fixed class membership, while feedback queues allow movement between queues based on CPU usage or waiting behavior.

questions.prompt: A multilevel feedback queue moves a job to a lower-priority queue after it uses its entire quantum. Which behavior is being favored?
options: Short or interactive jobs that yield early
Long CPU-bound jobs that exhaust quanta
Only jobs with earliest arrival time
Processes with the largest memory footprint
answer: Short or interactive jobs that yield early
questions.explanation: Using the full quantum suggests CPU-bound behavior and can demote a job. Interactive jobs often yield early and remain at higher priority.

questions.prompt: A process blocks for I/O before consuming its whole quantum in a feedback queue. What may the scheduler infer?
options: It may be interactive or I/O-bound and retain higher priority
It used more CPU than a process exhausting the quantum
answer: It may be interactive or I/O-bound and retain higher priority
questions.explanation: Yielding early often signals interactive or I/O-bound behavior, so feedback policies may keep the process in a higher-priority queue.

questions.prompt: A scheduler is work-conserving. What does that mean?
options: It does not leave the CPU idle when a ready process exists
It always minimizes average waiting time
answer: It does not leave the CPU idle when a ready process exists
questions.explanation: A work-conserving scheduler assigns the CPU whenever at least one process is ready. It does not imply optimality or fairness.

questions.prompt: Two processes have identical priority and arrival time. The scheduler?s tie-breaking rule is FCFS. Which runs first?
options: The one with larger PID always
answer: The one enqueued first
questions.explanation: When priority ties, FCFS tie-breaking selects the process that entered the ready queue first. Other tie-breaking rules could produce another result.

questions.prompt: A preemptive scheduler incurs context-switch cost c each time. Why can a very small quantum reduce useful CPU efficiency?
options: A larger fraction of time is spent switching rather than executing jobs
It increases the total CPU burst requirements
answer: A larger fraction of time is spent switching rather than executing jobs
questions.explanation: Frequent quanta cause more switches. With nonzero cost, switching overhead consumes CPU time that could otherwise perform useful work.

questions.prompt: Which algorithm minimizes average waiting time when all jobs are known and available together and context-switch costs are ignored?
answer: Non-preemptive SJF
questions.explanation: For a known set of jobs available at the same time, ordering by increasing burst minimizes average waiting time by placing short jobs ahead of longer ones.

questions.prompt: A scheduler claims to minimize response time for all workloads. Which issue undermines such a universal claim?
options: Workload arrivals and burst lengths may be unknown and objectives conflict
Response time is independent of scheduling
All algorithms produce the same order
Only disk scheduling affects response time
answer: Workload arrivals and burst lengths may be unknown and objectives conflict
questions.explanation: Scheduling policies trade off response, turnaround, fairness, and overhead; future arrivals and bursts are not generally known exactly.

questions.prompt: P1 arrives at 0 with burst 8. P2 arrives at 3 with burst 2. Under SRTF, when does P2 complete?
questions.explanation: P1 runs from 0 to 3, leaving 5. P2 arrives and preempts; it runs for 2 units and completes at time 5.

questions.prompt: P1 arrives at 0 with burst 8. P2 arrives at 3 with burst 2. Under non-preemptive SJF, when does P2 complete?
questions.explanation: Non-preemptive SJF does not interrupt P1, so P1 completes at 8. P2 then runs for 2 units and completes at 10.

questions.prompt: P1 arrives at 0 with burst 6 and P2 at 2 with burst 1. Under SRTF, what is P1?s completion time?
questions.explanation: P1 runs 0?2, then P2 preempts and completes at 3. P1 resumes with 4 remaining and completes at 7.

questions.prompt: Round Robin has quantum 3 and processes A=5, B=4 arriving at 0 in order A,B. Ignoring switching overhead, when does A complete?
questions.explanation: A runs 0?3 leaving 2; B runs 3?6 leaving 1; A runs 6?8 and completes.

questions.prompt: Round Robin q=2; A burst 3 and B burst 3, both arrive at 0 in order A,B. What is B?s completion time?
questions.explanation: A runs 0?2, B 2?4, A 4?5 and completes, then B runs its last unit from 5?6.

questions.prompt: Three jobs arrive at time 0 with bursts 2, 4, and 6. Under FCFS in that order, what is the average waiting time?
questions.explanation: Waiting times are 0, 2, and 6. Their sum is 8 and the mean is 8/3 time units.

questions.prompt: For bursts 2, 4, and 6 arriving together, SJF runs shortest first. What is average waiting time?
questions.explanation: Waiting times in SJF order are 0, 2, and 6, totaling 8; divided by three gives 8/3.

questions.prompt: A process arrives at time 4 and first receives CPU at time 9. What is its response time?
questions.explanation: Response time is the first CPU start minus arrival: 9 ? 4 = 5.

questions.prompt: A process arrives at time 6 and completes at time 19 after using 8 CPU units. What is its waiting time, assuming no other counted service?
questions.explanation: Turnaround is 19?6=13. Subtract its 8 CPU units to obtain 5 units of waiting.

questions.prompt: A process?s predicted burst is 10. With ?=0.25 and actual burst 6, what is the next exponential average estimate?
A process has CPU bursts 3 and 4 separated by I/O. Which scheduler decision can occur while it waits for the I/O?
options: The blocked process continues using CPU
answer: Another ready process can run
questions.explanation: When a process blocks for I/O, it leaves the ready/running set. The scheduler can dispatch another ready process.

questions.prompt: A non-preemptive scheduler starts a long job just before several short jobs arrive. What limitation does this illustrate?
options: It cannot preempt the running job for later arrivals
answer: It cannot preempt the running job for later arrivals
questions.explanation: Non-preemptive policies do not reconsider the CPU until the current job blocks or completes, so newly arrived short work can wait behind it.

questions.prompt: A scheduler uses preemptive priority and a newly ready process has lower priority than the running process. What happens?
options: The CPU switches to the lower-priority process immediately
answer: The current process continues running
questions.explanation: Under strict priority preemption, a lower-priority arrival does not displace the higher-priority running process.

questions.prompt: A scheduler grants each ready process at most q time units per turn. Which policy is this?
answer: Round Robin
questions.explanation: Round Robin rotates among ready processes, preempting after each quantum if the process has not completed or blocked.

questions.prompt: A job?s turnaround is 14 units and its waiting time is 9. Its CPU burst total is:
questions.explanation: Turnaround equals waiting plus CPU service. CPU burst total is 14 ? 9 = 5.

questions.prompt: Three jobs have equal arrival and burst times, and the scheduler uses FCFS. What determines their order?
answer: Ready-queue insertion or tie-breaking order
questions.explanation: With equal arrival/burst metrics, the scheduler?s FCFS queue order or explicit tie-breaking rule determines execution order.

questions.prompt: A scheduler maximizes CPU utilization. Which interpretation is correct?
options: Keep the CPU busy as much as possible
Guarantee shortest turnaround for each job
answer: Keep the CPU busy as much as possible
questions.explanation: CPU utilization is the fraction of time the CPU is busy. Maximizing it does not necessarily optimize individual latency or fairness.

questions.prompt: A workload has frequent short interactive bursts mixed with long CPU jobs. Which policy often gives good response and fairness tradeoffs?
options: Round Robin with a suitable quantum
answer: Round Robin with a suitable quantum
questions.explanation: Round Robin gives each ready process a turn, improving responsiveness. Quantum choice controls overhead and interaction; it does not ensure optimality.

questions.prompt: A process?s burst estimate is too short, so SJF repeatedly predicts it will finish early. What is a likely consequence?
options: Its actual burst may delay later jobs after it is selected
answer: Its actual burst may delay later jobs after it is selected
questions.explanation: SJF relies on burst estimates. An underestimated long burst can occupy the CPU longer than expected and increase waiting for jobs behind it.

questions.prompt: A scheduler chooses the process with the earliest deadline. Which scheduling criterion is it prioritizing?
answer: Deadline urgency
questions.explanation: Earliest-deadline-first schedules by deadline, a real-time objective distinct from burst length or arrival order.

questions.prompt: Under EDF, two jobs have deadlines 10 and 7 and are both ready. Which is selected?
answer: Deadline 7
questions.explanation: Earliest Deadline First chooses the ready job with the earliest absolute deadline, which is 7.

questions.prompt: A real-time job finishes after its deadline. Which metric has failed?
answer: Deadline satisfaction
questions.explanation: A real-time deadline requirement is violated if completion occurs after the specified deadline, regardless of eventual completion.

questions.prompt: A scheduler uses fixed-priority preemption for periodic real-time tasks. What may happen to a low-priority task under sustained high-priority load?
options: It can starve or miss deadlines
It always completes before high-priority tasks
answer: It can starve or miss deadlines
questions.explanation: Strict priority can indefinitely delay lower-priority tasks if higher-priority work continually occupies the processor.

questions.prompt: A scheduler has response time 2 for one job and 10 for another. What is their average response time?
questions.explanation: The mean is (2+10)/2 = 6 time units, using the standard arithmetic average of the two response times.

questions.prompt: Processes arrive at 0, 2, and 4 with CPU bursts 5, 2, and 1. Under FCFS, what is the completion time of the third process?
questions.explanation: P1 runs 0?5, P2 5?7, then P3 7?8. The third completion time is 8.

questions.prompt: For the same arrivals/bursts (0:5, 2:2, 4:1), under SRTF what is the completion time of the third process?
questions.explanation: P1 runs 0?2 (remaining 3), P2 arrives with burst 2 and runs 2?4, then P3 arrives with burst 1 and runs 4?5, completing at 5.

questions.prompt: A process with burst 2 arrives at time 5 while another process with 2 units remaining is running under SRTF. What decides the next CPU choice?
answer: The scheduler?s tie-breaking rule
questions.explanation: The remaining times tie. SRTF alone does not resolve ties, so the specified queue or scheduler tie-break rule determines the outcome.

questions.prompt: A system measures waiting time in the ready queue only. Does time blocked for I/O count?
options: Only if the process is high priority
answer: No
questions.explanation: Waiting time in CPU scheduling typically counts time in the ready queue, not time blocked waiting for I/O. Definitions should be explicit for a problem.

questions.prompt: A scheduler switches processes at every I/O completion, even if the current process still has CPU burst remaining. What kind of event can cause this?
options: A newly ready process may trigger preemption under the chosen policy
I/O completion always terminates the current process
The running process becomes a zombie
The CPU burst is reset to zero
answer: A newly ready process may trigger preemption under the chosen policy
questions.explanation: I/O completion moves a blocked process to ready. A preemptive policy may then select it if its priority or remaining-time criterion warrants.

questions.prompt: A scheduling algorithm is non-preemptive. Which event can still cause the running process to relinquish the CPU?
answer: It blocks or terminates
questions.explanation: Non-preemptive scheduling does not interrupt a running process due to another arrival; the process relinquishes the CPU when it blocks or completes.

questions.prompt: Two processes arrive at time 0 with bursts 4 and 2 in FCFS order. What is P2?s waiting time?
questions.explanation: P2 waits while P1 executes its four-unit burst, so its waiting time is 4.

questions.prompt: Processes P1=3 and P2=5 arrive at time 0. Under FCFS order P1 then P2, what is the average turnaround time?
questions.explanation: Completion and turnaround times are 3 and 8. Their mean is (3+8)/2=5.5 time units.

questions.prompt: A job arrives at time 7 and completes at time 20. What is its turnaround time?
questions.explanation: Turnaround equals completion minus arrival: 20?7=13.

questions.prompt: A process has turnaround 18 and CPU service 11. How much time did it spend waiting in the ready queue?
questions.explanation: Under the stated accounting, waiting = turnaround ? CPU service = 18?11=7.

questions.prompt: Round Robin quantum is 4. A CPU burst is 17 and there are no competing processes or switch costs. How many CPU turns does the process receive?
questions.explanation: The process consumes four full quanta four times (16 units), then a final 1-unit turn, for five turns.

questions.prompt: A round-robin system has q=5 and a process needs 12 CPU units. How many timer expirations occur before it finishes?
questions.explanation: It uses two complete five-unit quanta; on the third turn it finishes after two units, so there are two expirations before completion.

questions.prompt: A CPU-burst predictor has ?=0.4, previous estimate 5, and actual burst 10. What is the next estimate?
A process starts at time 12 and first runs at time 17. What is its response time?
questions.explanation: Response time is first CPU start minus arrival: 17?12=5.

questions.prompt: A process?s ready-queue waiting time is 14, and its CPU burst is 6. What is its turnaround time, ignoring other states?
questions.explanation: Turnaround is waiting plus CPU execution: 14+6=20.

questions.prompt: Four jobs finish in a 20-second interval. What is throughput in jobs per second?
questions.explanation: Throughput is completions divided by elapsed time: 4/20 = 0.2 jobs per second.

questions.prompt: A CPU is busy for 45 seconds of a 60-second observation period. What is utilization as a percentage?
questions.explanation: Utilization is 45/60 = 0.75, or 75 percent.

questions.prompt: A round-robin process needs 15 units of CPU and q=4. How many units remain after its first two full turns?
questions.explanation: Two full turns provide 8 units of service. Remaining burst is 15?8=7.

questions.prompt: A process?s exponential estimate is 6, actual burst is 10, and ?=0.5. What is the next estimate?
questions.explanation: The next estimate is 0.5?10 + 0.5?6 = 8.

questions.prompt: Two jobs have response times 3 and 9. What is their mean response time?
questions.explanation: The arithmetic mean is (3+9)/2=6 time units.

questions.prompt: An SRTF process has 9 units initially, runs for 4, then is preempted. How many units remain?
questions.explanation: Remaining burst equals initial minus executed: 9?4=5 units.

questions.prompt: Which are standard CPU-scheduling criteria?
answer: CPU utilization
Throughput
Turnaround time
questions.explanation: Utilization, throughput, turnaround, waiting, and response are scheduling criteria. Color depth is unrelated to CPU scheduling.

questions.prompt: Which claims about FCFS are correct?
options: It can cause the convoy effect
It always minimizes average waiting time
answer: It is usually non-preemptive
It can cause the convoy effect
It is simple to implement
questions.explanation: FCFS is simple and typically non-preemptive, but a long job can delay short jobs. SJF, not FCFS, minimizes average waiting for known simultaneous jobs.

questions.prompt: Which statements about SJF are correct?
options: It selects the smallest next CPU burst estimate
It can be preemptive as SRTF
It requires exact knowledge of future bursts in practice
answer: It selects the smallest next CPU burst estimate
It can be non-preemptive
It can be preemptive as SRTF
questions.explanation: SJF uses burst estimates and has preemptive SRTF form. Actual future bursts are generally unknown and must be estimated.

questions.prompt: Which effects can result from choosing a very small Round Robin quantum?
options: Lower response delay for short jobs in some workloads
answer: More context switches
Lower response delay for short jobs in some workloads
Higher scheduling overhead
questions.explanation: Small quanta improve service opportunities but increase preemption and overhead. FCFS is approached with a very large quantum, not a small one.

questions.prompt: Which statements about priority scheduling are correct?
options: Lower numeric values may encode higher priority by convention
Priority ties need a tie-break rule
answer: Aging can reduce starvation
Lower numeric values may encode higher priority by convention
Priority ties need a tie-break rule
questions.explanation: Priority conventions vary and ties need resolution. Aging helps starvation, but strict priority alone does not guarantee fairness.

questions.prompt: Which statements about response and turnaround are correct?
options: Response time ends at first CPU service
Turnaround is always equal to response time
answer: Response time ends at first CPU service
Turnaround ends at process completion
Waiting time excludes CPU service
questions.explanation: Response measures arrival to first service; turnaround measures arrival to completion. Waiting is ready-queue time and is distinct from CPU execution.

questions.prompt: Which events can make a running process relinquish the CPU?
options: Its time quantum expires under RR
A lower-priority process arrives under strict priority scheduling
answer: It blocks for I/O
Its time quantum expires under RR
It terminates
questions.explanation: Blocking, quantum expiration, and termination relinquish the CPU. A lower-priority arrival does not preempt a higher-priority running process under strict priority.

questions.prompt: Which statements about preemptive scheduling are correct?
options: A running process can be interrupted for another ready process
It can improve response for high-priority arrivals
answer: A running process can be interrupted for another ready process
It can improve response for high-priority arrivals
It may incur context-switch overhead
questions.explanation: Preemption improves responsiveness in some cases but adds overhead. It does not eliminate starvation without an appropriate fairness policy.

questions.prompt: Which workloads are likely to benefit from short CPU scheduling quanta?
options: Many short tasks sharing one CPU
Real-time tasks requiring bounded response (with suitable policy)
A single non-preemptible long batch job only
answer: Interactive workloads
Many short tasks sharing one CPU
Real-time tasks requiring bounded response (with suitable policy)
questions.explanation: Short quanta can improve responsiveness and sharing, though real-time guarantees need a suitable policy. A lone batch job gains little and incurs extra switching.

questions.prompt: Which statements about multilevel feedback queues are correct?
options: Observed CPU usage can affect queue placement
Queue membership is always fixed at process creation
answer: Processes can move between queues
Observed CPU usage can affect queue placement
They can favor interactive jobs
questions.explanation: Feedback queues dynamically adjust process priority or queue based on behavior. Fixed membership characterizes a basic multilevel queue.

questions.prompt: Which statements about exponential burst prediction are correct?
options: Larger ? gives more weight to recent actual burst
?=1 uses only the latest actual burst
answer: Larger ? gives more weight to recent actual burst
?=0 keeps the previous estimate unchanged
?=1 uses only the latest actual burst
questions.explanation: The recurrence weights recent actual burst by ? and old estimate by 1??. It predicts CPU burst length, not arrival time.

questions.prompt: Which are concerns with SJF/SRTF?
options: Long jobs may starve under a stream of short jobs
SRTF can preempt a running job
They require no scheduler decisions after dispatch
answer: Burst lengths must be estimated
Long jobs may starve under a stream of short jobs
SRTF can preempt a running job
questions.explanation: Shortest-job policies rely on estimates and can starve long work if short jobs continually arrive. SRTF reevaluates and can preempt.

questions.prompt: Which statements about work-conserving scheduling are correct?
options: The CPU is not idle if a ready job exists
It does not by itself imply fairness
It does not guarantee minimum average turnaround
It guarantees every ready process runs immediately
answer: The CPU is not idle if a ready job exists
It does not by itself imply fairness
It does not guarantee minimum average turnaround
questions.explanation: Work-conserving means no idle CPU when work is ready. Fairness, optimal turnaround, and immediate service do not follow.

questions.prompt: Which scheduler properties are required for a real-time deadline guarantee?
options: A policy that accounts for deadlines or task timing
answer: A policy that accounts for deadlines or task timing
Feasibility analysis under execution demands
Bounded relevant scheduling overhead
questions.explanation: Meeting deadlines requires timing-aware policy, schedulability analysis, and bounded overhead. High average throughput alone cannot ensure each deadline.

questions.prompt: Which statements distinguish multilevel queue from multilevel feedback queue?
options: Basic multilevel queues use fixed class assignment
Feedback queues allow movement between queues
Feedback may use CPU behavior to adjust priority
Both necessarily use Round Robin in every queue
answer: Basic multilevel queues use fixed class assignment
Feedback queues allow movement between queues
Feedback may use CPU behavior to adjust priority
questions.explanation: The key difference is dynamic movement in feedback queues versus fixed classification in basic multilevel queues. Per-queue algorithms can vary.

questions.prompt: Four processes arrive together with bursts 1, 2, 3, and 4. Under non-preemptive SJF, what is the average waiting time?
questions.explanation: SJF order is 1, 2, 3, 4. Waiting times are 0, 1, 3, and 6, giving mean 10/4 = 2.5.

questions.prompt: Two processes arrive together with bursts 3 and 7 in that order. Under FCFS, what is the average waiting time?
questions.explanation: The first waits 0 and the second waits 3, so the mean is (0+3)/2=1.5.

questions.prompt: P1 arrives at time 0 with burst 6. P2 arrives at time 4 with burst 1. Under SRTF, when does P2 finish?
questions.explanation: P1 has 2 units remaining when P2 arrives at time 4. P2?s 1-unit burst is shorter, so it runs and completes at time 5.

questions.prompt: A CPU scheduler completes 9 jobs in 3 seconds. What is throughput in jobs per second?
questions.explanation: Throughput is completed jobs divided by elapsed time: 9/3 = 3 jobs per second.

questions.prompt: A process arrives at 2 and first runs at 6. It completes at 15. What is its turnaround time?
questions.explanation: Turnaround is completion minus arrival: 15?2=13. The first-start time is relevant to response time, not turnaround.

questions.prompt: Four processes arrive together with bursts 1,2,3,4. Under SJF, what is the average waiting time?
questions.explanation: Waiting times are 0,1,3,6. The average is 10/4=2.5.

questions.prompt: A scheduler completes 15 jobs in 5 seconds. What is throughput in jobs per second?
questions.explanation: Throughput equals 15/5 = 3 completed jobs per second.

questions.prompt: Round Robin quantum is 3 and a job needs 11 CPU units. How many full quanta does it consume before its final partial turn?
questions.explanation: It consumes three full quanta for 9 units, then needs a final 2-unit turn.

questions.prompt: An I/O device completes 15 requests during a 5-second interval. What is its request throughput per second?
questions.explanation: Throughput is completed requests divided by elapsed time: 15/5 = 3 requests per second.

questions.prompt: A CPU is busy for 54 seconds in a 90-second interval. What is utilization percentage?
questions.explanation: Utilization is 54/90=0.6, or 60 percent.

questions.prompt: A system has one instance of each resource type. Its resource-allocation graph contains a directed cycle. What follows?
options: Deadlock is possible but not implied
answer: The system is deadlocked
questions.explanation: With single-instance resource types, a directed cycle is sufficient for deadlock: each process waits for a resource held by the next process in the cycle.

questions.prompt: A resource-allocation graph has a cycle, but some resource types have multiple instances. What is the strongest conclusion?
options: Deadlock may exist, but the cycle alone is not conclusive
answer: Deadlock may exist, but the cycle alone is not conclusive
questions.explanation: Multiple instances may allow an additional available unit to satisfy a request and break the cycle, so a cycle is necessary but not sufficient.

questions.prompt: In a wait-for graph, an edge Pi ? Pj means:
options: Pi is waiting for a resource held by Pj
Pj is waiting for Pi to terminate
Pi has allocated a resource to Pj
Pi and Pj share a CPU
answer: Pi is waiting for a resource held by Pj
questions.explanation: A wait-for edge represents a process blocked for a resource currently held by another process. A cycle can identify deadlock under single-instance assumptions.

questions.prompt: Three single-instance resources are held in a cycle P0?P1?P2?P0. Which processes are deadlocked?
options: No process because cycle length is odd
answer: P0, P1, and P2
questions.explanation: Each process in the cycle waits on the next for a resource held within the same cycle. With single instances, all three are deadlocked.

questions.prompt: A process requests resources only when it can obtain its entire maximum claim at once. Which deadlock condition is removed?
answer: Hold and wait
questions.explanation: Granting a process its entire resource requirement before it begins prevents it from holding some resources while waiting for additional ones.

questions.prompt: A system requires resources to be acquired in an increasing global order. Which condition is prevented?
answer: Circular wait
questions.explanation: Strictly increasing acquisition order makes it impossible to follow a cycle of decreasing dependencies back to the start, preventing circular wait.

questions.prompt: A system can forcibly reclaim a resource from a process when its request cannot be met. Which condition is relaxed?
answer: No preemption
questions.explanation: Permitting preemption means an allocated resource can be taken away under defined conditions. This removes the no-preemption condition.

questions.prompt: A request is denied even though resources are free because granting it would leave no safe sequence. This is:
answer: deadlock avoidance
questions.explanation: Avoidance evaluates whether a tentative allocation preserves a safe sequence and may defer a feasible request if it would produce an unsafe state.

questions.prompt: A state is unsafe. Which statement is correct?
options: Deadlock is not guaranteed, but safe completion cannot be guaranteed
The system has no allocated resources
answer: Deadlock is not guaranteed, but safe completion cannot be guaranteed
questions.explanation: Unsafe means there is no guaranteed safe sequence under the model. Some executions may still finish, so it does not prove present deadlock.

questions.prompt: In Banker?s algorithm, a process has Max=(7,4), Allocation=(2,1). What is Need?
questions.explanation: Need is the maximum additional demand: Max ? Allocation = (7?2, 4?1) = (5,3).

questions.prompt: Available=(2,3). P0 Need=(1,2), P1 Need=(3,1). Which process can finish first in the safety test?
answer: P0 only
questions.explanation: P0?s need fits componentwise within Available. P1 needs three units of the first resource while only two are free.

questions.prompt: Available=(1,2), P0 Need=(1,1) with Allocation=(2,0), and P1 Need=(2,1). Is P0?P1 a safe sequence?
options: No, P1 needs to finish first
answer: Yes
questions.explanation: P0 can finish using (1,1) and releases (2,0), yielding Available=(3,2), which covers P1?s Need=(2,1).

questions.prompt: Available=(1,0). P0 Need=(2,0), P1 Need=(1,0), and P2 Need=(0,1). Which process can finish first?
answer: P1 only
questions.explanation: P1?s need fits the available vector. P0 lacks one unit of the first resource, and P2 lacks the second resource entirely.

questions.prompt: A process requests (1,0) resources. Available=(2,1), Need=(1,1). What checks does Banker?s request algorithm perform before tentative allocation?
options: Only whether the process has the smallest PID
Only whether Max is less than Allocation
answer: Request ? Need and Request ? Available
questions.explanation: A request exceeding declared remaining need is invalid; one exceeding current availability must wait. If both checks pass, the state is tentatively updated and tested for safety.

questions.prompt: A Banker?s request passes Request?Need and Request?Available but makes the state unsafe. What should the algorithm do?
options: Restore the old state and make the process wait
answer: Restore the old state and make the process wait
questions.explanation: The algorithm tentatively grants the request only for the safety test. If no safe sequence exists, it rolls back the tentative allocation and delays the request.

questions.prompt: A system uses deadlock detection rather than avoidance. Which policy is characteristic?
options: It may grant requests and periodically search for deadlock
It refuses every request that could be unsafe
It requires processes to declare maximum claims
It prevents circular wait by resource ordering
answer: It may grant requests and periodically search for deadlock
questions.explanation: Detection permits allocations without ensuring a safe state, then searches for deadlock and invokes recovery if needed.

questions.prompt: A detection algorithm identifies P0 and P1 deadlocked. Which action is a recovery strategy?
options: Terminate one process to release its resources
answer: Terminate one process to release its resources
questions.explanation: Terminating a victim process releases its held resources and can break the deadlock. Priority changes alone do not release resources.

questions.prompt: A recovery algorithm rolls a process back to a checkpoint from before it acquired a resource. What is the purpose?
options: Release resources and allow other processes to make progress
Make the process hold more resources
Prevent all future deadlocks by definition
answer: Release resources and allow other processes to make progress
questions.explanation: Rolling back can undo the resource-holding state and free allocations so other processes can continue. It does not necessarily prevent future deadlocks.

questions.prompt: A recovery method repeatedly chooses the same low-priority process as victim. What risk arises?
options: The resource graph loses all edges
answer: That process may starve
questions.explanation: Repeated victimization can prevent one process from completing, which is starvation. Recovery policies should account for past victim choices.

questions.prompt: A system has a deadlocked set of processes but also unrelated runnable processes. What is possible?
options: Some processes continue executing while the deadlocked set remains stuck
The entire CPU must be idle
answer: Some processes continue executing while the deadlocked set remains stuck
questions.explanation: Deadlock affects the processes in the cycle; unrelated processes can continue to execute and make progress.

questions.prompt: A process holds a printer and waits for a scanner, while another holds the scanner and waits for the printer. Both resources have one instance. What is the state?
options: No deadlock because devices are different types
answer: Deadlock
questions.explanation: Each process waits for the single resource held by the other, creating a cycle with no available instance. This is deadlock.

questions.prompt: A process holds a resource and requests another, but the requested resource is free. Is it deadlocked?
options: No; the request can be granted, subject to policy
Yes, because it holds and waits
Yes, because two resources are involved
answer: No; the request can be granted, subject to policy
questions.explanation: A free requested resource can be granted, so the process is not blocked on that request. Hold-and-wait alone is not sufficient for deadlock.

questions.prompt: Which distinction between deadlock and starvation is correct?
options: Deadlock involves a circular wait set; starvation can affect one process while others progress
Starvation always includes a resource cycle
Deadlock means a process waits too long for CPU only
